[Power of the F test increases with \gamma] For fixed r,s\ge1 and c>0,  eta(\gamma)=\Pr\{F(r,s,\gamma)>c\} is continuous and strictly increasing in \gamma\ge0, and  eta(\gamma)	o1 as \gamma	o\infty. In particular, the level-\alpha test that rejects when F>F_\alpha(r,s) has power greater than \alpha at every \gamma>0. With U,V as in @def-qf-noncentral-f, F>c iff U>crV/s. Condition on V, which is independent of U:  eta(\gamma)=\E igl[\psi_\gamma(crV/s) igr],\qquad \psi_\gamma(x)=\Pr\{\chi^2(r,\gamma)>x\}. Since V>0 with probability one, @prp-qf-ncchisq-monotone gives, for \gamma<\gamma', \psi_\gamma(crV/s)<\psi_{\gamma'}(crV/s) almost surely, so  eta(\gamma)< eta(\gamma'). Continuity and the limit follow from the same proposition by dominated convergence, since 0\le\psi_\gamma\le1. Two further monotonicity facts hold for fixed \gamma>0 and fixed level. The power decreases as the numerator degrees of freedom r grow, and increases as the denominator degrees of freedom s grow (Ghosh 1973). The first says that spreading a fixed amount of signal over more dimensions makes it harder to detect. The second says that estimating \sigma^2 better helps. We use both only qualitatively, and Figure 4.4.1 in Section 4.4 shows the first. Because T^2\sim F(1,s,\delta^2), @thm-qf-f-power also shows that the power of the two-sided t test increases with \lvert\deltavert (@exr-qf-t-square). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Show that \chi^2(2) is the exponential distribution with mean 2. Use @thm-qf-ncchisq(d) to show that \Pr\{\chi^2(2,\gamma)>x\}=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\gamma/2} rac{(\gamma/2)^k}{k!}\;e^{-x/2}\sum_{j=0}^k rac{(x/2)^j}{j!} . [A2] Show that T\sim t(s,\delta) implies T^2\sim F(1,s,\delta^2). Deduce that the power of the two-sided level-\alpha t test depends on \delta only through \lvert\deltavert and increases with it. Show directly, by conditioning on the denominator, that the power of the one-sided test that rejects for T>c increases with \delta. T^2=X^2/(V/s) with X^2\sim\chi^2(1,\delta^2) independent of V, which is @def-qf-noncentral-f. The two-sided test rejects when \lvert Tvert>t_{\alpha/2}(s), that is, when T^2>F_\alpha(1,s). Its power is therefore \Pr\{F(1,s,\delta^2)>F_\alpha(1,s)\}, a strictly increasing function of \delta^2 by @thm-qf-f-power. For the one-sided test, \Pr(T>c)=\E\,\Pr\{X>c\sqrt{V/s}\mid V\} =\E\,\Phi(\delta-c\sqrt{V/s}), and \Phi is strictly increasing. B. Practice [B1] Show that the kth cumulant of \chi^2(r,\gamma) is 2^{k-1}(k-1)!\,(r+k\gamma). Deduce that its skewness tends to zero like 3/\sqrt{\gamma} as \gamma	o\infty with r fixed. Using -	frac12\log(1-2t)=\sum_{k\ge1}(2t)^k/(2k) and t/(1-2t)=\sum_{k\ge1}2^{k-1}t^k, the cumulant generating function is K(t)=\sum_{k\ge1}t^k\,2^{k-1}\Bigl( rac rk+\gamma\Bigr)=\sum_{k\ge1} rac{t^k}{k!}\,2^{k-1}(k-1)!\,(r+k\gamma). The kth cumulant is k! times the coefficient of t^k. In particular \kappa_2=2(r+2\gamma) and \kappa_3=8(r+3\gamma), so the skewness is \kappa_3/\kappa_2^{3/2}=8(r+3\gamma)/\{2(r+2\gamma)\}^{3/2}. As \gamma	o\infty this behaves like 24\gamma/(4\gamma)^{3/2}=3/\sqrt\gamma. [B2] Show that \chi^2(1,\gamma) has density (2\pi x)^{-1/2}e^{-(x+\gamma)/2}\cosh\sqrt{\gamma x} for x>0. Verify that expanding \cosh in a power series reproduces @eq-qf-ncchisq-density. Hint: \Gamma(k+	frac12)=\sqrt\pi\,(2k)!/(4^kk!). Let X=(W+\sqrt\gamma)^2 with W\sim\Normal(0,1). For x>0, X\le x iff -\sqrt x-\sqrt\gamma\le W\le\sqrt x-\sqrt\gamma. Differentiating with \phi the standard normal density, f(x)= rac{\phi(\sqrt x-\sqrt\gamma)+\phi(\sqrt x+\sqrt\gamma)}{2\sqrt x} = rac{e^{-(x+\gamma)/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\cdot rac{e^{\sqrt{\gamma x}}+e^{-\sqrt{\gamma x}}}{2}. Expanding, f(x)=(2\pi x)^{-1/2}e^{-(x+\gamma)/2}\sum_k(\gamma x)^k/(2k)!. The kth term of @eq-qf-ncchisq-density is  rac{e^{-\gamma/2}(\gamma/2)^k\,x^{k-1/2}e^{-x/2}}{k!\,2^{k+1/2}\,\Gamma(k+ rac12)} . By the hint the denominator is k!\,2^{k+1/2}\sqrt\pi\,(2k)!/(4^kk!)=\sqrt{2\pi}\,2^{-k}(2k)!, and the kth term becomes (2\pi x)^{-1/2}e^{-(x+\gamma)/2}(\gamma x)^k/(2k)!, as required. [B3] Let U_\gamma\sim\chi^2(r,\gamma) with r fixed. Show that (U_\gamma-r-\gamma)/\sqrt{2r+4\gamma} converges in distribution to \Normal(0,1) as \gamma	o\infty. Hint: U_\gamma has the law of (W_1+\sqrt\gamma)^2+W_2^2+\dots+W_r^2 with W_1,\dots,W_r independent standard normal. [B4] Let U\sim\chi^2(a) and V\sim\chi^2(b) be independent. Show that B=U/(U+V) has the \mathrm{Beta}(a/2,b/2) distribution and is independent of U+V, and that F=(U/a)/(V/b)=(b/a)\,B/(1-B). Deduce the null distribution of R^2 asked for in Chapter 6. The joint density of (U,V) is proportional to u^{a/2-1}v^{b/2-1}e^{-(u+v)/2}. Change variables to w=u/(u+v)\in(0,1) and s=u+v>0, so that u=ws, v=(1-w)s and the Jacobian is s. The density of (W,S) is proportional to w^{a/2-1}(1-w)^{b/2-1}\cdot s^{(a+b)/2-1}e^{-s/2}, a product of a function of w and a function of s. So B and U+V are independent, B\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a/2,b/2) and U+V\sim\chi^2(a+b). Also U/V=B/(1-B). For R^2 in a model with intercept, R^2=	ext{SSR}/(	ext{SSR}+	ext{SSE}), where 	ext{SSR}=
orm{(\M- P_1)\Y}^2 and 	ext{SSE}=
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2 come from orthogonal projections of ranks r-1 and n-r. If  mu=\mu one, both noncentralities vanish, and @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections with a=r-1, b=n-r gives R^2\sim\mathrm{Beta} igl((r-1)/2,(n-r)/2 igr). [B5] Show that f_{r,\gamma}(x)/g_r(x) is strictly increasing in x>0 for every \gamma>0. Conclude that among tests based on one observation U\sim\chi^2(r,\gamma) of \gamma=0 against a fixed \gamma>0, rejecting for large U is most powerful. C. Going deeper [C1] Let W_1,W_2 be independent \Normal(0,1) and U=W_1^2+\sigma^2W_2^2 with \sigma^2>0. A weighted sum of squares like this is what a general quadratic form in a normal vector turns out to be (Section 4.2), so it is worth knowing that it is almost never noncentral chi-squared. 1. Show that matching the mean and variance of U to those of \chi^2(r,\gamma) forces \gamma=\sigma^4-\sigma^2 and r=1+2\sigma^2-\sigma^4. Deduce that no \chi^2(r,\gamma) has the first two moments of U when \sigma^2<1. 2. Show more: if cU\sim\chi^2(r,\gamma) for some c>0, r\ge1 and \gamma\ge0, then c=\sigma^2=1. Hint: by @exr-qf-cumulants the kth cumulant of \chi^2(r,\gamma) is 2^{k-1}(k-1)!\,(r+k\gamma), and that of cU is 2^{k-1}(k-1)!\,(c^k+(c\sigma^2)^k). Use k=1,2,3. 3. Check that \sigma^2=1 does give a member of the family, and say which one. (a) By @thm-qf-ncchisq(b), matching gives r+\gamma=\E U=1+\sigma^2 and 2r+4\gamma=\Var U=2(1+\sigma^4), since \Var(W_1^2)=2 and \Var(\sigma^2W_2^2)=2\sigma^4. The second equation is r+2\gamma=1+\sigma^4; subtracting the first gives \gamma=\sigma^4-\sigma^2=\sigma^2(\sigma^2-1) and then r=1+2\sigma^2-\sigma^4. A noncentrality must be nonnegative, so \sigma^2<1 is impossible. (b) Write e=c and d=c\sigma^2, both positive. The cumulants of cU are 2^{k-1}(k-1)!(e^k+d^k), because cumulants of a sum of independent variables add and those of aW^2 are a^k times those of \chi^2(1). Equating with 2^{k-1}(k-1)!(r+k\gamma) for k=1,2,3 gives e+d=r+\gamma,\qquad e^2+d^2=r+2\gamma,\qquad e^3+d^3=r+3\gamma . Each consecutive difference equals \gamma, so e^2-e+d^2-d=e^3-e^2+d^3-d^2, that is e(e-1)^2+d(d-1)^2=0. Both terms are nonnegative, so e=d=1, which is c=1 and \sigma^2=1. (c) With \sigma^2=1, U=W_1^2+W_2^2\sim\chi^2(2), and the three equations are indeed satisfied by c=1, r=2, \gamma=0. The conclusion is that the noncentral chi-squared family is not closed under weighting: only equal weights give a member of it, which is why Section 4.3 will ask for an idempotent matrix. [C2] @prp-qf-ncchisq-monotone says the power of a chi-squared test increases with \gamma. How fast? 1. For z>0, show that \Pr\{\chi^2(1,\gamma)>z^2\}=\Phi(-z+\sqrt\gamma)+\Phi(-z-\sqrt\gamma), where \Phi is the standard normal distribution function. This is the power of the two-sided test based on a single \Normal(\sqrt{\gamma},1) observation. 2. Show that the right side equals \alpha+z\varphi(z)\,\gamma+o(\gamma) as \gamma\downarrow0, where \alpha=2\Phi(-z) and \varphi is the standard normal density. The power rises linearly in \gamma, with no first-order term in \sqrt\gamma. 3. For general r, show from the Poisson mixture in the proof of @prp-qf-ncchisq-monotone that  rac{d}{d\gamma}\Pr\{\chi^2(r,\gamma)>x\}\Big|_{\gamma=0} =	frac12 igl[\Pr\{\chi^2(r+2)>x\}-\Pr\{\chi^2(r)>x\} igr]. Check that this agrees with (b) when r=1 and x=z^2, given that \Pr\{\chi^2(3)>x\}=\Pr\{\chi^2(1)>x\}+2\sqrt x\,\varphi(\sqrt x). (a) By @def-qf-noncentral-chisq, X^2\sim\chi^2(1,\gamma) when X\sim\Normal(\sqrt\gamma,1). Then \Pr(X^2>z^2)=\Pr(X>z)+\Pr(X<-z), and \Pr(X>z)=1-\Phi(z-\sqrt\gamma)=\Phi(-z+\sqrt\gamma), \Pr(X<-z)=\Phi(-z-\sqrt\gamma). (b) Put \delta=\sqrt\gamma and  eta(\delta)=\Phi(-z+\delta)+\Phi(-z-\delta). Then  eta(0)=2\Phi(-z)=\alpha,  eta'(\delta)=\varphi(-z+\delta)-\varphi(-z-\delta), which vanishes at \delta=0, and  eta''(\delta)=\varphi'(-z+\delta)+\varphi'(-z-\delta). Since \varphi'(u)=-u\varphi(u),  eta''(0)=2z\varphi(z). Taylor’s theorem gives  eta(\delta)=\alpha+z\varphi(z)\delta^2+o(\delta^2), which is the claim because \delta^2=\gamma. The even symmetry in \delta is what kills the \sqrt\gamma term: a two-sided test cannot tell the sign of the shift. (c) In the notation of that proof, with its \phi written \Psi here to keep \varphi for the normal density, the tail probability is \Psi(\lambda)=\sum_kp_k(\lambda)h(k) with \lambda=\gamma/2 and h(k)=\Pr\{\chi^2(r+2k)>x\}, and \Psi'(\lambda)=\sum_kp_k(\lambda)\{h(k+1)-h(k)\}. At \lambda=0 only p_0=1 survives, so \Psi'(0)=h(1)-h(0), and d\gamma=2\,d\lambda gives the stated derivative. For r=1 and x=z^2 the bracket is 2\sqrt x\varphi(\sqrt x)=2z\varphi(z), and half of it is z\varphi(z), matching (b). The same calculation for a general r shows how much a design must raise \gamma to buy a given amount of power near the null.

title: 4.2 Mean and variance of quadratic forms
content:
Mean and variance of quadratic forms The mean needs no normality @thm-rv-quadform-mean computed \E(\Y\T\A\Y) for any random vector with mean  mu and covariance  Sigma: \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=	r(\A Sigma)+ mu\T\A mu . {#eq-qf-mean} The formula has two parts with distinct roles. The trace term is what the noise contributes. The term  mu\T\A mu is what the signal contributes. For nonnegative definite \A it vanishes exactly when \A mu= zero, which describes the mean vectors a well-designed estimator is meant to ignore. [Two estimators of \sigma^2 under a drifting mean] Let Y_1,\dots,Y_n be uncorrelated with common variance \sigma^2, and consider S^2= rac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i- ar{Y})^2,\qquad Q= rac{1}{2(n-1)}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(Y_{i+1}-Y_i)^2 , the sample variance and the mean square successive difference. In matrix form S^2=\Y\T\mathbf{C}\Y/(n-1) with \mathbf{C}=\I-n^{-1} one one\T, and Q=\Y\T D\T D\Y/\{2(n-1)\}, where  D is the (n-1)	imes n first-difference matrix with rows (\dots,-1,1,\dots). Both matrices annihilate  one, so both estimators ignore a constant mean. Since 	r(\mathbf{C})=n-1 and 	r( D\T D)=	r( D D\T)=2(n-1), @eq-qf-mean with  Sigma=\sigma^2\I shows that both are unbiased when the mean is constant. Now let the mean drift linearly, \mu_i=\mu_0+	heta i. Then \mathbf{C} mu is the centred trend and  D mu=	heta one_{n-1}, so \E(S^2)=\sigma^2+	heta^2 rac{n(n+1)}{12},\qquad \E(Q)=\sigma^2+ rac{	heta^2}{2}. The bias of S^2 grows quadratically with the length of the series, while that of Q does not grow at all. With n=20, \sigma=1 and 	heta=0.1, the means are 1.350 and 1.005. Differencing removes smooth trends, and this is why Q was proposed for series whose level may wander (von Neumann 1941). The price of robustness to drift is paid in variance, which we compute below. A canonical representation Higher moments and distributions need normality, and one representation answers all such questions at once. [Canonical form of a normal quadratic form] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma) and let \A be symmetric. Write  Sigma= L L\T with  L of size n	imes k, and take a spectral decomposition  L\T\A L=\Q Lambda\Q\T with  Lambda=\diag(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k). Put  b=\Q\T L\T\A mu. Then \Y\T\A\Y\;\overset{d}{=}\; mu\T\A mu+\sum_{j=1}^k igl(\lambda_jW_j^2+2b_jW_j igr), \qquad \W\sim\Normal_k( zero,\I_k). {#eq-qf-canonical} For \lambda_j
e0 the jth term equals \lambda_j(W_j+b_j/\lambda_j)^2-b_j^2/\lambda_j. The nonzero \lambda_j are the nonzero eigenvalues of \A Sigma. Such an  L exists. By @thm-mat-spectral,  Sigma= U D U\T with  U orthogonal and  D diagonal with entries d_i\ge0, and  L= U D^{1/2} works with k=n. Let \Z\sim\Normal_k( zero,\I). The vector  mu+ L\Z is normal with mean  mu and covariance  L L\T= Sigma (@thm-mvn-linear). A normal distribution is determined by its mean and covariance (@thm-mvn-mgf), so \Y and  mu+ L\Z have the same law, and so do \Y\T\A\Y and ( mu+ L\Z)\T\A( mu+ L\Z)= mu\T\A mu+2 mu\T\A L\Z+\Z\T L\T\A L\Z . Put \W=\Q\T\Z, again \Normal_k( zero,\I). Then \Z\T L\T\A L\Z=\W\T Lambda\W=\sum\lambda_jW_j^2 and  mu\T\A L\Z= b\T\W, which is @eq-qf-canonical. The completed square is algebra. Finally,  L\T\A L= H\mathbf{F} with \mathbf{F}=\A L and  H= L\T, and \mathbf{F} H=\A Sigma. By @prp-mat-eigen-basic(d) these two products have the same nonzero eigenvalues, with the same multiplicities. So a normal quadratic form is a constant plus a sum of independent pieces. Each piece is either a scaled noncentral \chi^2(1) variable, with scale \lambda_j, or a normal variable with mean zero, when \lambda_j=0 but b_j
e0. Because the \lambda_j may be negative, \Y\T\A\Y need not be positive. The linear pieces are special to singular covariances. If  Sigma is positive definite,  L can be taken square and nonsingular, and then \lambda_j=0 gives \A L\mathbf{q}_j= zero for the jth column \mathbf{q}_j of \Q, so b_j=(\A L\mathbf{q}_j)\T mu=0. A linear piece needs a direction in which \A responds to the mean while the noise is absent. [Moment generating function] In the setting of @thm-qf-canonical, for \lvert tvert<1/(2\max_j\lvert\lambda_jvert) (any t if all \lambda_j=0), \E\,e^{t\Y\T\A\Y}=e^{t mu\T\A mu}\prod_{j=1}^k(1-2\lambda_jt)^{-1/2} \exp\Bigl( rac{2b_j^2t^2}{1-2\lambda_jt}\Bigr). The terms of @eq-qf-canonical are independent. If \lambda_j=0, the term 2b_jW_j has mgf e^{2b_j^2t^2}. If \lambda_j
e0, apply @lem-qf-shifted-square to W_j+
u_j with 
u_j=b_j/\lambda_j at the argument \lambda_jt, and multiply by e^{-tb_j^2/\lambda_j}. The exponent is b_j^2t/\{\lambda_j(1-2\lambda_jt)\}-b_j^2t/\lambda_j=2b_j^2t^2/(1-2\lambda_jt). Variance and covariances [Moments of normal quadratic forms] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma), let \A and \B be symmetric n	imes n matrices, and let \mathbf{K} be an m	imes n matrix. Then 1. \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=	r(\A Sigma)+ mu\T\A mu; 2. \Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=2	r\{(\A Sigma)^2\}+4 mu\T\A Sigma\A mu; 3. \Cov(\mathbf{K}\Y,\Y\T\A\Y)=2\mathbf{K} Sigma\A mu; 4. \Cov(\Y\T\A\Y,\Y\T\B\Y)=2	r(\A Sigma\B Sigma)+4 mu\T\A Sigma\B mu. (a) is @eq-qf-mean. For (b), use @eq-qf-canonical. Independent terms have additive variances, and for W\sim\Normal(0,1), \Var(\lambda W^2+2bW)=2\lambda^2+4b^2, because \Cov(W^2,W)=\E W^3=0. Hence \Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=2\sum_j\lambda_j^2+4
orm{ b}^2 =2	r\{( L\T\A L)^2\}+4 mu\T\A L\Q\Q\T L\T\A mu . Now 	r\{( L\T\A L)^2\}=	r( L\T\A Sigma\A L)=	r(\A Sigma\A Sigma) by @thm-mat-trace-cyclic, and \Q\Q\T=\I, so the second term is 4 mu\T\A Sigma\A mu. For (c), write \Y= mu+ L\Z as in the proof of @thm-qf-canonical. Then \Y\T\A\Y-\E(\Y\T\A\Y)=\Z\T L\T\A L\Z-	r(\A Sigma)+2 mu\T\A L\Z and \mathbf{K}\Y-\E(\mathbf{K}\Y)=\mathbf{K} L\Z. Every entry of \E[\Z(\Z\T\mathbf{G}\Z)] is a sum of third moments of a \Normal_k( zero,\I) vector, which vanish. So only the linear term contributes, and \E[\mathbf{K} L\Z\cdot2\Z\T L\T\A mu]=2\mathbf{K} L L\T\A mu. For (d), apply (b) to \A, \B and \A+\B, and use \Var(X+Y)=\Var X+\Var Y+2\Cov(X,Y). For  mu= zero, part (b) can also be read off the fourth moments of a normal vector (@exr-mvn-fourth-moments). The variance has the same two-part structure as the mean: a pure-noise term, plus a term that is present only when \A responds to the mean. Part (c) shows that a quadratic form and a linear form are uncorrelated when \mathbf{K} Sigma\A=\mathbf{0}. Under normality this will turn out to give independence (@thm-qf-indep-linear). [@exm-qf-drift, continued] With  Sigma=\sigma^2\I and a constant mean, @thm-qf-mean-var(b) gives \Var(S^2)=2\sigma^4	r(\mathbf{C}^2)/(n-1)^2=2\sigma^4/(n-1). For Q, the matrix  D D\T is tridiagonal with 2 on the diagonal and -1 beside it, so 	r\{( D\T D)^2\}=	r\{( D D\T)^2\}=4(n-1)+2(n-2)=6n-8 and \Var(Q)= rac{2\sigma^4(6n-8)}{4(n-1)^2}= rac{\sigma^4(3n-4)}{(n-1)^2}. The ratio \Var(Q)/\Var(S^2)=(3n-4)/\{2(n-1)\} tends to 3/2. With n=20 the two variances are 0.1551 and 0.1053, a ratio of 1.474. So with no drift, Q needs about half as many observations again to match S^2. Under the drift 	heta=0.1, the signal term 4 mu\T\A Sigma\A mu raises the variances to 0.1552 and 0.1789. Combining variance and bias, the root mean squared errors are 0.394 for Q and 0.549 for S^2. The listing evaluates the formulas, and the script confirms all eight moments with 400{,}000 simulated series. import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(4402) n, sigma, theta = 20, 1.0, 0.1 t = np.arange(1, n + 1) mu = 5.0 + theta * t # mean with a linear trend Sigma = sigma**2 * np.eye(n) def qf_moments(A, mu, Sigma): """Mean and variance of Y^T A Y for Y ~ N(mu, Sigma), A symmetric.""" AS = A @ Sigma mean = np.trace(AS) + mu @ A @ mu var = 2 * np.trace(AS @ AS) + 4 * mu @ AS @ A @ mu return mean, var C = np.eye(n) - np.ones((n, n)) / n # centring matrix D = np.diff(np.eye(n), axis=0) # (n-1) x n first differences A_s2 = C / (n - 1) A_q = D.T @ D / (2 * (n - 1)) for name, A in [("S2", A_s2), ("Q", A_q)]: print(name, qf_moments(A, mu, Sigma), qf_moments(A, 0 * mu, Sigma)) Normality enters (b)–(d) through the third and fourth moments of \Y. For independent coordinates with excess kurtosis the variance acquires an extra term that involves only the diagonal of \A (@thm-rv-quadform-variance). Variance formulas for sums of squares derived under normality can be badly wrong for heavy-tailed errors, a point taken up in Chapter 19 (@prp-dep-sigma-interval, @prp-dep-balance). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_2( zero,\I) and \A= egin{psmallmatrix}0&1\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}. Compute \Var(\Y\T\A\Y) directly, and compare with 2	r(\A^2) and with 2	r(\A_s^2), where \A_s=	frac12(\A+\A\T). B. Practice [B1] Let (U_i,W_i), i=1,\dots,n, be independent copies of a bivariate normal pair with variances \sigma_U^2, \sigma_W^2 and covariance \sigma_{UW}, and let s_{UW}=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_i(U_i- ar{U})(W_i- ar{W}). Write s_{UW}=\Y\T\A\Y for the stacked vector \Y=(\mathbf{U}\T,\mathbf{W}\T)\T and a symmetric 2n	imes2n matrix \A, and use @thm-qf-mean-var to show that \Var(s_{UW})=(\sigma_U^2\sigma_W^2+\sigma_{UW}^2)/(n-1). Check the answer against \Var(S^2) when \mathbf{U}=\mathbf{W}. [B2] Let Y_1,\dots,Y_n be independent with mean 0, variance \sigma^2 and \E Y_i^4=\mu_4. By @exr-rv-cov-quadforms, for symmetric \A and \B, \Cov(\Y\T\A\Y,\Y\T\B\Y)=(\mu_4-3\sigma^4)\sum_ia_{ii}b_{ii}+2\sigma^4	r(\A\B). Show that in a one-way layout with g\ge2 groups, not all of size one, the between-group and within-group sums of squares are correlated unless \mu_4=3\sigma^4. Which sign does the correlation have for heavy-tailed errors? In the one-way layout the between-group matrix is \A=\M- P_1 and the within-group matrix is \B=\I-\M. They satisfy \A\B=\mathbf{0}, so 	r(\A\B)=0 and the covariance reduces to (\mu_4-3\sigma^4)\sum_ia_{ii}b_{ii}. An observation in group \ell has a_{ii}=1/n_\ell-1/n and b_{ii}=1-1/n_\ell, so \sum_ia_{ii}b_{ii}=\sum_\ell n_\ell\Bigl( rac1{n_\ell}- rac1n\Bigr)\Bigl(1- rac1{n_\ell}\Bigr) =\sum_\ell\Bigl(1- rac{n_\ell}{n}\Bigr)\Bigl(1- rac1{n_\ell}\Bigr). With g\ge2 every first factor is positive, and the second is positive for any group with two or more observations. So the sum is positive, and the covariance vanishes iff \mu_4=3\sigma^4. For heavy-tailed errors, \mu_4>3\sigma^4, the two sums of squares are positively correlated: a large error inflates both. [B3] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I), and let \M be symmetric idempotent of rank r with \M mu
eq mu, as when a regression model omits a needed regressor. Show that 
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-r,
orm{(\I-\M) mu}^2/\sigma^2), and find the bias of 
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2/(n-r) as an estimator of \sigma^2. In the setting of @thm-qf-nested-f without the assumption  P mu= mu, which parts of the conclusion survive? [B4] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( zero, Sigma). Use @cor-qf-mgf and @prp-mat-eigen-basic(d) to show that \E\,e^{t\Y\T\A\Y}=\det(\I_n-2t\A Sigma)^{-1/2} for \lvert tvert small. C. Going deeper [C1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n(\mu one,\sigma^2\I) with \mu and \sigma^2 unknown. Among symmetric \A with \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=\sigma^2 for all \mu and \sigma^2, show that \A=\mathbf{C}/(n-1), which gives S^2, uniquely minimizes \Var(\Y\T\A\Y) at every parameter value. (Compare @exr-rv-best-quadratic, where the mean is known to be zero.) Since \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=\sigma^2	r\A+\mu^2 one\T\A one, unbiasedness means 	r\A=1 and  one\T\A one=0. By @thm-qf-mean-var, \Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=2\sigma^4	r(\A^2)+4\mu^2\sigma^2
orm{\A one}^2. The map \A\mapsto\mathbf{C}\A\mathbf{C} is an orthogonal projection for the inner product 	r(\A\B) on symmetric matrices, so 	r(\A^2)\ge	r\{(\mathbf{C}\A\mathbf{C})^2\}, with equality iff \A=\mathbf{C}\A\mathbf{C}. Also 	r(\mathbf{C}\A\mathbf{C})=	r\A- one\T\A one/n=1. The symmetric matrix \mathbf{C}\A\mathbf{C} has rank at most n-1. If \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{n-1} are its eigenvalues on  one\perpc, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives 1=(\sum\lambda_i)^2\le(n-1)\sum\lambda_i^2. Hence 	r(\A^2)\ge1/(n-1), with equality iff \A=\mathbf{C}\A\mathbf{C} and all \lambda_i=1/(n-1), that is, iff \A=\mathbf{C}/(n-1). That matrix also has \A one= zero, so it minimizes both variance terms at once.

title: 4.3 When a quadratic form is chi-squared
content:
When a quadratic form is chi-squared A quadratic form is a weighted sum of independent noncentral \chi^2(1) pieces, and the weights are eigenvalues. It is itself chi-squared when every nonzero weight equals one. This section turns that observation into checkable conditions on \A and  Sigma, and shows that for the spherical case the condition is necessary as well as sufficient. Spherical normal vectors [Chi-squared forms in a spherical normal vector] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\I_n), let \A be symmetric, and let r\ge1 be an integer and \gamma\ge0. Then \Y\T\A\Y\sim\chi^2(r,\gamma) if and only if \A is idempotent with ank(\A)=r and \gamma= mu\T\A mu. Sufficiency. By @thm-mat-idempotent, \A=\Q_1\Q_1\T, where the n	imes r matrix \Q_1 has orthonormal columns and r=ank(\A)=	r(\A). Then \Y\T\A\Y=
orm{\Q_1\T\Y}^2 and \Q_1\T\Y\sim\Normal_r(\Q_1\T mu,\Q_1\T\Q_1)=\Normal_r(\Q_1\T mu,\I_r), so by definition \Y\T\A\Y\sim\chi^2(r,
orm{\Q_1\T mu}^2), and 
orm{\Q_1\T mu}^2= mu\T\A mu. Necessity. Apply @thm-qf-canonical with  L=\I, so that \A=\Q Lambda\Q\T. Let  oldsymbol{\upnu}=\Q\T mu. Then  b=\Q\T\A mu= Lambda oldsymbol{\upnu}, so b_j=\lambda_j
u_j. The constant left after completing squares is  mu\T\A mu-\sum_{\lambda_j
e0}\lambda_j
u_j^2= oldsymbol{\upnu}\T Lambda oldsymbol{\upnu}-\sum_j\lambda_j
u_j^2=0. Hence \Y\T\A\Y has the law of \sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j(W_j+
u_j)^2, where J indexes the nonzero eigenvalues. J is not empty, because a \chi^2(r,\gamma) variable with r\ge1 is not identically zero. By @lem-qf-shifted-square, near t=0 the logarithm of the mgf of this sum is \sum_{j\in J}\{-	frac12\log(1-2\lambda_jt)+\lambda_j
u_j^2t/(1-2\lambda_jt)\}. Expanding -	frac12\log(1-x)=\sum_{k\ge1}x^k/(2k) and x/(1-x)=\sum_{k\ge1}x^k, the coefficient of t^k is (2^{k-1}/k)\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j^k(1+k
u_j^2). The same expansion of @eq-qf-ncchisq-mgf gives (2^{k-1}/k)(r+k\gamma). Equal distributions have equal mgfs, and two power series that agree on an interval have equal coefficients, so \sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j^k\,(1+k
u_j^2)=r+k\gamma\qquad	ext{for every }k\ge1 . {#eq-qf-cumulant-match} Let ho=\max_{j\in J}\lvert\lambda_jvert. For even k every term on the left is nonnegative and one of them is at least ho^k. The right side grows only linearly in k, so ho\le1. Split J into J_+=\{\lambda_j=1\}, J_-=\{\lambda_j=-1\} and J_0=\{0<\lvert\lambda_jvert<1\}, and write N_\pm=\lvert J_\pmvert and S_\pm=\sum_{J_\pm}
u_j^2. The terms over J_0 tend to zero as k	o\infty, so N_++(-1)^kN_-+k igl(S_++(-1)^kS_- igr)-r-k\gamma\;\longrightarrow\;0 . Dividing by k and letting k	o\infty through even and through odd values gives S_++S_-=\gamma=S_+-S_-. Then the same limit without the factor k gives N_++N_-=r=N_+-N_-. So N_-=S_-=0, N_+=r and S_+=\gamma. The terms over J_+ in @eq-qf-cumulant-match now account for all of r+k\gamma, and with k=2 the remaining sum \sum_{J_0}\lambda_j^2(1+2
u_j^2) is zero. Every term of that sum is positive, so J_0 is empty. Thus every eigenvalue of \A is 0 or 1, \A is idempotent, ank(\A)=N_+=r, and  mu\T\A mu=\sum_{J_+}
u_j^2=\gamma. The necessity half is the one that makes the theorem a tool for recognizing distributions. If a quadratic form in a spherical normal vector is chi-squared at all, then it is the squared length of a projection. There is no other way. General covariance matrices When a quadratic form is chi-squared Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma) and let \A be symmetric. 1. (Projections.) If  Sigma=\sigma^2\I with \sigma>0 and  P is symmetric and idempotent, then  rac{
orm{ P\Y}^2}{\sigma^2}= rac{\Y\T P\Y}{\sigma^2} \sim\chi^2\Bigl(ank( P),\, rac{
orm{ P mu}^2}{\sigma^2}\Bigr). 2. (Positive definite  Sigma.) If  Sigma is positive definite, then \Y\T\A\Y has a \chi^2(r,\gamma) distribution for some r\ge1 and \gamma\ge0 iff \A Sigma is idempotent and \A
e\mathbf{0}. In that case r=ank(\A)=	r(\A Sigma) and \gamma= mu\T\A mu. 3. (Any  Sigma.) If 	ext{(i) }  Sigma\A Sigma\A Sigma= Sigma\A Sigma,\qquad 	ext{(ii) }  Sigma\A Sigma\A mu= Sigma\A mu,\qquad 	ext{(iii) }  mu\T\A Sigma\A mu= mu\T\A mu, then \Y\T\A\Y\sim\chi^2 igl(	r(\A Sigma), mu\T\A mu igr). The three conditions hold in particular when \A Sigma\A=\A, and when \A Sigma is idempotent and  mu\in\C( Sigma). (a) \sigma^{-1}\Y\sim\Normal_n(\sigma^{-1} mu,\I). Apply @thm-qf-chisq-identity with \A= P, using  P\T P= P to write \Y\T P\Y=
orm{ P\Y}^2 and  mu\T P mu=
orm{ P mu}^2. (b) Let  Sigma^{1/2} be the positive definite square root (@thm-mat-square-root). Then \Z= Sigma^{-1/2}\Y\sim\Normal_n( Sigma^{-1/2} mu,\I) and \Y\T\A\Y=\Z\T\B\Z with \B= Sigma^{1/2}\A Sigma^{1/2} symmetric. By @thm-qf-chisq-identity, \Y\T\A\Y is noncentral chi-squared iff \B is idempotent and nonzero. Now \B^2= Sigma^{1/2}\A Sigma\A Sigma^{1/2}, so \B^2=\B iff \A Sigma\A=\A (multiply by  Sigma^{-1/2} on both sides) iff \A Sigma\A Sigma=\A Sigma (multiply by  Sigma or  Sigma^{-1} on the right). Also \B
e\mathbf{0} iff \A
e\mathbf{0}. The degrees of freedom are ank(\B)=ank(\A), which equals 	r(\B)=	r(\A Sigma), and the noncentrality is  mu\T Sigma^{-1/2}\B Sigma^{-1/2} mu= mu\T\A mu. (c) Take  L of size n	imes k with full column rank k=ank( Sigma) and  L L\T= Sigma, for instance  L= U_1 D_1^{1/2} from the eigenvectors  U_1 for the positive eigenvalues  D_1 of  Sigma. (If  Sigma=\mathbf{0} the claim is trivial.) As in @thm-qf-canonical, \Y\overset{d}{=} mu+ L\Z with \Z\sim\Normal_k( zero,\I). Since  L has full column rank,  L\T has full row rank, so  L\mathbf{G} L\T= L H L\T implies \mathbf{G}= H, and  L\mathbf{g}= L\mathbf{h} implies \mathbf{g}=\mathbf{h}. Put \B= L\T\A L and \mathbf{c}= L\T\A mu. Condition (i) reads  L\B^2 L\T= L\B L\T, so \B^2=\B. Condition (ii) reads  L\B\mathbf{c}= L\mathbf{c}, so \B\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c}. Condition (iii) reads \mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{c}= mu\T\A mu. Hence ( mu+ L\Z)\T\A( mu+ L\Z)= mu\T\A mu+2\mathbf{c}\T\Z+\Z\T\B\Z =(\Z+\mathbf{c})\T\B(\Z+\mathbf{c}), because (\Z+\mathbf{c})\T\B(\Z+\mathbf{c})=\Z\T\B\Z+2\mathbf{c}\T\B\Z+\mathbf{c}\T\B\mathbf{c} and \B\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c}. Now \Z+\mathbf{c}\sim\Normal_k(\mathbf{c},\I), and @thm-qf-chisq-identity gives the law \chi^2(ank\B,\mathbf{c}\T\B\mathbf{c}), where ank\B=	r\B=	r(\A Sigma) and \mathbf{c}\T\B\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{c}= mu\T\A mu. If \B=\mathbf{0}, then \mathbf{c}=\B\mathbf{c}= zero and the form is identically 0, which is \chi^2(0). If \A Sigma\A=\A, all three conditions follow by substitution. If \A Sigma is idempotent and  mu= Sigma v, then (i) follows from multiplying \A Sigma\A Sigma=\A Sigma by  Sigma on the left, and (ii) and (iii) from the same identity applied to  v. Part (a) is the case used most often in this book. For the linear model \Y\sim\Normal_n(\X beta,\sigma^2\I) and the projection \M onto \C(\X), Chapter 6 shows that the residual sum of squares is 	ext{SSE}=
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2. Since (\I-\M)\X beta= zero, part (a) gives 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2 igl(n-ank(\X) igr), a central distribution whatever the value of  beta. The projections that define test statistics, by contrast, do not annihilate the mean under the alternative, and their noncentrality 
orm{ P\X beta}^2/\sigma^2 measures how far the truth is from the hypothesis in the metric that the test can see. In part (c) idempotence of \A Sigma alone is not enough when  Sigma is singular. A mean with a component outside \C( Sigma) is a deterministic shift that the form may pick up as a constant or as a linear term (@exr-qf-singular). Part (c) also covers the natural generalization of the Mahalanobis distance. [Mahalanobis forms] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma). 1. If  Sigma is positive definite, (\Y- mu)\T Sigma^{-1}(\Y- mu)\sim\chi^2(n) and \Y\T Sigma^{-1}\Y\sim\chi^2(n, mu\T Sigma^{-1} mu). 2. If \G is a symmetric generalized inverse of  Sigma and  mu\in\C( Sigma), then \Y\T\G\Y\sim\chi^2 igl(ank( Sigma), mu\T\G mu igr). (a) \A= Sigma^{-1} satisfies \A Sigma\A=\A, and \Y- mu\sim\Normal_n( zero, Sigma). The central statement was already obtained by whitening in @prp-mvn-mahalanobis. (b) \G Sigma is idempotent because  Sigma\G Sigma= Sigma, so part (c) of the theorem applies and the degrees of freedom are 	r(\G Sigma)=	r( L\T\G L). With  L as in that proof,  L L\T\G L L\T= L L\T gives  L\T\G L=\I_k, whose trace is k=ank( Sigma). A symmetric generalized inverse always exists (@prp-mat-ginverse-props(d)). The value of \Y\T\G\Y does not depend on which one is chosen, with probability one (@exr-qf-ginverse-form). [Correlated observations about a common level] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma) with  Sigma positive definite, and suppose we want to measure how far \Y is from a common level m one. The generalized least squares level is \hat{m}= one\T Sigma^{-1}\Y/ one\T Sigma^{-1} one, and the natural discrepancy is (\Y-\hat{m} one)\T Sigma^{-1}(\Y-\hat{m} one)=\Y\T\A\Y with \A= Sigma^{-1}- rac{ Sigma^{-1} one one\T Sigma^{-1}}{ one\T Sigma^{-1} one}. A direct multiplication gives \A Sigma\A=\A, and 	r(\A Sigma)=n-1. By @thm-qf-chisq(b) the form is noncentral chi-squared with n-1 degrees of freedom and noncentrality  mu\T\A mu, which is zero exactly when  mu is constant. The listing takes n=8, an autoregressive correlation  Sigma=(ho^{\lvert i-jvert}) with ho=0.6, and a linear trend in the mean, for which \gamma=4.200. Figure 4.3.1(a) compares 200{,}000 simulated values with the \chi^2(7,4.200) density. import numpy as np from scipy import integrate, stats rng = np.random.default_rng(31415) n, rho = 8, 0.6 idx = np.arange(n) Sigma = rho ** np.abs(idx[:, None] - idx[None, :]) # AR(1) correlation matrix mu = 0.4 * (idx - idx.mean()) # linear trend, mean zero one = np.ones(n) W = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) A = W - np.outer(W @ one, W @ one) / (one @ W @ one) # GLS-centred form AS = A @ Sigma print("A Sigma idempotent:", np.allclose(AS @ AS, AS)) df, gamma = np.trace(AS), mu @ A @ mu # chi^2(df, gamma) L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma) # Y = mu + L Z Z = rng.standard_normal((200_000, n)) Y = mu + Z @ L.T q_gls = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Y, A, Y) print(df, gamma, stats.kstest(q_gls, stats.ncx2(df, gamma).cdf).pvalue) [Figure 4.3.1. Two quadratic forms measuring spread about a common level, for n=8 autoregressive observations with a trending mean. (a) With generalized least squares centring, \A Sigma is idempotent and the form is exactly noncentral chi-squared. (b) With ordinary centring it is a weighted sum of noncentral \chi^2(1) terms. A two-moment scaled chi-squared fits closely. The chi-squared law that would hold for independent observations does not.] Figure 4.3.1. Two quadratic forms measuring spread about a common level, for n=8 autoregressive observations with a trending mean. (a) With generalized least squares centring, \A Sigma is idempotent and the form is exactly noncentral chi-squared. (b) With ordinary centring it is a weighted sum of noncentral \chi^2(1) terms. A two-moment scaled chi-squared fits closely. The chi-squared law that would hold for independent observations does not. [Two quadratic forms measuring spread about a common level, for n=8 autoregressive observations with a trending mean. (a) With generalized least squares centring, \A Sigma is idempotent and the form is exactly noncentral chi-squared. (b) With ordinary centring it is a weighted sum of noncentral \chi^2(1) terms. A two-moment scaled chi-squared fits closely. The chi-squared law that would hold for independent observations does not.] Two quadratic forms measuring spread about a common level, for n=8 autoregressive observations with a trending mean. (a) With generalized least squares centring, \A Sigma is idempotent and the form is exactly noncentral chi-squared. (b) With ordinary centring it is a weighted sum of noncentral \chi^2(1) terms. A two-moment scaled chi-squared fits closely. The chi-squared law that would hold for independent observations does not. Forms that are not chi-squared Most quadratic forms fail the conditions of @thm-qf-chisq. The ordinary sum of squares about the mean, \Y\T\mathbf{C}\Y with \mathbf{C}=\I-n^{-1} one one\T, is an example as soon as the observations are correlated. Then \mathbf{C} Sigma is not idempotent, and by @thm-qf-canonical the law is that of \sum_j\lambda_j(W_j+
u_j)^2, with weights \lambda_j equal to the nonzero eigenvalues of \mathbf{C} Sigma. In @exm-qf-gls-centring these range from 0.259 to 1.832. Two practical ways to handle such a law are the following. Exact computation. The characteristic function of the weighted sum is known in closed form (put t=iu in @cor-qf-mgf), and a distribution function can be recovered from a characteristic function \varphi by the inversion formula of Gil-Pelaez (1951), \Pr(X>x)= rac12+ rac1\pi\int_0^\infty rac{\operatorname{Im}\{e^{-iux}\varphi(u)\}}{u}\,du . For a weighted sum of k chi-squared terms the integrand decays like u^{-1-k/2}, so ordinary quadrature works well. Imhof (1961) gave the real-variable form of this integral that most software uses. The listing implements it directly and checks it against simulation. Two-moment approximation. Match a\chi^2(
u) to the mean m and variance v from @thm-qf-mean-var. Since a\chi^2(
u) has mean a
u and variance 2a^2
u, this gives a=v/(2m) and 
u=2m^2/v, with 
u usually not an integer (Satterthwaite 1946; Patnaik 1949). In @exm-qf-gls-centring, the simulated 95th percentile of \Y\T\mathbf{C}\Y is 26.51. The exact tail probability beyond it is 0.0490, and the approximation with a=2.488 and 
u=4.68 gives 0.0484. Treating the observations as independent, and so using \chi^2(7,6.720), gives 0.040. Figure 4.3.1(b) shows the three laws. Here the error from ignoring correlation is modest at the 5\% point but visible in the shape. It is not a monotone function of ho, but strong correlation makes it severe: with ho=0.9 and the same mean, the naive tail probability at the true 95th percentile is 0.197. def canonical(A, mu, L): """Y^T A Y = sum_j lam_j (W_j + nu_j)^2 + c (all lam_j nonzero here), W ~ N(0, I).""" lam, Qm = np.linalg.eigh(L.T @ A @ L) b = Qm.T @ L.T @ A @ mu keep = np.abs(lam) > 1e-10 assert np.allclose(b[~keep], 0) # no linear terms in this example c = mu @ A @ mu - np.sum(b[keep] ** 2 / lam[keep]) return lam[keep], b[keep] / lam[keep], c def tail_prob(x, lam, nu, c=0.0): """P(sum lam_j (W_j + nu_j)^2 + c > x) by Gil-Pelaez inversion.""" def integrand(u): z = 1 - 2j * lam * u phi = np.prod(z ** -0.5 * np.exp(1j * u * lam * nu**2 / z)) return (np.exp(-1j * u * (x - c)) * phi).imag / u edges = np.linspace(0, 400, 401) # integrand decays like u^(-1-k/2) val = sum(integrate.quad(integrand, a, b)[0] for a, b in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:])) return 0.5 + val / np.pi Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( zero,\I) with n\ge2, and \A=\alpha\I+ eta one one\T. Find all (\alpha, eta) for which \Y\T\A\Y has a chi-squared distribution, and identify each form. \A has eigenvalue \alpha+n eta on  one and \alpha on  one\perpc. By @thm-qf-chisq-identity, the form is chi-squared iff \A
e\mathbf{0} and both eigenvalues lie in \{0,1\}. The three solutions are (1,0), giving 
orm{\Y}^2\sim\chi^2(n); (0,1/n), giving n ar{Y}^2\sim\chi^2(1); and (1,-1/n), giving \sum(Y_i- ar{Y})^2\sim\chi^2(n-1). [A2] Two independent samples of sizes m and k come from \Normal(\mu_1,\sigma^2) and \Normal(\mu_2,\sigma^2). Write the pooled within-sample sum of squares as 
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2 for a suitable projection, and show that the two-sample t statistic has the t igl(m+k-2,(\mu_1-\mu_2)/(\sigma\sqrt{1/m+1/k}) igr) distribution. B. Practice [B1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n igl(\mu one,\sigma^2\{(1-ho)\I+ho one one\T\} igr) with -1/(n-1)<ho<1, and let  ar{Y} and S^2 be the sample mean and variance. Show that (n-1)S^2/\{\sigma^2(1-ho)\}\sim\chi^2(n-1) and that S^2 is independent of  ar{Y}. Deduce that \sqrt n( ar{Y}-\mu)/S has the law of \{(1+(n-1)ho)/(1-ho)\}^{1/2} times a t(n-1) variable, and describe what a positive ho does to the coverage of the usual 95\% t interval for \mu. [B2] Let  Sigma=\diag(1,0),  mu=(0,1)\T, \A=\I_2 and \Y\sim\Normal_2( mu, Sigma). Show that \A Sigma is idempotent but \Y\T\A\Y is not chi-squared. Which of the conditions of @thm-qf-chisq(c) fail? What changes if  mu=(m,0)\T? Repeat the first part with \A= egin{psmallmatrix}1&1\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}, where the shift enters through a linear term. \A Sigma= Sigma is idempotent. But Y_2=1 with probability one, so \Y\T\A\Y=Y_1^2+1\ge1, while every \chi^2(r,\gamma) with r\ge1 gives positive probability to (0,1). Conditions (i) and (ii) hold, since  Sigma^3= Sigma and  Sigma^2 mu= zero= Sigma mu. Condition (iii) fails, since  mu\T Sigma mu=0
e1= mu\T mu. The part of the mean outside \C( Sigma) adds a constant. If  mu=(m,0)\T\in\C( Sigma), then \Y\T\A\Y=Y_1^2\sim\chi^2(1,m^2), as @thm-qf-chisq(c) predicts. For \A= egin{psmallmatrix}1&1\1&0\end{psmallmatrix} and  mu=(0,1)\T, \A Sigma= egin{psmallmatrix}1&0\1&0\end{psmallmatrix} is again idempotent, and \Y\T\A\Y=Y_1^2+2Y_1Y_2=Y_1^2+2Y_1=(Y_1+1)^2-1, which is negative with positive probability. Conditions (i) and (ii) hold, since  Sigma\A Sigma= Sigma and  Sigma\A Sigma\A mu= Sigma\A mu=(1,0)\T, but (iii) fails because  mu\T\A Sigma\A mu=1
e0= mu\T\A mu. The shift now enters through the linear term 2Y_1. [B3] In @cor-qf-mahalanobis(b), show that \Y\T\G\Y takes the same value for every generalized inverse \G of  Sigma, with probability one. Hint: @thm-rv-cov-nnd. By @thm-rv-cov-nnd, \Y- mu\in\C( Sigma) with probability one. Since  mu\in\C( Sigma), also \Y\in\C( Sigma), so \Y= Sigma v for some (random)  v. For any generalized inverse \G, \Y\T\G\Y= v\T Sigma\G Sigma v= v\T Sigma v, which does not involve \G. [B4] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( zero, Sigma) with  Sigma positive definite, and let \A
e\mathbf{0} be nonnegative definite. Show that the two-moment approximation a\chi^2(
u) to \Y\T\A\Y has 
u=\{	r(\A Sigma)\}^2/	r\{(\A Sigma)^2\}, and that 
u\leank(\A), with equality iff all nonzero eigenvalues of \A Sigma are equal. C. Going deeper [C1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma) with  Sigma possibly singular, and suppose \Y\T\A\Y\sim\chi^2(r,\gamma) with r\ge1. Show that  Sigma\A Sigma\A Sigma= Sigma\A Sigma. Hint: in @cor-qf-mgf, compare the coefficients of t^k for k\ge3 with those of @eq-qf-ncchisq-mgf, and adapt the argument of @thm-qf-chisq-identity.

title: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content:
Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms An F or t statistic is a ratio, and its distribution is known only if numerator and denominator are independent. For normal vectors, uncorrelated linear functions are independent (@thm-mvn-independence). Quadratic forms are not linear, but the following observation brings them within reach of that result. A quadratic form is a function of a linear form: for any generalized inverse \A\ginv of \A, \Y\T\A\Y=\Y\T\A\A\ginv\A\Y=(\A\Y)\T\A\ginv(\A\Y). So \Y\T\A\Y is independent of anything that is independent of the vector \A\Y. The independence theorems [Linear and quadratic forms] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma), let \B be m	imes n and \A symmetric n	imes n. If \B Sigma\A=\mathbf{0}, then \B\Y and \Y\T\A\Y are independent. Conversely, if \B\Y and \Y\T\A\Y are independent for every  mu\in\Real^n, with  Sigma fixed, then \B Sigma\A=\mathbf{0}. The vector (\B\Y,\A\Y) is a linear function of \Y, hence jointly normal (@thm-mvn-linear), and its cross-covariance is \Cov(\B\Y,\A\Y)=\B Sigma\A\T=\B Sigma\A (@thm-rv-linear). If this is zero, \B\Y and \A\Y are independent by @thm-mvn-independence, and so are \B\Y and the function (\A\Y)\T\A\ginv(\A\Y) of \A\Y, which is \Y\T\A\Y by the key idea above. Conversely, independent variables with finite variances are uncorrelated, so @thm-qf-mean-var(c) gives 2\B Sigma\A mu= zero for every  mu, that is, \B Sigma\A=\mathbf{0}. [Two quadratic forms] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma) and let \A,\B be symmetric. If \A Sigma\B=\mathbf{0}, equivalently \B Sigma\A=\mathbf{0}, then \Y\T\A\Y and \Y\T\B\Y are independent. The two conditions are transposes of each other. As before, \A\Y and \B\Y are jointly normal with \Cov(\A\Y,\B\Y)=\A Sigma\B=\mathbf{0}, hence independent, and each form is a function of one of them. The condition is sufficient for every  mu and every  Sigma. When  Sigma is singular one might hope that the weaker requirement  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma=\mathbf{0} suffices, since only directions in \C( Sigma) carry noise. For nonnegative definite \A and \B the two requirements turn out to be equivalent (@exr-qf-singular-independence). In the other direction, the condition is necessary under mild assumptions, a result usually credited to Craig (1943). Its general proof is surprisingly delicate, and the history of incorrect published proofs is recounted by Driscoll and Gundberg (1986). The case that matters most for sums of squares has a short proof. [Necessity for nonnegative definite forms] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( zero,\I) and let \A,\B be nonnegative definite. If \Y\T\A\Y and \Y\T\B\Y are independent, then \A\B=\mathbf{0}. Independence makes the covariance zero, and by @thm-qf-mean-var(d) the covariance is 2	r(\A\B). With the square roots of @thm-mat-square-root, 	r(\A\B)=	r(\A^{1/2}\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}\B^{1/2})=	r igl\{(\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2})\T(\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}) igr\}, the sum of squares of the entries of \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}. So \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}=\mathbf{0}, and \A\B=\A^{1/2}(\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2})\B^{1/2}=\mathbf{0}. For nonnegative definite forms in a standard normal vector, then, zero correlation and independence coincide, just as for jointly normal linear forms. This fails for general symmetric matrices (@exr-qf-uncorrelated-dependent). Orthogonal projections of a spherical normal vector The situation in regression is the tidiest one: a spherical normal vector and several projections onto mutually orthogonal subspaces. [Independent projections] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I), and let  P_1,\dots, P_k be symmetric idempotent matrices with  P_i P_j=\mathbf{0} for i
e j, and ranks r_1,\dots,r_k. Then  P_1\Y,\dots, P_k\Y are mutually independent normal vectors,  P_i\Y\sim\Normal_n( P_i mu,\sigma^2 P_i), and the sums of squares  rac{
orm{ P_i\Y}^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2\Bigl(r_i, rac{
orm{ P_i mu}^2}{\sigma^2}\Bigr), \qquad i=1,\dots,k, are mutually independent. Stack the vectors  P_i\Y into one nk-vector. It is a linear function of \Y, so it is normal, and the covariance between blocks i and j is  P_i(\sigma^2\I) P_j\T=\sigma^2 P_i P_j. This is \mathbf{0} for i
e j and \sigma^2 P_i for i=j. By the block form of @thm-mvn-independence the blocks are mutually independent, and functions of them, the squared lengths, are then mutually independent. Their laws are @thm-qf-chisq(a). In geometric language, which Chapter 6 develops: the coordinates of a spherical normal vector in mutually orthogonal subspaces are independent. It is the reason the rows of an analysis of variance table can be treated separately. [Sample mean and sample variance] Let Y_1,\dots,Y_n (n\ge2) be independent \Normal(\mu,\sigma^2), with sample mean  ar{Y} and sample variance S^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i- ar{Y})^2. Then 1.  ar{Y} and S^2 are independent, and  ar{Y}\sim\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2/n); 2. (n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-1); 3. for any \mu_0, T=\sqrt n( ar{Y}-\mu_0)/S\sim t(n-1,\delta) with \delta=\sqrt n(\mu-\mu_0)/\sigma. In particular T\sim t(n-1) when \mu=\mu_0. Here \Y\sim\Normal_n(\mu one,\sigma^2\I). Let  P_1=n^{-1} one one\T and \mathbf{C}=\I- P_1. Both are symmetric and idempotent,  P_1\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{0}, and ank(\mathbf{C})=	r(\mathbf{C})=n-1. Since  P_1\Y= ar{Y} one and 
orm{\mathbf{C}\Y}^2=(n-1)S^2, @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections gives (a), which @exm-mvn-mean-deviations obtained directly, and, because \mathbf{C}\mu one= zero, also (b). For (c), X=\sqrt n( ar{Y}-\mu_0)/\sigma\sim\Normal(\delta,1) and V=(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-1) are independent, and T=X/\sqrt{V/(n-1)}. Apply @def-qf-noncentral-t. The independence in (a) characterizes the normal distribution: for n\ge2 independent identically distributed observations with finite variance,  ar{Y} and S^2 are independent only under normality (Lukacs 1942). We will not need this, but it shows that normality is used essentially here. It is not a technicality that more careful arguments could remove. Preview: the F statistic for nested models The main use of these results comes in Chapter 11. Its core fits in a few lines. [F statistic for nested subspaces] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I), and let  P_0 and  P be symmetric idempotent matrices of ranks r_0<r<n with  P P_0= P_0. Suppose that  P mu= mu. Then F= rac{\Y\T( P- P_0)\Y/(r-r_0)}{\Y\T(\I- P)\Y/(n-r)} \sim F\Bigl(r-r_0,\;n-r,\; rac{
orm{( P- P_0) mu}^2}{\sigma^2}\Bigr), and the noncentrality is zero iff  P_0 mu= mu. Transposing  P P_0= P_0 gives  P_0 P= P_0. Hence ( P- P_0)^2= P-2 P_0+ P_0= P- P_0, so  P- P_0 is symmetric idempotent with rank 	r( P)-	r( P_0)=r-r_0. Also ( P- P_0)(\I- P)= P- P- P_0+ P_0=\mathbf{0}, and \I- P is symmetric idempotent of rank n-r. By @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections the numerator and denominator sums of squares are independent, with \sigma^{-2} times them distributed as \chi^2(r-r_0,
orm{( P- P_0) mu}^2/\sigma^2) and \chi^2(n-r,
orm{(\I- P) mu}^2/\sigma^2). The second noncentrality is 0 since  P mu= mu. The unknown \sigma^2 cancels in the ratio, and @def-qf-noncentral-f applies. Finally, ( P- P_0) mu= mu- P_0 mu. In a linear model,  P=\M projects onto the column space of the full model matrix \X and  P_0=\Mo onto that of a submodel \X_0. The numerator is the drop in residual sum of squares from the submodel to the full model (Chapter 6). The theorem says three things. The test that rejects for large F has an exactly known null distribution. Its power depends on the unknown parameters only through \gamma=
orm{(\M-\Mo)\X beta}^2/\sigma^2. And, by @thm-qf-f-power, that power increases with \gamma. [Detecting curvature] Let x_1,\dots,x_n, n=15, be equally spaced on [0,1], and suppose Y_i=1+0.5x_i+ eta_2x_i^2+\varepsilon_i with independent \Normal(0,1) errors. To test for curvature, compare the straight line (\X_0=[ one,\x]) with the quadratic (\X=[ one,\x,\x^2]). The F statistic has 1 and 12 degrees of freedom, and the 5\% critical value is 4.747. For  eta_2=8.0, the listing finds \gamma=6.873 and power 0.673 from the noncentral F, and the rejection rate in 100{,}000 simulated data sets is 0.674. The noncentrality has a clear meaning. It is  eta_2^2 times the squared length of the part of \x^2 orthogonal to  one and \x, divided by \sigma^2. It grows roughly in proportion to n for a fixed design pattern. Keeping the same design on [0,1], the smallest n with power at least 0.8 is 21, where \gamma=8.97. Figure 4.4.1 places the example on the power curve and shows the loss of power when the same noncentrality is spread over more numerator degrees of freedom r. At \gamma=10 the power is 0.827, 0.606 and 0.421 for r=1,3,6. import numpy as np from scipy import stats rng = np.random.default_rng(1104) alpha, s = 0.05, 12 def power(gamma, q, s, alpha=0.05): crit = stats.f.ppf(1 - alpha, q, s) return stats.ncf.sf(crit, q, s, np.maximum(gamma, 1e-12)) gammas = np.linspace(0, 30, 301) gamma_ref, rs = 10.0, (1, 3, 6) # r = numerator degrees of freedom curves = {q: power(gammas, q, s) for q in rs} n, sigma, beta0, beta1, beta2, reps = 15, 1.0, 1.0, 0.5, 8.0, 100_000 x = np.linspace(0, 1, n) X0 = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x]) # straight line X = np.column_stack([X0, x**2]) # adds curvature def proj(Z): Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(Z) return Q @ Q.T M, M0 = proj(X), proj(X0) mean = X @ np.array([beta0, beta1, beta2]) gamma = mean @ (M - M0) @ mean / sigma**2 # noncentrality q, df_resid = 1, n - 3 crit = stats.f.ppf(0.95, q, df_resid) exact_power = stats.ncf.sf(crit, q, df_resid, gamma) Y = mean + sigma * rng.standard_normal((reps, n)) num = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Y, M - M0, Y) / q den = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Y, np.eye(n) - M, Y) / df_resid print(gamma, exact_power, np.mean(num / den > crit)) [Figure 4.4.1. Power \Pr\{F(r,12,\gamma)>F_{0.05}(r,12)\} of the level-0.05 F test as a function of the noncentrality. Every curve starts at 0.05 and increases to 1 (@thm-qf-f-power). For a fixed \gamma, power falls as the number r of numerator degrees of freedom grows. The dot is the curvature test of @exm-qf-curvature.] Figure 4.4.1. Power \Pr\{F(r,12,\gamma)>F_{0.05}(r,12)\} of the level-0.05 F test as a function of the noncentrality. Every curve starts at 0.05 and increases to 1 (@thm-qf-f-power). For a fixed \gamma, power falls as the number r of numerator degrees of freedom grows. The dot is the curvature test of @exm-qf-curvature. [Power \Pr\{F(r,12,\gamma)>F_{0.05}(r,12)\} of the level-0.05 F test as a function of the noncentrality. Every curve starts at 0.05 and increases to 1 (@thm-qf-f-power). For a fixed \gamma, power falls as the number r of numerator degrees of freedom grows. The dot is the curvature test of @exm-qf-curvature.] Power \Pr\{F(r,12,\gamma)>F_{0.05}(r,12)\} of the level-0.05 F test as a function of the noncentrality. Every curve starts at 0.05 and increases to 1 (@thm-qf-f-power). For a fixed \gamma, power falls as the number r of numerator degrees of freedom grows. The dot is the curvature test of @exm-qf-curvature. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] In @exm-qf-drift let \Y\sim\Normal_n(\mu one,\sigma^2\I) with n\ge3. Use @thm-qf-mean-var(d) to show that \Cov(S^2,Q)=\Var(S^2), and deduce that S^2 and Q are dependent with correlation \{2(n-1)/(3n-4)\}^{1/2}. Which linear forms \mathbf{a}\T\Y are independent of Q for every mean vector  mu\in\Real^n? With  Sigma=\sigma^2\I, part (d) of @thm-qf-mean-var gives \Cov(S^2,Q)=2\sigma^4	r(\mathbf{C} D\T D)/\{2(n-1)^2\}. Since  D one= zero, \mathbf{C} D\T D= D\T D, whose trace is 2(n-1), so \Cov(S^2,Q)=2\sigma^4/(n-1)=\Var(S^2). The mean terms vanish because \mathbf{C} mu= D mu= zero. Using \Var(Q) from @exm-qf-drift-variance, the correlation is \{\Var(S^2)/\Var(Q)\}^{1/2}=\{2(n-1)/(3n-4)\}^{1/2}, which is nonzero, so the forms are dependent. By @thm-qf-indep-linear, \mathbf{a}\T\Y is independent of Q for every  mu iff \mathbf{a}\T D\T D= zero\T. Multiplying by \mathbf{a} gives 
orm{ D\mathbf{a}}^2=0, so  D\mathbf{a}= zero and \mathbf{a} is a multiple of  one; conversely such \mathbf{a} work. The only such linear forms are the multiples of  ar{Y}. B. Practice [B1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_2( zero,\I). Show that Y_1^2-Y_2^2 and 2Y_1Y_2 are uncorrelated but not independent. Why does @prp-qf-craig-nnd not apply? With \A=\diag(1,-1) and \B= egin{psmallmatrix}0&1\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}, 	r(\A\B)=0, so the covariance 2	r(\A\B) is zero. In polar coordinates Y_1=R\cos\Theta, Y_2=R\sin\Theta, with R^2\sim\chi^2(2) independent of \Theta uniform on [0,2\pi), the two forms are R^2\cos2\Theta and R^2\sin2\Theta. Now \E(R^4)=8 and \E(R^8)=384, so \E[(R^2\cos2\Theta)^2(R^2\sin2\Theta)^2]=384/8=48, but the product of the expected squares is (8/2)^2=16. The forms are dependent. @prp-qf-craig-nnd needs nonnegative definite matrices, and \A and \B are indefinite. [B2] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma) and let \A,\B be nonnegative definite with  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma=\mathbf{0}. Show that \A Sigma\B=\mathbf{0}, so that \Y\T\A\Y and \Y\T\B\Y are independent. Show by an example that the implication can fail when \A is not nonnegative definite. Write \A=\R\R\T and \B= S S\T, for instance with symmetric square roots, and  Sigma= L L\T with  L of full column rank. Cancelling  L on both sides of  L( L\T\A L)( L\T\B L) L\T=\mathbf{0} gives  L\T\A L L\T\B L=\mathbf{0}. The trace of this matrix is 	r( L\T\R\R\T L L\T S S\T L)=	r\{(\R\T Sigma S)(\R\T Sigma S)\T\}=
orm{\R\T Sigma S}_F^2, so \R\T Sigma S=\mathbf{0}. Hence \A Sigma\B=\R(\R\T Sigma S) S\T=\mathbf{0}, and @thm-qf-indep-quadratic applies. For nonnegative definite matrices the two conditions are therefore equivalent, since \A Sigma\B=\mathbf{0} trivially implies  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma=\mathbf{0}. Without nonnegative definiteness the argument breaks at the trace step. Take  Sigma=\diag(1,0), \A= egin{psmallmatrix}0&1\1&0\end{psmallmatrix} and \B=\I_2. Then  Sigma\A Sigma=\mathbf{0}, so  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma=\mathbf{0}, but \A Sigma\B= egin{psmallmatrix}0&0\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}
e\mathbf{0}. With  mu=(0,m)\T and m
e0 we have Y_2=m with probability one, so the forms are 2mY_1 and Y_1^2+m^2. The second is a nonconstant function of the first, so they are dependent. [B3] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n(\X beta,\sigma^2\I) with \X of full column rank p<n, let \hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\Y, \M=\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T and s^2=
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2/(n-p). With v_{jj} the jth diagonal entry of (\X\T\X)^{-1}, show that (\hat{ eta}_j-b)/(s\sqrt{v_{jj}})\sim t igl(n-p,( eta_j-b)/(\sigma\sqrt{v_{jj}}) igr). Here \M is symmetric and idempotent with 	r\M=	r\{(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\X\}=p, and \M\X=\X. So (n-p)s^2/\sigma^2=
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-p) by @thm-qf-chisq(a), because (\I-\M)\X beta= zero. With \B=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T, \B(\sigma^2\I)(\I-\M)=\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1}(\X\T-\X\T\M)=\mathbf{0}, so \hbeta=\B\Y is independent of s^2 (@thm-qf-indep-linear). Since \hbeta\sim\Normal_p( beta,\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1}), the variable X=(\hat{ eta}_j-b)/(\sigma\sqrt{v_{jj}}) is \Normal igl(( eta_j-b)/(\sigma\sqrt{v_{jj}}),1 igr). The statistic is X/\sqrt{V/(n-p)} with V=(n-p)s^2/\sigma^2, and @def-qf-noncentral-t applies. [B4] Show that F_\alpha(r,s)	o\chi^2_\alpha(r)/r as s	o\infty, where \chi^2_\alpha(r) is the upper \alpha point of \chi^2(r), and that the power \Pr\{F(r,s,\gamma)>F_\alpha(r,s)\} tends to \Pr\{\chi^2(r,\gamma)>\chi^2_\alpha(r)\}, the power of the test that knows \sigma^2. C. Going deeper [C1] Keep the notation of @thm-qf-nested-f and assume the null hypothesis  P_0 mu= mu. Put a=r-r_0, b=n-r, U=\Y\T( P- P_0)\Y, V=\Y\T(\I- P)\Y, and consider R= rac{\Y\T( P- P_0)\Y}{\Y\T(\I- P_0)\Y}= rac{U}{U+V}, the share of the reduced model’s residual sum of squares that the full model removes. 1. Show that the numerator and the denominator of R are not independent, and that their correlation is \sqrt{a/(a+b)}=\sqrt{(r-r_0)/(n-r_0)}. 2. Show nevertheless that R\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a/2,b/2) exactly, that R is independent of \Y\T(\I- P_0)\Y, and that F=(b/a)R/(1-R), so the two tests are the same test. 3. Which hypothesis of @thm-qf-indep-quadratic fails for the pair \{\Y\T( P- P_0)\Y,\ \Y\T(\I- P_0)\Y\}, and why does its failure not damage the exact null distribution? (a) The matrices  P- P_0 and \I- P are symmetric idempotent with zero product (proof of @thm-qf-nested-f), so U and V are independent with U/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(a) and V/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(b) by @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections; the noncentralities vanish because  P mu= mu and  P_0 mu= mu. The denominator is U+V, so \Cov(U,U+V)=\Var(U) and \operatorname{corr}(U,U+V)= rac{\Var(U)}{\sqrt{\Var(U)\Var(U+V)}} =\sqrt{ rac{2a\sigma^4}{2(a+b)\sigma^4}}=\sqrt{ rac{a}{a+b}} , which is positive: a large U inflates the denominator too. (b) This is @exr-qf-beta applied to the independent pair (U/\sigma^2,V/\sigma^2): the ratio U/(U+V) is \mathrm{Beta}(a/2,b/2) and is independent of U+V, and U/V=R/(1-R) gives F=(U/a)/(V/b)=(b/a)R/(1-R), a strictly increasing function of R. So rejecting for large R and rejecting for large F are the same rule at the same level, and \sigma^2 has cancelled in both. (c) Independence would require ( P- P_0)(\I- P_0)=\mathbf{0}, whereas ( P- P_0)(\I- P_0)= P- P_0 
e\mathbf{0}. What the theorems supply is a decomposition of the denominator into two independent pieces, one of which is the numerator. Dependence between numerator and denominator is not a problem in itself; what an exact distribution needs is that the pair be a function of independent chi-squared variables, which it is. [C2] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n(\X beta,\sigma^2\V) with \V positive definite and \X of full column rank p<n. Write \mathbf{K}=(\X\T\V^{-1}\X)^{-1}, 	ilde{ beta}=\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1}\Y,\qquad \A=\V^{-1}-\V^{-1}\X\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1},\qquad Q=\Y\T\A\Y . 1. Show that Q=(\Y-\X	ilde{ beta})\T\V^{-1}(\Y-\X	ilde{ beta}), that 	ilde{ beta}\sim\Normal_p( beta,\sigma^2\mathbf{K}) and Q/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-p), and that 	ilde{ beta} and Q are independent. Deduce an exact t distribution for  lambda\T	ilde{ beta} studentized by Q/(n-p). 2. Now take the ordinary least squares \hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\Y and 	ext{RSS}=\Y\T(\I-\M)\Y with \M=\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T. Show that they are independent for every  beta if and only if \C(\V\X)\subseteq\C(\X). 3. Check that the condition holds for equicorrelated errors, \V=(1-ho)\I+ho one one\T, in any model whose columns include  one, and fails for \X= one, n=3 and \V=\diag(1,1,4). (a) Since \Y-\X	ilde{ beta}=(\I-\X\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1})\Y, expanding (\I-\X\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1})\T\V^{-1}(\I-\X\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1}) gives \V^{-1}-2\V^{-1}\X\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1}+\V^{-1}\X\mathbf{K}(\X\T\V^{-1}\X)\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1}=\A. By @thm-mvn-linear, 	ilde{ beta} is normal with mean \mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1}\X beta= beta and covariance \sigma^2\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1}\V\V^{-1}\X\mathbf{K}=\sigma^2\mathbf{K}. Next, with  Sigma=\sigma^2\V, the matrix (\A/\sigma^2) Sigma=\A\V is idempotent, because \A\V\A=\A by the same expansion, and 	r(\A\V)=n-	r(\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1}\X)=n-p; also \A\X beta= zero because \A\X=\V^{-1}\X-\V^{-1}\X=\mathbf{0}. So Q/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-p) by @thm-qf-chisq(b). For independence take \B=\mathbf{K}\X\T\V^{-1} in @thm-qf-indep-linear: \B Sigma\A=\sigma^2\mathbf{K}\X\T\A=\mathbf{0}, again because \A\X=\mathbf{0}. Hence  lambda\T(	ilde{ beta}- beta)/\sqrt{ lambda\T\mathbf{K} lambda\,Q/(n-p)}\sim t(n-p), exactly as in @exr-qf-regression-t. (b) With \B=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T and \A=\I-\M, @thm-qf-indep-linear says that independence for every mean vector \X beta holds iff \B Sigma\A=\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\V(\I-\M)=\mathbf{0}, that is, iff \X\T\V(\I-\M)=\mathbf{0}. Transposing, this says (\I-\M)\V\X=\mathbf{0}, that is, \V\X=\M\V\X, which is \C(\V\X)\subseteq\C(\X). (Necessity is for all  beta; for one particular  beta the covariance may vanish by accident.) (c) For the equicorrelated \V and a model with  one\in\C(\X), \V\X=(1-ho)\X+ho one( one\T\X), and each column of  one one\T\X is a multiple of  one, so \C(\V\X)\subseteq\C(\X): ordinary least squares keeps its exact t and F theory. For \X= one and \V=\diag(1,1,4), \V one=(1,1,4)\T is not a multiple of  one, so  ar{Y} and the residual sum of squares are dependent, and the usual t statistic has no t distribution. The condition \C(\V\X)\subseteq\C(\X) is the same one under which ordinary and generalized least squares coincide (Chapter 31).

title: 4.5 The Cochran theorem
content:
The Cochran theorem An analysis of variance starts from an identity \Y\T\Y=\Y\T\A_1\Y+\dots+\Y\T\A_k\Y,\qquad \A_1+\dots+\A_k=\I, that splits the total sum of squares into pieces attributed to sources of variation. @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections says the pieces are independent chi-squared variables when the \A_i are mutually orthogonal projections. Checking that directly means checking k idempotence conditions and  inom k2 orthogonality conditions. Cochran’s theorem shows that one count of ranks does all of it. The algebra The matrix algebra behind this was done in Chapter 1. For symmetric matrices, any two of the three properties “each \A_i is idempotent”, “\A_i\A_j=\mathbf{0} for i
e j” and “the sum is idempotent” imply the third, and symmetric matrices that add to \I with ranks adding to n are idempotent and mutually orthogonal (@thm-mat-idempotent-sum). The next theorem adds the rank count for a sum that is idempotent but not necessarily \I, which is what nested models need. [Cochran, algebraic form] Let \A_1,\dots,\A_k be symmetric n	imes n matrices and \A=\sum_i\A_i. Consider 1. each \A_i is idempotent; 2. \A_i\A_j=\mathbf{0} for all i
e j; 3. \A is idempotent; 4. ank(\A)=\sum_iank(\A_i). Then any two of (a), (b), (c) imply all four, and (c) together with (d) implies all four. Any two of (a), (b), (c). By @thm-mat-idempotent-sum, any two of them imply the third. When all three hold, rank equals trace for symmetric idempotent matrices (@thm-mat-idempotent), so ank(\A)=	r(\A)=\sum_i	r(\A_i)=\sum_iank(\A_i), which is (d). (c) and (d) imply (a) and (b). Let r=ank(\A) and r_i=ank(\A_i). Every \A v=\sum_i\A_i v lies in \C(\A_1)+\dots+\C(\A_k), whose dimension is at most \sum_ir_i=r=\dim\C(\A). So the two spaces coincide, and in particular \C(\A_i)\subseteq\C(\A). By @thm-mat-idempotent(a), \A=\Q\Q\T with \Q of size n	imes r and \Q\T\Q=\I_r. Since \A is symmetric and idempotent it fixes every vector of its column space, so \A\A_i=\A_i, and transposing, \A_i\A=\A_i. Hence \A_i=\A\A_i\A=\Q\B_i\Q\T with \B_i=\Q\T\A_i\Q. The r	imes r matrices \B_i are symmetric, satisfy \sum_i\B_i=\Q\T\A\Q=\I_r, and have ank(\B_i)=r_i because \Q has orthonormal columns. By the last statement of @thm-mat-idempotent-sum, \B_i^2=\B_i and \B_i\B_j=\mathbf{0} for i
e j, and multiplying by \Q on the left and \Q\T on the right transfers both identities to the \A_i. The distributional statement [Cochran] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I), and let \A_1,\dots,\A_k be symmetric with ranks r_1,\dots,r_k, whose sum \A=\sum_i\A_i is idempotent of rank r (for example \A=\I, r=n). The following are equivalent: 1. the forms \Y\T\A_i\Y/\sigma^2 are mutually independent, and \Y\T\A_i\Y/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(r_i, mu\T\A_i mu/\sigma^2) for each i; 2. r_1+\dots+r_k=r; 3. each \A_i is idempotent; 4. \A_i\A_j=\mathbf{0} for all i
e j. Condition (c) of @thm-qf-cochran-algebra holds by assumption, so that theorem shows that (ii), (iii) and (iv) are equivalent, and each implies the other two. If (iii) and (iv) hold, @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections gives (i). If (i) holds, apply @thm-qf-chisq-identity to \sigma^{-1}\Y\sim\Normal_n(\sigma^{-1} mu,\I). Each \A_i with r_i\ge1 is idempotent, and an \A_i of rank zero is \mathbf{0}. This is (iii). In words: if the degrees of freedom add up, the sums of squares are independent chi-squared variables. Independence in (i) is not needed to reach (iii). The marginal chi-squared laws alone force the whole structure. [The one-way layout] Let observations fall into g groups of sizes n_1,\dots,n_g, with Y_{\ell j} independent \Normal(\mu_\ell,\sigma^2). Let \M replace each observation by its group mean, and  P_1=n^{-1} one one\T by the grand mean. Then \I= P_1+(\M- P_1)+(\I-\M) splits 
orm{\Y}^2 into n ar{Y}^2, the between-group sum of squares \sum_\ell n_\ell( ar{Y}_\ell- ar{Y})^2 and the within-group sum of squares \sum_{\ell,j}(Y_{\ell j}- ar{Y}_\ell)^2. The three matrices are symmetric with ranks 1, g-1 and n-g, which add to n. Cochran’s theorem needs nothing more. The three sums of squares, divided by \sigma^2, are independent noncentral chi-squared variables. Their noncentralities are n ar{\mu}^2/\sigma^2, \sum_\ell n_\ell(\mu_\ell- ar{\mu})^2/\sigma^2 with  ar{\mu}=\sum_\ell n_\ell\mu_\ell/n, and 0. The last is zero because \M mu= mu. The ratio of the between and within mean squares is F(g-1,n-g,\gamma) by @thm-qf-nested-f, and it is central iff all group means are equal. The script uses g=3 groups of sizes 3, 5, 4, means 2, 3, 1.5, and \sigma=1, and draws 200{,}000 data sets. Table 4.5.1 compares the theoretical means r_i+\gamma_i and variances 2r_i+4\gamma_i with the simulated ones. The largest absolute correlation between the three sums of squares is 0.0013. As a check that goes beyond correlation, the proportion of data sets in which both the between and the within sums of squares exceed their medians is 0.2497, against 0.25 for independent variables. import numpy as np from scipy import stats rng = np.random.default_rng(5150) sizes, means, sigma = [3, 5, 4], [2.0, 3.0, 1.5], 1.0 groups = np.repeat(np.arange(3), sizes) n = len(groups) Z = (groups[:, None] == np.arange(3)).astype(float) # group indicators M = Z @ np.diag(1 / np.array(sizes)) @ Z.T # group-mean projection J = np.ones((n, n)) / n pieces = [J, M - J, np.eye(n) - M] ranks = [np.linalg.matrix_rank(P) for P in pieces] print("ranks", ranks, "sum", sum(ranks), "n", n) mu = np.array(means)[groups] gammas = [mu @ P @ mu / sigma**2 for P in pieces] Y = mu + sigma * rng.standard_normal((200_000, n)) Q = np.stack([np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Y, P, Y) for P in pieces], axis=1) / sigma**2 print(np.corrcoef(Q, rowvar=False).round(3)) Table 4.5.1. Cochran decomposition for a one-way layout with n=12: theory against 200{,}000 simulated data sets. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Sum of squares r_i \gamma_i mean simulated variance simulated ---------------- ---------- ---------- ---------- ----------- ---------- ----------- grand mean 1 60.750 61.750 61.763 245.00 244.95 between groups 2 5.250 7.250 7.230 25.00 24.85 within groups 9 0.000 9.000 8.994 18.00 17.96 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ [What the theorem does not cover] Two assumptions carry the weight. The first is normality. Without it, @thm-qf-mean-var(d) fails, and with independent nonnormal errors the between and within sums of squares are in general correlated, with a correlation driven by the fourth cumulant (@exr-qf-kurtosis). The second is the spherical covariance \sigma^2\I. With \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\V, \V positive definite, apply the theorem to \V^{-1/2}\Y, whose forms have matrices \V^{1/2}\A_i\V^{1/2}. Their ranks are those of the \A_i, so the rank count is unchanged. What changes is the condition on the sum: \V^{1/2}\A\V^{1/2} is idempotent iff \A\V\A=\A (for example \sum_i\A_i=\V^{-1}), and conditions (iii) and (iv) become \A_i\V\A_i=\A_i and \A_i\V\A_j=\mathbf{0}. These are the generalized least squares decompositions of Chapter 31 (@thm-ggm-inference). Most analysis of variance tables in this book come from a chain of nested model spaces. The successive differences of their projections are mutually orthogonal projections whose ranks add up, so Cochran’s theorem applies without further work (@exr-qf-sequential, @thm-ss-decomposition). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let \A_1=\diag(2,0) and \A_2=\diag(-1,1), so that \A_1+\A_2=\I_2. Which hypotheses of @thm-qf-cochran fail, and what are the laws of the two forms when \Y\sim\Normal_2( zero,\I)? The sum \I_2 is idempotent, but every one of the conditions (ii)–(iv) fails. The ranks are 1 and 2, which add to 3
e2. Neither matrix is idempotent, since \A_1^2=\diag(4,0) and \A_2^2=\I_2. And \A_1\A_2=\diag(-2,0)
e\mathbf{0}. The forms are 2Y_1^2, which is twice a \chi^2(1) variable, and Y_2^2-Y_1^2, the difference of two independent \chi^2(1) variables, which takes negative values. Neither is chi-squared. They are dependent, because \Cov(2Y_1^2,\,Y_2^2-Y_1^2)=2\Cov(Y_1^2,Y_2^2)-2\Var(Y_1^2)=0-2\cdot2=-4
e0 . B. Practice [B1] A two-way layout has one observation Y_{ij} for each of a rows and b columns. Write 
orm{\Y}^2 as the sum of the grand-mean, row, column and residual sums of squares, identify the four matrices, and use @thm-qf-cochran to show that under Y_{ij}\sim\Normal(\mu+\alpha_i+ eta_j,\sigma^2) independently the four sums of squares are independent, with degrees of freedom 1, a-1, b-1 and (a-1)(b-1). [B2] Let  P_1,\dots, P_m be symmetric idempotent with \C( P_1)\subset\C( P_2)\subset\dots\subset\C( P_m), and put  P_0=\mathbf{0},  P_{m+1}=\I. Show that the matrices  P_i- P_{i-1}, i=1,\dots,m+1, satisfy the conditions of @thm-qf-cochran, so that the sequential sums of squares 
orm{( P_i- P_{i-1})\Y}^2 are independent noncentral chi-squared variables when \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I). C. Going deeper [C1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( zero,\I), and Q=Q_1+Q_2 with Q=\Y\T\A\Y\sim\chi^2(r), Q_1=\Y\T\A_1\Y\sim\chi^2(r_1) and Q_2=\Y\T\A_2\Y for a nonnegative definite \A_2. Show that Q_1 and Q_2 are independent and Q_2\sim\chi^2(r-r_1). By @thm-qf-chisq-identity, \A and \A_1 are idempotent, with ranks r and r_1. If \A v= zero, then 0= v\T\A_1 v+ v\T\A_2 v with both terms nonnegative, so 
orm{\A_1 v}^2= v\T\A_1 v=0. Thus \Null(\A)\subseteq\Null(\A_1), hence \C(\A_1)\subseteq\C(\A) and \A\A_1=\A_1=\A_1\A. Then \A_2^2=(\A-\A_1)^2=\A-2\A_1+\A_1=\A_2, so \A_2 is idempotent, and \A_1\A_2=\A_1\A-\A_1=\mathbf{0}. By @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections, Q_1 and Q_2 are independent and Q_2\sim\chi^2(	r\A_2)=\chi^2(r-r_1).

title: 4.6 Summary and Notes
content:
Summary and Notes Summary 1. If \Z\sim\Normal_r( mu,\I) then 
orm{\Z}^2\sim\chi^2(r,\gamma) with \gamma=
orm{ mu}^2, mean r+\gamma and variance 2r+4\gamma. The law is a Poisson(\gamma/2) mixture of \chi^2(r+2k) laws, and its tails increase strictly with \gamma (@thm-qf-ncchisq and @prp-qf-ncchisq-monotone). 2. F(r,s,\gamma) and t(s,\delta) put a noncentral numerator over an independent central denominator. The power of an F test increases strictly with \gamma, and T^2\sim F(1,s,\delta^2) (@thm-qf-f-power). 3. \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=	r(\A Sigma)+ mu\T\A mu for any distribution. Under normality \Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=2	r\{(\A Sigma)^2\}+4 mu\T\A Sigma\A mu,\qquad \Cov(\mathbf{K}\Y,\Y\T\A\Y)=2\mathbf{K} Sigma\A mu (@thm-qf-mean-var). 4. A normal quadratic form is a constant plus independent terms \lambda_j(W_j+
u_j)^2, and for singular  Sigma possibly normal terms. The weights \lambda_j are the nonzero eigenvalues of \A Sigma (@thm-qf-canonical). 5. For \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\I), \Y\T\A\Y is chi-squared iff \A is idempotent. Then the degrees of freedom are ank\A=	r\A and the noncentrality is  mu\T\A mu (@thm-qf-chisq-identity). For positive definite  Sigma the condition is that \A Sigma be idempotent. For projections, 
orm{ P\Y}^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(ank P,
orm{ P mu}^2/\sigma^2) (@thm-qf-chisq). 6. \B\Y and \Y\T\A\Y are independent if \B Sigma\A=\mathbf{0}, and \Y\T\A\Y and \Y\T\B\Y are independent if \A Sigma\B=\mathbf{0}, because a quadratic form is a function of \A\Y (@thm-qf-indep-linear and @thm-qf-indep-quadratic). 7. Projections of a spherical normal vector onto mutually orthogonal subspaces are independent. This gives the independence of  ar{Y} and S^2 and the exact F(r-r_0,n-r,\gamma) law of the nested-model F statistic (@thm-qf-orthogonal-projections, @cor-qf-sample-variance and @thm-qf-nested-f). 8. Cochran: if symmetric matrices add to an idempotent matrix and their ranks add up, the corresponding sums of squares are independent chi-squared variables (@thm-qf-cochran-algebra and @thm-qf-cochran). Notes and sources Source texts. Rencher and Schaalje (2008, chapter 5) cover the material of Section 4.2, Section 4.3, Section 4.4 and Section 4.5 for positive definite covariance matrices. They derive the mgf of a quadratic form by integrating against the normal density and obtain its variance by differentiating the logarithm of the mgf; the converse of the chi-squared theorem is referred to the literature. They use the noncentrality  mu\T mu/2. Seber and Lee (2003, section 2.4) reduce the general case to a spherical normal vector by an orthogonal diagonalization. They prove necessity of idempotence for central forms by factorizing the moment generating function, and give the eigenvalue criterion for singular covariance matrices. Christensen (2020, section 1.3) states the three conditions of @thm-qf-chisq(c) for arbitrary nonnegative definite  Sigma, and obtains independence by viewing quadratic forms as functions of linear ones, the approach followed in Section 4.4. The canonical representation (@thm-qf-canonical), the proof of necessity through the coefficients @eq-qf-cumulant-match, the monotonicity proof through the Poisson mixture, and the treatment of the Cochran algebra are this book’s own arrangements of standard material. Noncentral distributions. The noncentral chi-squared distribution first appeared in Fisher (1928). Patnaik (1949) studied its approximation by a scaled central chi-squared variable, and Satterthwaite (1946) used the same two-moment idea for linear combinations of mean squares, which reappears in the mixed models of Chapter 32 (@prp-mix-inference). Johnson et al. (1995, chapters 29–31) collect the properties of the noncentral chi-squared, F and t families. The monotonicity of power in the noncentrality and in the degrees of freedom is treated systematically by Ghosh (1973). General quadratic forms. The exact distribution of a quadratic form that is not chi-squared can be computed by numerical inversion of its characteristic function (Gil-Pelaez 1951; Imhof 1961). Mathai and Provost (1992) give a book-length treatment of quadratic forms in normal and nonnormal variables. The mean square successive difference of @exm-qf-drift goes back to von Neumann (1941), who derived the exact distribution of its ratio to S^2. Independence and Cochran’s theorem. Cochran (1934) proved the decomposition theorem that bears his name, in the context of the analysis of covariance. The necessity of \A Sigma\B=\mathbf{0} for independence of two forms is attributed to Craig (1943). Its full proof for arbitrary symmetric matrices and arbitrary means turned out to be subtle, and Driscoll and Gundberg (1986) trace the flawed and correct arguments. Searle (1971) gives general proofs of the independence and Cochran theorems in the style most linear-models texts follow. For nonnegative definite \A and \B, the condition  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma=\mathbf{0} of Christensen (2020, Theorem 1.3.8) is in fact equivalent to \A Sigma\B=\mathbf{0} (@exr-qf-singular-independence), so that theorem adds nothing to @thm-qf-indep-quadratic even for singular  Sigma, whereas his Theorem 1.3.9, for general symmetric \A and \B, does. That the independence of  ar{Y} and S^2 characterizes the normal distribution was shown by Lukacs (1942). References - Christensen, Ronald (2020). Plane Answers to Complex Questions: The Theory of Linear Models. 5th edition. Cham: Springer. - Cochran, William G. (1934). The Distribution of Quadratic Forms in a Normal System, with Applications to the Analysis of Covariance. Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 30(2), 178–191. - Craig, Allen T. (1943). Note on the Independence of Certain Quadratic Forms. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 14(2), 195–197. - Driscoll, Michael F. and Gundberg, William R. (1986). A History of the Development of Craig’s Theorem. The American Statistician 40(1), 65–70. - Fisher, Ronald A. (1928). The General Sampling Distribution of the Multiple Correlation Coefficient. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A 121(788), 654–673. - Ghosh, Bhaskar K. (1973). Some Monotonicity Theorems for \chi^2, F and t Distributions with Applications. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 35(3), 480–492. - Gil-Pelaez, J. (1951). Note on the Inversion Theorem. Biometrika 38(3/4), 481–482. - Imhof, Jean-Pierre (1961). Computing the Distribution of Quadratic Forms in Normal Variables. Biometrika 48(3/4), 419–426. - Johnson, Norman L., Kotz, Samuel and Balakrishnan, Narayanaswamy (1995). Continuous Univariate Distributions. 2nd edition. New York: Wiley. - Lukacs, Eugene (1942). A Characterization of the Normal Distribution. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 13(1), 91–93. - Mathai, Arak M. and Provost, Serge B. (1992). Quadratic Forms in Random Variables: Theory and Applications. New York: Marcel Dekker. - Patnaik, P. B. (1949). The Non-Central \chi^2- and F-Distributions and Their Applications. Biometrika 36(1/2), 202–232. - Rencher, Alvin C. and Schaalje, G. Bruce (2008). Linear Models in Statistics. 2nd edition. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. - Satterthwaite, Franklin E. (1946). An Approximate Distribution of Estimates of Variance Components. Biometrics Bulletin 2(6), 110–114. - Searle, Shayle R. (1971). Linear Models. New York: Wiley. - Seber, George A. F. and Lee, Alan J. (2003). Linear Regression Analysis. 2nd edition. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. - von Neumann, John (1941). Distribution of the Ratio of the Mean Square Successive Difference to the Variance. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 12(4), 367–395.

title: The Model, Least Squares and the Normal Equations
content: The Model, Least Squares and the Normal Equations A regression model is a claim about how the distribution of a response changes with a set of regressors, and the linear model is the simplest useful claim of that kind. It says that the mean of the response is a linear combination of known columns, that the errors around this mean have a common variance and are uncorrelated, and nothing more. This chapter sets the model up and draws out what follows from those assumptions alone. It starts with what the assumptions do and do not say, fits a straight line by calculus, and passes to the matrix form of the model, where polynomials, harmonics, indicator variables and interactions all turn out to be linear models. It then derives the least squares estimator and the normal equations, computes the mean and covariance of the estimator, estimates the error variance without bias, and asks what a fitted coefficient means. The last section surveys the models the rest of the book builds on this one. Throughout, the model matrix has full column rank. Chapter 6 retells the same story geometrically and removes that condition. What you need. Chapter 1: rank (@prp-mat-rank-product), inverses, nonnegative definite matrices (@prp-mat-pd-properties), traces (@thm-mat-trace-cyclic) and the derivatives of linear and quadratic forms (@thm-mat-quadform-derivative). Chapter 2: means and covariances of linear transformations (@thm-rv-linear), the mean and variance of a quadratic form (@thm-rv-quadform-mean, @thm-rv-quadform-variance) and the laws of total expectation and covariance (@prp-rv-total-covariance). Normality (Chapter 3) appears only in remarks.
