So the midrange minus \mu is symmetric about zero, and it has mean zero because \lvert\varepsilon_{(1)}+\varepsilon_{(n)}vert\le2\max_i\lvert\varepsilon_ivert is integrable. [C3] Let \E(\Y)=\X beta and \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\V with \V positive definite. Show that an LUE \mathbf{a}\T\Y of  lambda\T beta is a BLUE iff it is uncorrelated with every linear unbiased estimator of zero. Deduce that  lambda\T\hbeta (ordinary least squares) is the BLUE for every estimable  lambda\T beta iff \C(\V\X)\subseteq\C(\X), in agreement with @thm-proj-kruskal. Every LUE is \mathbf{a}\T\Y+ u\T\Y with  u\T\Y an unbiased estimator of zero, and \Var(\mathbf{a}\T\Y+t u\T\Y)=\Var(\mathbf{a}\T\Y)+2t\Cov(\mathbf{a}\T\Y, u\T\Y)+t^2\Var( u\T\Y) for every real t. If \mathbf{a}\T\Y is a BLUE, this quadratic in t is minimized at t=0, which forces the covariance to vanish. Conversely, if every such covariance vanishes, the variance of every competitor is \Var(\mathbf{a}\T\Y)+\Var( u\T\Y)\ge\Var(\mathbf{a}\T\Y). By @exr-opt-unbiased-zero, the unbiased estimators of zero are  w\T(\I-\M)\Y. So ordinary least squares  oldsymbol{\uprho}\T\M\Y is a BLUE for every  oldsymbol{\uprho} iff \sigma^2 oldsymbol{\uprho}\T\M\V(\I-\M) w=0 for all  oldsymbol{\uprho}, w, that is, iff \M\V(\I-\M)=\mathbf{0}. Transposing, this says (\I-\M)\V\M=\mathbf{0}, so every column of \V\M lies in \C(\X). Since \C(\V\M)=\C(\V\X), this is \C(\V\X)\subseteq\C(\X).

title: 7.3 Maximum likelihood under normality
content:
Maximum likelihood under normality The Gauss–Markov theorem needs only two moments. That is its strength, and also the reason it can say nothing about \sigma^2, nothing about nonlinear estimators, and nothing about the distribution of the estimates. From now on we assume more: the errors are normal. The linear model becomes a fully specified family of distributions, \Y\sim\Normal_n(\X beta,\sigma^2\I),\qquad  beta\in\Real^p,\ \sigma^2>0, {#eq-opt-normal-model} the normal linear model of @def-lm-linear-model. The first general-purpose method of estimation in such a family is maximum likelihood. This section shows that it gives back least squares for  beta, and gives a slightly different estimate of \sigma^2. The likelihood By @thm-mvn-density with  Sigma=\sigma^2\I, which is positive definite with \det(\sigma^2\I)=\sigma^{2n}, the density of \Y at the observed \y is L( beta,\sigma^2)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\Bigl\{- rac{
orm{\y-\X beta}^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\}. As a function of the parameters with \y held fixed, this is the likelihood. Its logarithm is \ell( beta,\sigma^2)=- rac n2\log(2\pi)- rac n2\log\sigma^2- rac{
orm{\y-\X beta}^2}{2\sigma^2}. {#eq-opt-loglik} The data enter the log-likelihood only through the sum of squares 
orm{\y-\X beta}^2. That is the first sign that normality and least squares belong together. The Gaussian density penalizes a residual by its square, so the most likely parameter values are those with the smallest squared residuals. One technical point matters. If \y\in\C(\X), the residual sum of squares at the least squares fit is zero, and \ell	o\infty as \sigma^2	o0, so no maximum exists. This happens with probability zero when n>r. The subspace \C(\X) has dimension r<n, so it has Lebesgue measure zero, and \Y has a density. We therefore assume n>r throughout, and 	ext{SSE}>0 for the observed data. The maximum likelihood estimates [Maximum likelihood in the normal linear model] Assume @eq-opt-normal-model with n>r, and let \y be such that 	ext{SSE}=
orm{(\I-\M)\y}^2>0. Then (	ilde{ beta},	ilde{\sigma}^2) maximizes the likelihood iff 	ilde{ beta} is a least squares estimate and 	ilde{\sigma}^2=\hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}= rac{	ext{SSE}}{n}. The maximized log-likelihood is \ell_{\max}=- rac n2 igl\{\log(2\pi\,	ext{SSE}/n)+1 igr\}. The maximum likelihood estimate of \X beta is \M\y, and for estimable  lambda\T beta it is  lambda\T\hbeta. Both are unique. Fix \sigma^2>0. By @eq-opt-loglik, \ell( b,\sigma^2) is a decreasing function of 
orm{\y-\X b}^2. So it is maximized over  b exactly at the least squares estimates, and there 
orm{\y-\X b}^2=	ext{SSE} (@thm-proj-ls-projection). This gives  egin{aligned} \ell( b,\sigma^2)&\le\ell(\hbeta,\sigma^2)=g(\sigma^2)\ &:=- rac n2\log(2\pi)- rac n2\log\sigma^2- rac{	ext{SSE}}{2\sigma^2}, \end{aligned} with equality iff  b is a least squares estimate. Now put v_0=	ext{SSE}/n and u=v_0/\sigma^2>0. Then 	ext{SSE}/(2\sigma^2)=nu/2 and \log\sigma^2=\log v_0-\log u, so g(v_0)-g(\sigma^2)= rac n2 igl(u-1-\log u igr)\ge0, because \log u\le u-1 for all u>0, with equality only at u=1. Hence \ell( b,\sigma^2)\le g(\sigma^2)\le g(v_0), with equality throughout iff  b is a least squares estimate and \sigma^2=v_0. The value g(v_0) is the stated maximum. The least squares estimates all give the fitted vector \M\y (@thm-proj-ls-projection), and all give the same value of  lambda\T\hbeta for  lambda\in\C(\X\T) (@thm-proj-invariant-functions). The proof finds a global maximum without solving any equations. Calculus gives the same answer and is the usual route in a first course: set the gradient \partial\ell/\partial beta=\X\T(\y-\X beta)/\sigma^2 to zero, which gives the normal equations, and \partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2=-n/(2\sigma^2)+
orm{\y-\X beta}^2/(2\sigma^4) to zero. But the stationarity argument still has to be completed by showing that the stationary point is a maximum (@exr-opt-mle-calculus). The inequality \log u\le u-1 handles existence, maximality and uniqueness together. When \X is rank deficient, the likelihood is constant along the affine set of least squares estimates \hbeta+\Null(\X), so the MLE of  beta is not unique. This is a general fact about nonidentified parameters. If \X beta_1=\X beta_2, the two parameter values give the same distribution of \Y and hence the same likelihood for every data set. Maximum likelihood cannot separate what the model itself does not separate. What it does determine uniquely, \X beta and the estimable functions, is exactly what least squares determines uniquely. [Stack loss] Brownlee’s stack loss data record n=21 days of operation of a plant that oxidizes ammonia to nitric acid. The response is the percentage of ammonia lost (times ten). The regressors are air flow, the temperature of the cooling water, and the acid concentration. With an intercept, p=4, and least squares gives \hbeta=(-39.9197,\ 0.7156,\ 1.2953,\ {-}0.1521)\T,\qquad 	ext{SSE}=178.830 . By @thm-opt-mle these are also the maximum likelihood estimates of  beta. The MLE of \sigma^2 is 178.830/21=8.516, while the unbiased estimate is s^2=178.830/17=10.519. The maximized log-likelihood is -52.288. A general-purpose numerical optimizer, started far from the answer and knowing nothing about least squares, arrives at the same point. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy import optimize, stats data = sm.datasets.stackloss.load_pandas().data y = data["STACKLOSS"].to_numpy() X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), data[["AIRFLOW", "WATERTEMP", "ACIDCONC"]]]) n, p = X.shape beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None) sse = np.sum((y - X @ beta_hat) ** 2) sigma2_mle, s2 = sse / n, sse / (n - p) loglik_max = -n / 2 * (np.log(2 * np.pi * sigma2_mle) + 1) print("beta_hat ", np.round(beta_hat, 4)) print(f"SSE = {sse:.3f} MLE of sigma^2 = {sigma2_mle:.3f} s^2 = {s2:.3f}") print(f"maximized log-likelihood = {loglik_max:.3f}") def negloglik(theta): """Minus the normal log-likelihood; theta = (beta, log sigma^2).""" b, log_s2 = theta[:p], theta[p] r = y - X @ b return n / 2 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + log_s2) + r @ r / (2 * np.exp(log_s2)) start = np.r_[np.zeros(p), np.log(np.var(y))] opt = optimize.minimize(negloglik, start, method="BFGS", options={"gtol": 1e-8}) print("numerical MLE of beta ", np.round(opt.x[:p], 4)) print("numerical MLE sigma^2 ", round(float(np.exp(opt.x[p])), 3)) The bias of the variance estimate Unlike least squares for  beta, the MLE of \sigma^2 is biased. Since \E(	ext{SSE})=\sigma^2(n-r) (@thm-lm-sigma2 in full rank, and Section 6.4 in general), \E\hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}= rac{n-r}{n}\,\sigma^2 . The bias is downward, by the fraction r/n. The residual vector lives in the (n-r)-dimensional space \C(\X)\perpc, and the MLE divides its squared length by n as if it had n dimensions. The r dimensions spent on fitting the mean are the dimensions in which the fit has pulled the data toward itself. With a few regressors and many observations the bias is negligible. It is not negligible when the number of parameters grows with the sample size. [Many means, one variance] Suppose m laboratories each make two measurements, Y_{i1},Y_{i2}\iid\Normal(\mu_i,\sigma^2), with a different \mu_i for each laboratory and a common measurement variance. This is a linear model with n=2m and r=m, one indicator column per laboratory. The fitted value for each pair is its mean, and  egin{aligned} \hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}&= rac{1}{2m}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^2(Y_{ij}- ar{Y}_{i\cdot})^2 = rac1{4m}\sum_{i=1}^m(Y_{i1}-Y_{i2})^2,\ \E\hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}&= rac{\sigma^2}{2}. \end{aligned} The bias does not disappear as m	o\infty. By the law of large numbers, \hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}	o\sigma^2/2 with probability one, so the MLE is inconsistent. The unbiased s^2=	ext{SSE}/(n-r) is exactly twice as large and is consistent. This is the example of Neyman and Scott (1948). It shows that the good large-sample behaviour of maximum likelihood can fail when the number of nuisance parameters grows with the data. Restricted maximum likelihood, which removes the mean before estimating the variance (@exr-opt-reml), repairs it, and Chapter 32 builds variance-component estimation on that idea (@def-mix-reml). Unbiasedness is not the only possible criterion for choosing a divisor. Under normality we can compare estimators of the form 	ext{SSE}/d by mean squared error. [The best multiple of SSE] Assume @eq-opt-normal-model with k=n-r\ge1. Among estimators 	ext{SSE}/d with d>0,  rac{\E igl(	ext{SSE}/d-\sigma^2 igr)^2}{\sigma^4}= rac{2k}{d^2}+\Bigl( rac kd-1\Bigr)^2, which is minimized at d=k+2, with minimum value 2/(k+2). The unbiased choice d=k gives 2/k, and the maximum likelihood choice d=n gives (2k+r^2)/n^2. Write 	ext{SSE}=\Y\T(\I-\M)\Y. By @thm-qf-mean-var with \A=\I-\M,  Sigma=\sigma^2\I and  mu=\X beta, for which \A mu= zero, \E(	ext{SSE})=\sigma^2	r(\I-\M)=\sigma^2k,\qquad \Var(	ext{SSE})=2\sigma^4	r igl((\I-\M)^2 igr)=2\sigma^4k . The mean squared error is variance plus squared bias: 2\sigma^4k/d^2+(k/d-1)^2\sigma^4. As a function of t=1/d, this is \sigma^4\{(2k+k^2)t^2-2kt+1\}, a convex quadratic minimized at t=k/(2k+k^2)=1/(k+2). Substituting d=k+2, k and n=k+r gives the three values. For the last, 2k/n^2+(k-n)^2/n^2=(2k+r^2)/n^2. For the stack loss data, k=17, and the three relative mean squared errors are 0.1176 for s^2, 0.1134 for the MLE and 0.1053 for 	ext{SSE}/(k+2). The unbiased estimator is the worst of the three by this criterion. Comparing (2k+r^2)/n^2 with 2/k shows that the MLE beats s^2 iff (r-4)k<2r. So it always does when r\le4, and it loses once many parameters are fitted relative to the residual degrees of freedom, as in @exm-opt-neyman-scott. In practice s^2 is used anyway, because it is what makes the t and F statistics of Section 7.5 exact. The choice of divisor matters for point estimation of \sigma^2 and for nothing else. Any fixed multiple of SSE leads to the same tests and intervals once the matching distribution is used. Profile likelihood In most problems only some parameters are of interest. The others, called nuisance parameters, still appear in the likelihood. A simple and general way to eliminate them is to maximize them out. Profile likelihood Let the parameter be  oldsymbol{\uptheta}=(\psi, oldsymbol{\upeta}), where \psi is of interest and  oldsymbol{\upeta} is a nuisance parameter. The profile log-likelihood of \psi is \ell_p(\psi)=\sup_{ oldsymbol{\upeta}}\ell(\psi, oldsymbol{\upeta}). The profile log-likelihood is maximized at the MLE of \psi, with maximum \ell_{\max}. The drop \ell_{\max}-\ell_p(\psi) measures how much less plausible the value \psi is than the best value. In the linear model the profiles have closed forms. The proof of @thm-opt-mle computed two of them. With \sigma^2 as nuisance, the profile of  beta is \ell_p( beta)=- rac n2\Bigl\{\log\Bigl( rac{2\pi
orm{\y-\X beta}^2}{n}\Bigr)+1\Bigr\}, a decreasing function of 
orm{\y-\X beta}^2. Its level sets are the level sets of the residual sum of squares. When \X has full rank they are ellipsoids centred at \hbeta, and they are the basis of the confidence ellipsoids of Chapter 12 (@thm-ci-ellipsoid). With  beta as nuisance, the profile of \sigma^2 is the function g in the proof. The most useful case is a single estimable function. Here the profile likelihood turns out to be a function of the familiar t statistic. [Profile likelihood of an estimable function] Assume @eq-opt-normal-model with n>r, and let  lambda\in\C(\X\T),  lambda
e zero. For \psi\in\Real, put t(\psi)= rac{ lambda\T\hbeta-\psi}{s\sqrt{ lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda}},\qquad s^2= rac{	ext{SSE}}{n-r}. Then the smallest residual sum of squares subject to  lambda\T beta=\psi is 	ext{SSE}(\psi)=	ext{SSE}+ rac{( lambda\T\hbeta-\psi)^2}{ lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda}, {#eq-opt-constrained-sse} and the profile log-likelihood of \psi= lambda\T beta, with ( beta,\sigma^2) otherwise free, satisfies 2\{\ell_{\max}-\ell_p(\psi)\}=n\log\Bigl(1+ rac{t(\psi)^2}{n-r}\Bigr). {#eq-opt-profile-t} Write  lambda=\X\T oldsymbol{\uprho} and \mathbf{c}=\M oldsymbol{\uprho}. Then \mathbf{c}
e zero, since \X\T\mathbf{c}=\X\T oldsymbol{\uprho}= lambda
e zero, and 
orm{\mathbf{c}}^2= lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda as in the proof of @thm-opt-gauss-markov(a). For any  b, @eq-proj-distance-split gives 
orm{\y-\X b}^2=	ext{SSE}+
orm{\X\hbeta-\X b}^2. Put  u=\X(\hbeta- b)\in\C(\X). The constraint  lambda\T b=\psi reads  oldsymbol{\uprho}\T\X(\hbeta- b)= lambda\T\hbeta-\psi=:\delta, that is,  oldsymbol{\uprho}\T u=\delta. Since  u\in\C(\X),  oldsymbol{\uprho}\T u= oldsymbol{\uprho}\T\M u=\mathbf{c}\T u. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, \lvert\deltavert=\lvert\mathbf{c}\T uvert\le
orm{\mathbf{c}}
orm{ u}, so 
orm{ u}^2\ge\delta^2/
orm{\mathbf{c}}^2. Equality holds for  u=\delta\mathbf{c}/
orm{\mathbf{c}}^2, which lies in \C(\X) and so equals \X(\hbeta- b) for some  b. That  b satisfies the constraint. This proves @eq-opt-constrained-sse. Maximizing over \sigma^2 as in the proof of @thm-opt-mle, with SSE replaced by 	ext{SSE}(\psi), gives \ell_p(\psi)=- rac n2\{\log(2\pi\,	ext{SSE}(\psi)/n)+1\}. Hence  egin{aligned} 2\{\ell_{\max}-\ell_p(\psi)\}&=n\log rac{	ext{SSE}(\psi)}{	ext{SSE}} =n\log\Bigl(1+ rac{\delta^2}{
orm{\mathbf{c}}^2\,	ext{SSE}}\Bigr)\ &=n\log\Bigl(1+ rac{t(\psi)^2}{n-r}\Bigr), \end{aligned} since \delta^2/(
orm{\mathbf{c}}^2\,	ext{SSE})=t(\psi)^2/(n-r). Two consequences show up immediately. First, any procedure based on the profile likelihood of  lambda\T beta is a procedure based on \lvert tvert, because @eq-opt-profile-t is increasing in t^2. The likelihood ratio test of  lambda\T beta=\psi_0 is therefore the t test, a fact Chapter 11 extends to general hypotheses (@thm-glh-lrt). Second, the large-sample calibration of the likelihood ratio, “reject when 2\{\ell_{\max}-\ell_p\} exceeds a \chi^2(1) quantile”, is only approximate. The exact calibration uses the t(n-r) distribution of Section 7.5. [Profile likelihood for the air-flow coefficient] For the stack loss model, Figure 7.3.1 plots \ell_p( eta_1)-\ell_{\max} for the air-flow coefficient  eta_1, computed by refitting the model with  eta_1 fixed on a grid. The listing confirms @eq-opt-profile-t to rounding error. The standard error of \hat{ eta}_1 is 0.1349. The set of  eta_1 with 2\{\ell_{\max}-\ell_p\}\le3.841, the 95\% point of \chi^2(1), is the likelihood interval (0.467,\ 0.965). By @eq-opt-profile-t it consists of the values with \lvert tvert\le1.847. The exact 95\% interval uses the t(17) quantile 2.110 instead, and is (0.431,\ 1.000). With only 17 residual degrees of freedom, the \chi^2 calibration makes the interval about 12\% too short. def profile_loglik(b1): """Profile log-likelihood of the air-flow coefficient: maximize over everything else.""" others = np.delete(X, 1, axis=1) z = y - b1 * X[:, 1] # move the fixed term to the left side coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(others, z, rcond=None) sse_b = np.sum((z - others @ coef) ** 2) # SSE(b1): smallest SSE with beta_1 = b1 return -n / 2 * (np.log(2 * np.pi * sse_b / n) + 1) se1 = np.sqrt(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)[1, 1]) grid = np.linspace(beta_hat[1] - 4 * se1, beta_hat[1] + 4 * se1, 201) lp = np.array([profile_loglik(b) for b in grid]) t = (beta_hat[1] - grid) / se1 print("max |2(l_max - l_p) - n log(1 + t^2/(n-p))| =", np.abs(2 * (loglik_max - lp) - n * np.log1p(t ** 2 / (n - p))).max()) [Figure 7.3.1. Profile log-likelihood of the air-flow coefficient in the stack loss regression, relative to its maximum. The ticks on the dashed cutoff line mark the \chi^2-calibrated likelihood interval, and the bar below it marks the exact 95\% t interval, which is wider.] Figure 7.3.1. Profile log-likelihood of the air-flow coefficient in the stack loss regression, relative to its maximum. The ticks on the dashed cutoff line mark the \chi^2-calibrated likelihood interval, and the bar below it marks the exact 95\% t interval, which is wider. [Profile log-likelihood of the air-flow coefficient in the stack loss regression, relative to its maximum. The ticks on the dashed cutoff line mark the \chi^2-calibrated likelihood interval, and the bar below it marks the exact 95\% t interval, which is wider.] Profile log-likelihood of the air-flow coefficient in the stack loss regression, relative to its maximum. The ticks on the dashed cutoff line mark the \chi^2-calibrated likelihood interval, and the bar below it marks the exact 95\% t interval, which is wider. [Other error distributions] The agreement between maximum likelihood and least squares is special to normal errors. If the errors have the Laplace density (2	au)^{-1}e^{-\lvert\varepsilonvert/	au}, the log-likelihood is -n\log(2	au)-\sum_i\lvert y_i-\x_{(i)}\T betavert/	au, and maximum likelihood minimizes the sum of absolute residuals; @exr-opt-laplace-mle works out the location case. For errors with a t distribution it downweights large residuals. For each error distribution the likelihood picks its own loss function. Least squares is the one that goes with the Gaussian. Section 20.6 uses robust fitting as a diagnostic, and Chapter 45 treats median and quantile regression. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] For Y_1,\dot{s},Y_n\iid\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2), write the model in the form @eq-opt-normal-model and read off the MLEs from @thm-opt-mle. Show that \hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}=(n-1)s^2/n, where s^2 is the sample variance. [A2] Let \C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X) with residual sums of squares 	ext{SSE}_0\ge	ext{SSE}. Show that the ratio of maximized likelihoods is L_{0,\max}/L_{\max}=(	ext{SSE}/	ext{SSE}_0)^{n/2}, and write it as a decreasing function of (	ext{SSE}_0-	ext{SSE})/	ext{SSE}. By @thm-opt-mle, L_{\max}=(2\pi\,	ext{SSE}/n)^{-n/2}e^{-n/2}, and similarly for the smaller model. The ratio is (	ext{SSE}_0/	ext{SSE})^{-n/2}=\{1+(	ext{SSE}_0-	ext{SSE})/	ext{SSE}\}^{-n/2}, which decreases in (	ext{SSE}_0-	ext{SSE})/	ext{SSE}. That quantity is, up to degrees of freedom, the F statistic of @thm-qf-nested-f. So the likelihood ratio test for nested normal linear models is the F test. Chapter 11 develops this (@thm-glh-lrt). B. Practice [B1] Assume ank(\X)=p. Compute the gradient and the Hessian of \ell( beta,\sigma^2), show that the only stationary point is (\hbeta,	ext{SSE}/n), and show that the Hessian there is negative definite. Why does this not by itself prove that the stationary point is a global maximum? What additional argument completes the proof? [B2] In @exm-opt-neyman-scott, verify the identity \sum_j(Y_{ij}- ar{Y}_{i\cdot})^2=(Y_{i1}-Y_{i2})^2/2, compute \E\hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}} and \Var\hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}, and prove that \hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}	o\sigma^2/2 in probability as m	o\infty. Y_{i1}- ar{Y}_{i\cdot}=(Y_{i1}-Y_{i2})/2=-(Y_{i2}- ar{Y}_{i\cdot}), so the sum of squares is 2\cdot(Y_{i1}-Y_{i2})^2/4. Now D_i=Y_{i1}-Y_{i2}\sim\Normal(0,2\sigma^2) independently, so D_i^2/(2\sigma^2)\sim\chi^2(1), with mean 1 and variance 2. Hence \hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}= rac1{4m}\sum_iD_i^2 has mean 2\sigma^2/4=\sigma^2/2 and variance m\cdot4\sigma^4\cdot2/(16m^2)=\sigma^4/(2m). The variance tends to zero, so by Chebyshev’s inequality \hat{\sigma}^2_{	ext{ML}}	o\sigma^2/2 in probability. [B3] Suppose \Y\sim\Normal_n(\X beta,\sigma^2\V) with \V known and positive definite and \X of full rank. Find the MLEs of  beta and \sigma^2. C. Going deeper [C1] In the location model Y_i=\mu+\varepsilon_i, i=1,\dot{s},n, let the errors be independent with the Laplace density (2	au)^{-1}e^{-\lvert\varepsilonvert/	au}, so \Var(\varepsilon_i)=2	au^2. 1. Show that every sample median maximizes the likelihood in \mu, whatever 	au is, and that the MLE of 	au is the mean absolute deviation n^{-1}\sum_i\lvert Y_i-	ilde{\mu}vert about a median 	ilde{\mu}. 2. The sample median of n observations from a density f that is positive and continuous at its median \mu has asymptotic variance 1/\{4nf(\mu)^2\}. Compute this for the Laplace density and compare it with \Var( ar{Y}). Which is larger, and by what factor? 3.  ar{Y} is the BLUE of \mu (@cor-opt-gm-consequences). Explain why (b) does not contradict @thm-opt-gauss-markov, and contrast the answer with @exm-opt-midrange, where the winning nonlinear estimator used the extremes rather than the middle of the sample. (a) The log-likelihood is -n\log(2	au)-	au^{-1}\sum_i\lvert Y_i-\muvert. For fixed 	au it is maximized by minimizing g(\mu)=\sum_i\lvert Y_i-\muvert. The function g is convex and piecewise linear, with slope \#\{i:Y_i<\mu\}-\#\{i:Y_i>\mu\} between data points. The slope is \le0 to the left of every median and \ge0 to the right, so the minimizers are exactly the sample medians. Substituting 	ilde{\mu} and maximizing -n\log	au-g(	ilde{\mu})/	au over 	au>0 gives \hat{	au}=g(	ilde{\mu})/n. (b) f(\mu)=1/(2	au), so the median has asymptotic variance 	au^2/n, while \Var( ar{Y})=2	au^2/n. The mean has twice the variance of the median. (c) The median is not a linear function of \Y: its weights depend on the ordering of the sample. The Gauss–Markov theorem compares  ar{Y} only with linear unbiased estimators. With Laplace errors, which have heavier tails than the normal, the extremes are unreliable and the median gains by ignoring them; with uniform errors the extremes are the most informative observations and the midrange gains by using only them. [C2] Let \Q_2 be an n	imes(n-r) matrix whose columns are an orthonormal basis of \C(\X)\perpc, and let \Z=\Q_2\T\Y (“error contrasts”). Show that \Z\sim\Normal_{n-r}( zero,\sigma^2\I), whatever  beta is, and that 
orm{\Z}^2=	ext{SSE}. Show that the MLE of \sigma^2 based on \Z alone is 	ext{SSE}/(n-r). This is restricted (or residual) maximum likelihood. \Q_2\T\X=\mathbf{0}, so \Z=\Q_2\T e\sim\Normal_{n-r}( zero,\sigma^2\Q_2\T\Q_2)=\Normal_{n-r}( zero,\sigma^2\I) by @thm-mvn-linear. Also \Q_2\Q_2\T=\I-\M (@prp-proj-orthonormal-formula), so 
orm{\Z}^2=\Y\T\Q_2\Q_2\T\Y=\Y\T(\I-\M)\Y=	ext{SSE}. The log-likelihood of \Z is - rac{n-r}2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-
orm{\Z}^2/(2\sigma^2), which is the function g of the proof of @thm-opt-mle with n replaced by n-r. It is maximized at 
orm{\Z}^2/(n-r)=	ext{SSE}/(n-r). In @exm-opt-neyman-scott this gives s^2, which is consistent.

title: 7.4 Sufficiency, completeness and minimum variance
content:
Sufficiency, completeness and minimum variance The Gauss–Markov theorem compares least squares only with linear unbiased estimators, and @exm-opt-midrange showed that the restriction matters: with uniform errors a nonlinear estimator wins easily. This section shows that under normality the restriction can be dropped. In the normal linear model,  lambda\T\hbeta has the smallest variance among all unbiased estimators of an estimable  lambda\T beta, and s^2 has the smallest variance among all unbiased estimators of \sigma^2. The argument is the classical one through sufficiency and completeness. It also produces best unbiased estimators of nonlinear functions, such as \sigma itself. At the end we compare the variances with the Cramér–Rao lower bound, which least squares attains for  beta and s^2 does not attain for \sigma^2. Two facts from mathematical statistics are quoted without proof: the factorization criterion for sufficiency and the completeness of full-rank exponential families. Both are proved in standard texts such as Lehmann and Casella (1998) and Lehmann and Romano (2005). Everything built on them is proved here. Sufficiency [Sufficient and complete statistics] Let \Y have a distribution P_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}} from a family indexed by  oldsymbol{\uptheta}\in\Theta, and let  T= T(\Y) be a statistic. 1.  T is sufficient for  oldsymbol{\uptheta} if the conditional law of \Y given  T is the same for every  oldsymbol{\uptheta}. 2.  T is complete if, for every function h with \E_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\lvert h( T)vert<\infty and \E_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}h( T)=0 for all  oldsymbol{\uptheta}\in\Theta, we have \Pr_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\{h( T)=0\}=1 for all  oldsymbol{\uptheta}. A sufficient statistic carries all the information about  oldsymbol{\uptheta} in the data. Once  T is known, the rest of \Y is noise whose distribution does not involve the parameter. Completeness says that  T carries no redundant information either: no nontrivial function of  T has expectation zero for every parameter value. Equivalently, an unbiased estimator that is a function of  T is unique. [Factorization criterion] Suppose \Y has a density f_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\y) on \Real^n. Then  T(\Y) is sufficient iff there are functions g_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}} and h, with h not depending on  oldsymbol{\uptheta}, such that f_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\y)=g_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}( T(\y))\,h(\y) for all \y and  oldsymbol{\uptheta}. [Completeness in exponential families] Suppose \Y has a density of the form f_{ oldsymbol{\upeta}}(\y)=c( oldsymbol{\upeta})\,h(\y)\exp\{ oldsymbol{\upeta}\T T(\y)\},\qquad  oldsymbol{\upeta}\in\mathcal E\subseteq\Real^k, with  T(\y)\in\Real^k. If \mathcal E contains a nonempty open subset of \Real^k, then  T(\Y) is complete and sufficient. Sufficiency follows from @lem-opt-factorization with g_{ oldsymbol{\upeta}}( T)=c( oldsymbol{\upeta})e^{ oldsymbol{\upeta}\T T}. Completeness rests on the uniqueness of Laplace transforms: \E_{ oldsymbol{\upeta}}h( T)=0 on an open set of  oldsymbol{\upeta} forces a certain two-sided Laplace transform to vanish on an open set, and hence h( T)=0 almost surely. For the normal linear model, expand the exponent of the density: 
orm{\y-\X beta}^2=\y\T\y-2 beta\T\X\T\y+ beta\T\X\T\X beta . So the density of @eq-opt-normal-model is f(\y)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\Bigl\{- rac{ beta\T\X\T\X beta}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\} \exp\Bigl\{ rac{ beta\T\X\T\y}{\sigma^2}- rac{\y\T\y}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\}, {#eq-opt-expfam} and the data enter only through \X\T\y and \y\T\y. [A complete sufficient statistic] In the normal linear model @eq-opt-normal-model, let \Q be an n	imes r matrix whose columns are an orthonormal basis of \C(\X). Then  T=(\Q\T\Y,\ \Y\T\Y) is complete and sufficient for ( beta,\sigma^2). The statistics (\X\T\Y,\Y\T\Y) and (\M\Y,	ext{SSE}) are one-to-one functions of  T, so they are complete and sufficient too. Since \X beta\in\C(\X), \X beta=\Q gamma with  gamma=\Q\T\X beta\in\Real^r, and  beta\T\X\T\y= gamma\T\Q\T\y. By @eq-opt-expfam the density has the form of @lem-opt-exponential-family with k=r+1,  T(\y)=(\Q\T\y,\ \y\T\y),\qquad  oldsymbol{\upeta}= igl( gamma/\sigma^2,\ {-}1/(2\sigma^2) igr). As  beta ranges over \Real^p,  gamma=\Q\T\X beta ranges over all of \Real^r: the r	imes p matrix \Q\T\X has rank r, because \Q\Q\T\X=\M\X=\X has rank r. Hence \mathcal E=\Real^r	imes(-\infty,0), which is open, and @lem-opt-exponential-family applies. For the equivalent statistics: \M\Y=\Q\Q\T\Y (@prp-proj-orthonormal-formula) and 	ext{SSE}=\Y\T\Y-
orm{\Q\T\Y}^2 are functions of  T, and conversely \Q\T\Y=\Q\T\M\Y and \Y\T\Y=	ext{SSE}+
orm{\M\Y}^2. Also \X\T\Y=\X\T\Q(\Q\T\Y), and \Q=\X\mathbf{K} for some \mathbf{K}, since the columns of \Q lie in \C(\X), so \Q\T\Y=\mathbf{K}\T\X\T\Y. A one-to-one function of a complete sufficient statistic is again complete and sufficient, since both definitions refer only to the information (the \sigma-field) the statistic generates. The reduction is dramatic. An n-dimensional data vector is replaced by r+1 numbers: the fitted values (equivalently, the least squares estimates of the estimable functions) and the residual sum of squares. Under normality the residual vector, apart from its length, carries no information about the parameters. Its direction is uniformly distributed over the unit sphere of \C(\X)\perpc whatever ( beta,\sigma^2) is (@exr-opt-residual-direction). This is the precise sense in which the residuals are “just noise”, and it is also why they are useful for checking the model. Their pattern can reveal departures from normality precisely because, under normality, it has a known and parameter-free distribution. Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé [Rao–Blackwell] Let  T be sufficient for  oldsymbol{\uptheta}, and let \delta(\Y) be an unbiased estimator of g( oldsymbol{\uptheta}) with \Var_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\delta<\infty for all  oldsymbol{\uptheta}. Then \delta^*=\E(\delta\mid T) is a statistic, it is unbiased for g( oldsymbol{\uptheta}), and  egin{aligned} \Var_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\delta)&=\Var_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\delta^*)+\E_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}} igl[(\delta-\delta^*)^2 igr]\ &\ge\Var_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\delta^*) \end{aligned} for every  oldsymbol{\uptheta}, with equality iff \delta=\delta^* with probability one. The law of \Y given  T does not depend on  oldsymbol{\uptheta}, so neither does \E(\delta(\Y)\mid T). It is therefore computable from the data, which makes it a statistic. By the law of total expectation (@prp-rv-total-covariance), \E\delta^*=\E\delta=g( oldsymbol{\uptheta}). By the law of total variance in the same result, \Var\delta=\E\{\Var(\delta\mid T)\}+\Var(\delta^*), and \E\{\Var(\delta\mid T)\}=\E\{\E[(\delta-\delta^*)^2\mid T]\}=\E(\delta-\delta^*)^2. This last term is zero iff \delta=\delta^* almost surely. Conditioning on a sufficient statistic averages out the part of an estimator that responds to parameter-free noise. It never hurts, and it helps unless the estimator was already a function of  T. [Lehmann–Scheffé] Let  T be complete and sufficient for  oldsymbol{\uptheta}. If \phi( T) is unbiased for g( oldsymbol{\uptheta}) and has finite variance, then \phi( T) is a uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE) of g( oldsymbol{\uptheta}): \Var_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\phi( T)\le\Var_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\delta for every unbiased \delta and every  oldsymbol{\uptheta}. It is the only unbiased function of  T and, up to sets of probability zero, the only UMVUE. If \phi_1( T) and \phi_2( T) are both unbiased, then \E_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\{\phi_1( T)-\phi_2( T)\}=0 for all  oldsymbol{\uptheta}, so \phi_1( T)=\phi_2( T) almost surely by completeness. Now let \delta be any unbiased estimator with finite variance. By @thm-opt-rao-blackwell, \E(\delta\mid T) is an unbiased function of  T, so it equals \phi( T) almost surely, and \Var\phi( T)\le\Var\delta, with equality iff \delta=\phi( T) almost surely. (If \delta has infinite variance there is nothing to prove.) Best unbiased estimators in the normal linear model [Minimum variance unbiased estimation] Assume the normal linear model @eq-opt-normal-model with n>r, and let s^2=	ext{SSE}/(n-r). 1. For every  lambda\in\C(\X\T),  lambda\T\hbeta is the UMVUE of  lambda\T beta. 2. s^2 is the UMVUE of \sigma^2. 3. More generally, every estimator of the form \phi(\M\Y,	ext{SSE}) with finite variance is the UMVUE of its expectation. In particular, for k=n-r, b_k=\sqrt{ rac2k}\, rac{\Gamma igl( rac{k+1}2 igr)}{\Gamma igl( rac k2 igr)}, s/b_k is the UMVUE of \sigma, and \x_0\T\hbeta+z\,s/b_k is the UMVUE of \x_0\T beta+z\sigma for every constant z and every \x_0\in\C(\X\T). By @prp-opt-complete-sufficient, (\M\Y,	ext{SSE}) is complete and sufficient, so by @thm-opt-lehmann-scheffe it suffices to show that each estimator is an unbiased function of it with finite variance. (a) Write  lambda=\X\T oldsymbol{\uprho}. Then  lambda\T\hbeta= oldsymbol{\uprho}\T\M\Y is a function of \M\Y, it is unbiased by @thm-opt-gauss-markov(a), and its variance is finite. (b) s^2 is a function of SSE, it is unbiased because \E(	ext{SSE})=\sigma^2(n-r) (@thm-rv-quadform-mean), and it has finite variance. (c) The first statement is @thm-opt-lehmann-scheffe again. For \sigma, note that 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2=\Y\T(\I-\M)\Y/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(k) by @thm-qf-chisq(a), since \I-\M is a projection of rank k and (\I-\M)\X beta= zero. If W\sim\chi^2(k), with density w^{k/2-1}e^{-w/2}/\{2^{k/2}\Gamma(k/2)\}, then  egin{aligned} \E\sqrt W&= rac{1}{2^{k/2}\Gamma(k/2)}\int_0^\infty w^{(k+1)/2-1}e^{-w/2}\,dw\ &= rac{2^{(k+1)/2}\Gamma igl( rac{k+1}2 igr)}{2^{k/2}\Gamma igl( rac k2 igr)} =\sqrt2\, rac{\Gamma igl( rac{k+1}2 igr)}{\Gamma igl( rac k2 igr)} . \end{aligned} Hence \E s=\sigma\,\E\sqrt{W/k}=b_k\sigma, and s/b_k is unbiased for \sigma, with variance at most \E s^2/b_k^2<\infty. The last estimator is a sum of two unbiased functions of (\M\Y,	ext{SSE}). Part (a) is the promised strengthening of Gauss–Markov. Under normality no unbiased estimator of  lambda\T beta, linear or not, beats least squares. The midrange of @exm-opt-midrange cannot help when the errors are normal. Part (c) shows the method at work beyond linear estimators. The obvious estimate s of \sigma is biased, because \E s<\sqrt{\E s^2} by Jensen’s inequality, and dividing by b_k removes the bias. [Estimating \sigma without bias] The constant b_k=\E(s)/\sigma depends only on the residual degrees of freedom. For the stack loss regression, k=17 and b_{17}=0.9854, so the UMVUE of \sigma is s/b_{17}=1.0148\,s. The correction is 1.5\% here. It is large for very small k, with b_2=0.8862, and negligible for large k, with b_{200}=0.9988. import numpy as np from scipy import special def mean_s_factor(k): """b_k = E(s)/sigma when k s^2 / sigma^2 ~ chi^2(k).""" return np.sqrt(2 / k) * np.exp(special.gammaln((k + 1) / 2) - special.gammaln(k / 2)) for k in [2, 5, 10, 17, 50, 200]: b = mean_s_factor(k) print(f"k = {k:3d} E(s)/sigma = {b:.4f} UMVUE of sigma = s / {b:.4f}") Rao–Blackwellization by reflection The Rao–Blackwell theorem is not only a device for proofs. In the normal linear model we can carry out the conditioning explicitly, and it takes every linear unbiased estimator to least squares. [Conditioning on the sufficient statistic] Let \mathbf{a}\T\Y be any LUE of an estimable  lambda\T beta, such as the end-point slope of @exm-opt-three-slopes. Let \R=2\M-\I, the reflection that fixes \C(\X) and reverses \C(\X)\perpc. It is symmetric and orthogonal (\R^2=\I) and \R\X=\X. Consequently: - \R\Y\sim\Normal_n(\R\X beta,\sigma^2\R\R\T)=\Normal_n(\X beta,\sigma^2\I) by @thm-mvn-linear, so \R\Y has the same distribution as \Y; - the sufficient statistic is unchanged: \X\T\R\Y=\X\T\Y and 
orm{\R\Y}=
orm{\Y}. So the pairs (\mathbf{a}\T\Y, T(\Y)) and (\mathbf{a}\T\R\Y, T(\Y)) have the same joint distribution, where  T=(\X\T\Y,\Y\T\Y). Hence \E(\mathbf{a}\T\Y\mid T)=\E(\mathbf{a}\T\R\Y\mid T), and averaging, \E(\mathbf{a}\T\Y\mid T)=\E\Bigl(\mathbf{a}\T rac{\Y+\R\Y}2\,\Big|\, T\Bigr)=\E(\mathbf{a}\T\M\Y\mid T)=\mathbf{a}\T\M\Y= lambda\T\hbeta , because \mathbf{a}\T\M\Y is a function of  T and \M\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{a}_* (@prp-opt-lue-set). The Rao–Blackwell improvement of every LUE is the least squares estimate. The listing checks the identity 	frac12(\mathbf{a}\T\y+\mathbf{a}\T\R\y)= lambda\T\hbeta for simulated data and the end-point slope. import numpy as np x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.5, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0, 10.5, 12.0]) n = len(x) X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x]) M = X @ np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T) R = 2 * M - np.eye(n) # reflection: keeps C(X), flips C(X)-perp rng = np.random.default_rng(71) y = X @ np.array([2.0, 0.5]) + rng.normal(size=n) y_ref = R @ y print("X^T y unchanged:", np.allclose(X.T @ y_ref, X.T @ y)) print("y^T y unchanged:", np.isclose(y_ref @ y_ref, y @ y)) a_end = np.zeros(n) a_end[[0, -1]] = [-1.0, 1.0] a_end /= x[-1] - x[0] # the end-point slope estimator a_ls = X @ np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, [0.0, 1.0]) print("average of a^T y over the two points:", (a_end @ y + a_end @ y_ref) / 2) print("least squares slope: ", a_ls @ y) The reflection argument uses the normal distribution only through its invariance under orthogonal maps that fix the mean. It makes concrete what “the residuals are noise” means. Reversing the residual vector changes neither the likelihood nor the sufficient statistic, so an estimator should not depend on the residuals’ direction. An LUE that uses the residuals is replaced by the average of its value at \y and at the reflected data, and that average no longer involves the residuals. The Cramér–Rao bound A different route to optimality bounds the variance of every unbiased estimator from below and checks whether the bound is attained. We state the bound for the full-rank normal linear model, where every ingredient can be computed. Write  oldsymbol{\uptheta}=( beta\T,v)\T with v=\sigma^2. The score is the gradient of the log-likelihood @eq-opt-loglik, evaluated at the random \Y: \mathbf{S}= egin{pmatrix}\partial\ell/\partial beta\ \partial\ell/\partial v\end{pmatrix} = egin{pmatrix}\X\T e/v\[2pt] -\dfrac{n}{2v}+\dfrac{ e\T e}{2v^2}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad  e=\Y-\X beta . [Score and information] In @eq-opt-normal-model with ank(\X)=p, \E\mathbf{S}= zero and  oldsymbol{\mathcal I}( oldsymbol{\uptheta})=\Cov(\mathbf{S})= egin{pmatrix}\X\T\X/\sigma^2& zero\  zero\T&n/(2\sigma^4)\end{pmatrix}.  e\sim\Normal_n( zero,v\I). Hence \E(\X\T e/v)= zero and \Cov(\X\T e/v)=\X\T\X/v by @thm-rv-linear. Next,  e\T e/v\sim\chi^2(n) by @thm-qf-chisq(a) with  P=\I, so it has mean n and variance 2n. So the last coordinate has mean -n/(2v)+nv/(2v^2)=0 and variance 2n/(4v^2)=n/(2v^2). Finally, by @thm-qf-mean-var(c) with \mathbf{K}=\X\T, \A=\I and  mu= zero, \Cov(\X\T e, e\T e)= zero. [Cramér–Rao bound in the normal linear model] Assume @eq-opt-normal-model with ank(\X)=p. Let \delta(\Y) have finite variance and satisfy \E_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\delta=g( oldsymbol{\uptheta}) for all  oldsymbol{\uptheta}, with g differentiable. Then  egin{aligned} \Var_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\delta)&\ge
abla g( oldsymbol{\uptheta})\T oldsymbol{\mathcal I}( oldsymbol{\uptheta})^{-1}
abla g( oldsymbol{\uptheta})\ &=\sigma^2\,\mathbf{g}_{ beta}\T(\X\T\X)^{-1}\mathbf{g}_{ beta}+ rac{2\sigma^4}{n}\,g_v^2, \end{aligned} where \mathbf{g}_{ beta}=\partial g/\partial beta and g_v=\partial g/\partial v. Write f_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}} for the density. Differentiating g( oldsymbol{\uptheta})=\int\delta(\y)f_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\y)\,d\y under the integral sign, which is justified because the normal family is an exponential family (Lehmann and Casella 1998, chapter 1), gives  egin{aligned} 
abla g( oldsymbol{\uptheta})&=\int\delta(\y)\,
abla\log f_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\y)\,f_{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\y)\,d\y\ &=\E(\delta\mathbf{S})=\Cov(\delta,\mathbf{S}), \end{aligned} the last step because \E\mathbf{S}= zero. For any constant vector \mathbf{c}, 0\le\Var(\delta-\mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{S})=\Var\delta-2\mathbf{c}\T
abla g+\mathbf{c}\T oldsymbol{\mathcal I}\mathbf{c}. Choosing \mathbf{c}= oldsymbol{\mathcal I}^{-1}
abla g gives \Var\delta\ge
abla g\T oldsymbol{\mathcal I}^{-1}
abla g. The block-diagonal form of @prp-opt-information gives the right-hand side. For g( oldsymbol{\uptheta})= lambda\T beta the bound is \sigma^2 lambda\T(\X\T\X)^{-1} lambda, exactly the variance of  lambda\T\hbeta. Least squares attains the bound, which gives a second proof of @thm-opt-umvue(a) in full rank. For g=\sigma^2 the bound is 2\sigma^4/n, while \Var(s^2)= rac{\sigma^4}{(n-p)^2}\Var\{\chi^2(n-p)\}= rac{2\sigma^4}{n-p}> rac{2\sigma^4}n . So s^2 does not attain the bound, although by @thm-opt-umvue(b) no unbiased estimator does better. The bound is simply not sharp here. Its ratio to the attained minimum, the efficiency of s^2, is (n-p)/n. That is 0.810 for the stack loss regression, and it tends to one as n	o\infty with p fixed. The same happens for \sigma: the UMVUE s/b_k has variance 0.0298\,\sigma^2 when k=17, against the bound \sigma^2/(2n)=0.0238\,\sigma^2, an efficiency of 0.798. The equality condition in the proof explains why. The bound is attained iff \Var(\delta-\mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{S})=0, that is, iff \delta=g( oldsymbol{\uptheta})+
abla g\T oldsymbol{\mathcal I}^{-1}\mathbf{S} with probability one. For g=\sigma^2 the right-hand side is \sigma^2+(2\sigma^4/n)\{-n/(2\sigma^2)+ e\T e/(2\sigma^4)\}=
orm{\Y-\X beta}^2/n. This is not a statistic, because it involves the unknown  beta, so no unbiased estimator of \sigma^2 attains the bound. The Cramér–Rao bound is a lower bound, not a target. An estimator that fails to attain it may still be the best unbiased estimator, as s^2 is. When an estimator does attain it, the bound certifies optimality without any appeal to completeness. The Lehmann–Scheffé route is stronger in one respect: it needs no differentiability and covers every estimable function in every rank. What changes without normality Every result of this section uses the normal density. Without it the conclusions can fail. Under uniform errors the midrange beats  ar{Y} (@exm-opt-midrange). Under Laplace errors the sample median has asymptotic variance \sigma^2/(2n), half that of  ar{Y}. Under the second-moment assumptions alone, the best that can be said for s^2 is a result in the spirit of Gauss–Markov. Among quadratic unbiased estimators \Y\T\A\Y of \sigma^2 with \A nonnegative definite, s^2 has the smallest variance when the errors have zero excess kurtosis, or when all leverages are equal. @exr-opt-quadratic-sigma2 outlines this result of Atiqullah (1962). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Assume ank(\X)=p. Use @lem-opt-factorization and the identity 
orm{\y-\X beta}^2=	ext{SSE}+(\hbeta- beta)\T\X\T\X(\hbeta- beta) to show directly that (\hbeta,	ext{SSE}) is sufficient for ( beta,\sigma^2). Is \hbeta alone sufficient? [A2] Suppose \sigma^2=\sigma_0^2 is known. Show that \X\T\Y alone is complete and sufficient for  beta, and that  lambda\T\hbeta is still the UMVUE of every estimable  lambda\T beta. Why is \X\T\Y not sufficient when \sigma^2 is unknown? B. Practice [B1] For estimable  lambda\T beta, find the UMVUE of ( lambda\T beta)^2 in the normal linear model. Can it be negative? Comment. \E( lambda\T\hbeta)^2=( lambda\T beta)^2+\sigma^2 lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda and \E s^2=\sigma^2, so ( lambda\T\hbeta)^2-s^2 lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda is unbiased. It is a function of (\M\Y,	ext{SSE}), so it is the UMVUE by @thm-opt-umvue(c). It is negative whenever \lvert tvert<1 for the t statistic of @prp-opt-profile-t at \psi=0, which has positive probability. An estimator of a nonnegative quantity that can be negative is clearly improvable, for example by its positive part. The positive part is biased but has smaller mean squared error. Unbiasedness can be a costly requirement. [B2] Compute the observed information -
abla^2\ell at ( beta,v), take its expectation, and confirm @prp-opt-information by this second route. [B3] For the stack loss model, the 90\% quantile of the response at a new operating condition \x_0 is \x_0\T beta+1.2816\,\sigma. Write down its UMVUE, and explain why \x_0\T\hbeta+1.2816\,s is biased. By how much, in units of \sigma? C. Going deeper [C1] In the normal linear model with n-r\ge2, let  U=(\I-\M)\Y/
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}. Show that  U is independent of (\M\Y,	ext{SSE}), and that its distribution (uniform on the unit sphere of \C(\X)\perpc) does not depend on ( beta,\sigma^2). Hint: write (\I-\M)\Y=\Q_2\Z as in @exr-opt-reml, and use the rotation invariance of \Normal( zero,\sigma^2\I). With \Q_2 as in @exr-opt-reml, (\I-\M)\Y=\Q_2\Z with \Z\sim\Normal_{n-r}( zero,\sigma^2\I), and \Z is independent of \M\Y by @thm-mvn-independence, since \Cov(\M\Y,\Z)=\sigma^2\M\Q_2=\mathbf{0}. Then 	ext{SSE}=
orm{\Z}^2 and  U=\Q_2\Z/
orm{\Z}. For any orthogonal \mathbf{H}, \mathbf{H}\Z has the same law as \Z, so the law of \Z/
orm{\Z} is invariant under all rotations. The only such law on the sphere is the uniform one. The independence of the direction \Z/
orm{\Z} and the length 
orm{\Z} follows from the polar form of the density of \Z, which is a function of 
orm{ z} only. Hence  U is independent of (\M\Y,	ext{SSE}), and its law involves neither  beta nor \sigma^2. [C2] Assume only that the errors are independent with common variance \sigma^2, zero third moment and fourth moment \mu_4. Let \Y\T\A\Y be an unbiased estimator of \sigma^2 with \A symmetric nonnegative definite. (a) Show that \A\X=\mathbf{0} and 	r\A=1. (b) Using @thm-rv-quadform-variance, show that \Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=(\mu_4-3\sigma^4)\sum_ia_{ii}^2+2\sigma^4	r(\A^2). (c) Show that 	r(\A^2)\ge1/(n-r), with equality iff \A=(\I-\M)/(n-r). (d) Conclude that s^2 has the smallest variance in this class when \mu_4=3\sigma^4. Hint for (c): \A=(\I-\M)\A(\I-\M), so the eigenvalues of \A live on \C(\X)\perpc.

title: 7.5 Sampling distributions of the estimates
content:
Sampling distributions of the estimates A point estimate is of little use without a measure of its uncertainty. Under the second-moment assumptions we know the mean and variance of  lambda\T\hbeta and the mean of s^2, but not their distributions. Under normality we know everything. The estimates of the estimable functions are jointly normal, the residual sum of squares is a scaled chi-squared variable, and the two are independent. These three facts are what the whole of Part III rests on. Tests, confidence intervals, confidence ellipsoids and prediction intervals are all built from them. The machinery was assembled in Chapter 3 and Chapter 4. Here we apply it. The main theorem [Sampling distributions in the normal linear model] Assume @eq-opt-normal-model with r=ank(\X)<n. Let  Lambda be p	imes q with \C( Lambda)\subseteq\C(\X\T), let (\X\T\X)\ginv be any generalized inverse, and let s^2=	ext{SSE}/(n-r). 1.  Lambda\T\hbeta\sim\Normal_q igl( Lambda\T beta,\ \sigma^2 Lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv Lambda igr). In particular \hY=\M\Y\sim\Normal_n(\X beta,\sigma^2\M), and if ank(\X)=p, \hbeta\sim\Normal_p igl( beta,\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1} igr). 2. 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2=(n-r)s^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-r). 3. \M\Y and 	ext{SSE} are independent. Hence  Lambda\T\hbeta, and every function of the fitted values, is independent of s^2. 4. \E(s^2)=\sigma^2 and \Var(s^2)=2\sigma^4/(n-r). Write  Lambda=\X\T\mathbf{P} for an n	imes q matrix \mathbf{P}. As in the proof of @thm-opt-gauss-markov(d),  Lambda\T\hbeta=\mathbf{P}\T\M\Y for every least squares estimate \hbeta. (a) By @thm-mvn-linear, \mathbf{P}\T\M\Y is normal with mean \mathbf{P}\T\M\X beta=\mathbf{P}\T\X beta= Lambda\T beta and covariance \sigma^2\mathbf{P}\T\M\M\T\mathbf{P}=\sigma^2\mathbf{P}\T\M\mathbf{P}=\sigma^2 Lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv Lambda, by @thm-proj-M-formula. The special cases are  Lambda=\X\T, with \mathbf{P}=\I, and  Lambda=\I_p in full rank. (b) 	ext{SSE}=\Y\T(\I-\M)\Y, and \I-\M is symmetric and idempotent of rank n-r (@thm-proj-sym-idem and @prp-proj-trace-rank). By @thm-qf-chisq(a), 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2 igl(n-r,
orm{(\I-\M)\X beta}^2/\sigma^2 igr), and the noncentrality is zero because (\I-\M)\X=\mathbf{0}. (c) Apply @thm-qf-indep-linear with \B=\M, \A=\I-\M and  Sigma=\sigma^2\I. Then \B Sigma\A=\sigma^2\M(\I-\M)=\mathbf{0}, so \M\Y and \Y\T(\I-\M)\Y are independent. Functions of independent random vectors are independent. (d) A \chi^2(k) variable has mean k and variance 2k (@thm-qf-ncchisq(b) with \gamma=0). So \E\,	ext{SSE}=\sigma^2(n-r) and \Var(	ext{SSE})=2\sigma^4(n-r). Divide by n-r and (n-r)^2. The proof is short because the work was done earlier. It is worth seeing where each ingredient comes from geometrically. The fitted vector \M\Y and the residual vector (\I-\M)\Y are projections of \Y onto orthogonal subspaces. For a spherical normal vector, orthogonal projections are independent (@thm-qf-orthogonal-projections). Everything about  beta lives in the first projection. The second is pure noise, and its squared length, measured in units of \sigma^2, counts n-r independent squared standard normals. The independence in (c) has no analogue under the second-moment assumptions. If the errors are independent with zero third moment,  lambda\T\hbeta and s^2 are still uncorrelated, but in general they are not independent. The simulation at the end of the section shows the difference. Standardizing: the t statistic The distribution in (a) involves the unknown \sigma. Since \E(s^2)=\sigma^2, the matrix s^2 Lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv Lambda is an unbiased estimate of \Cov( Lambda\T\hbeta), and in full rank s^2(\X\T\X)^{-1} is unbiased for \Cov(\hbeta); this needs only the second-moment assumptions. The square roots of its diagonal entries are the standard errors reported by regression software. Replacing \sigma by s changes the normal distribution into a t distribution, and independence is what makes the change exact. [The t statistic for an estimable function] Assume @eq-opt-normal-model with r<n, let  lambda\in\C(\X\T) with  lambda
e zero, and put 	ext{se}( lambda\T\hbeta)=s\sqrt{ lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda}. For every constant d, T_d= rac{ lambda\T\hbeta-d}{	ext{se}( lambda\T\hbeta)}\sim t(n-r,\delta),\qquad \delta= rac{ lambda\T beta-d}{\sigma\sqrt{ lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda}} . In particular T=( lambda\T\hbeta- lambda\T beta)/	ext{se}( lambda\T\hbeta)\sim t(n-r), and \Pr igl\{\lvert lambda\T\hbeta- lambda\T betavert\le t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,	ext{se}( lambda\T\hbeta) igr\}=1-\alpha, {#eq-opt-t-interval} where t_{n-r,\alpha/2} is the upper \alpha/2 point of t(n-r). Put c^2= lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda. Then c>0, since c^2=
orm{\M oldsymbol{\uprho}}^2 with \X\T\M oldsymbol{\uprho}= lambda
e zero. By @thm-opt-sampling(a), Z=( lambda\T\hbeta-d)/(\sigma c)\sim\Normal(\delta,1). By (b), V=(n-r)s^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-r), and by (c) Z and V are independent. Now T_d=Z/\sqrt{V/(n-r)}, which is t(n-r,\delta) by @def-qf-noncentral-t. With d= lambda\T beta, \delta=0, and @eq-opt-t-interval restates \Pr\{\lvert Tvert\le t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\}=1-\alpha. @eq-opt-t-interval is the familiar confidence interval  lambda\T\hbeta\pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,	ext{se}, and T_d is the statistic for testing  lambda\T beta=d. Its noncentrality \delta governs the power. Chapter 11 and Chapter 12 develop both. For the air-flow coefficient in the stack loss regression this interval was (0.431,\ 1.000) (@exm-opt-stackloss-profile). Two features of the corollary are easy to overlook. The degrees of freedom are n-r, the dimension of the residual space. They are not n, and when \X is rank deficient they are not n-p either. And the interval is exact for every sample size, which no large-sample argument delivers. Several functions at once For a vector of estimable functions, the natural summary of @thm-opt-sampling(a) is a quadratic form. The covariance matrix  Lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv Lambda may be singular when the columns of  Lambda are linearly dependent, so a generalized inverse is needed. [A chi-squared pivot for several functions] In the setting of @thm-opt-sampling, let \mathbf{W}= Lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv Lambda, let \mathbf{W}\ginv be any generalized inverse of \mathbf{W}, and put \mathbf{D}= Lambda\T\hbeta- Lambda\T beta. Then Q= rac{\mathbf{D}\T\mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{D}}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2 igl(ank( Lambda) igr), Q does not depend on the choice of \mathbf{W}\ginv (with probability one), and Q is independent of SSE. Consequently  rac{\mathbf{D}\T\mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{D}/ank( Lambda)}{s^2}\sim F igl(ank( Lambda),\ n-r igr). By @thm-opt-sampling(a), \mathbf{D}\sim\Normal_q( zero,\sigma^2\mathbf{W}). The quadratic form is unchanged if \mathbf{W}\ginv is replaced by its symmetric part  rac12(\mathbf{W}\ginv+\mathbf{W}^{-	op}), which is again a generalized inverse of the symmetric matrix \mathbf{W} (@prp-mat-ginverse-props(d)). So we may assume \mathbf{W}\ginv symmetric. Apply @thm-qf-chisq(c) with  Sigma=\sigma^2\mathbf{W},  mu= zero and \A=\mathbf{W}\ginv/\sigma^2. Conditions (ii) and (iii) hold trivially because  mu= zero. Condition (i) is  Sigma\A Sigma\A Sigma=\sigma^2\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{W}=\sigma^2\mathbf{W}= Sigma\A Sigma, by two uses of \mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{W}. So Q\sim\chi^2(	r(\A Sigma)), where 	r(\A Sigma)=	r(\mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{W})=ank(\mathbf{W}), because \mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{W} is idempotent with the same rank as \mathbf{W} (@prp-mat-ginverse-props(a)), and the trace of an idempotent matrix is its rank (@prp-mat-idempotent-basic). It remains to show ank(\mathbf{W})=ank( Lambda). With  Lambda=\X\T\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{W}=\mathbf{P}\T\M\mathbf{P}=(\M\mathbf{P})\T(\M\mathbf{P}), so ank\mathbf{W}=ank(\M\mathbf{P}). Also  Lambda=\X\T\mathbf{P}=\X\T\M\mathbf{P}. If \X\T\M\mathbf{P} u= zero, then \M\mathbf{P} u\in\C(\X)\cap\C(\X)\perpc=\{ zero\}, so \X\T is one-to-one on \C(\M\mathbf{P}) and ank Lambda=ank(\M\mathbf{P}). For invariance: \mathbf{D}\in\C(\mathbf{W}) with probability one by @thm-rv-cov-nnd(d). If \mathbf{D}=\mathbf{W} u, then \mathbf{D}\T\mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{D}= u\T\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}\ginv\mathbf{W} u= u\T\mathbf{W} u, whatever \mathbf{W}\ginv is. Independence follows from @thm-opt-sampling(c), since \mathbf{D} is a function of \M\Y. The F ratio is then a ratio of independent chi-squared variables divided by their degrees of freedom (@def-qf-noncentral-f). The set of  Lambda\T beta values for which this F ratio stays below an F quantile is a confidence ellipsoid. Chapter 12 studies these regions, and Chapter 11 turns the same statistic into the test of the general linear hypothesis. Here we note only that the degrees of freedom in the numerator are the number of linearly independent functions being estimated, not the number of rows of  Lambda\T. [A rank-deficient model, simulated] Consider a one-way layout with three groups of sizes 4, 5, 6, an intercept, one indicator column per group, and a covariate. So n=15 and p=5, but the rank is r=4, because the indicators add up to the intercept. The contrast  lambda\T beta=\alpha_1-\alpha_2, with  lambda=(0,1,-1,0,0)\T, is estimable. With \sigma=2, @thm-opt-sampling gives \Var( lambda\T\hbeta)=\sigma^2 lambda\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda=1.9007, computed with the Moore–Penrose inverse. In 100{,}000 simulated data sets the variance of the estimated contrast is 1.9017, and the average of 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2 is 11.001, against n-r=11. The sample correlation between the contrast estimate and s^2 is 0.0036. The standardized contrast T falls within \pm2.201, the 97.5\% point of t(11), in a proportion 0.9498 of the samples. Figure 7.5.1 compares the simulated distributions with the theory. Near the centre the t(11) and \Normal(0,1) densities are hard to tell apart, so panel (b) uses a logarithmic density scale, on which the tails separate: the simulated points follow t(11), and the normal density falls away too fast. The tail mass says the same in numbers. A proportion 0.0758 of the samples have |T|>1.96, against 0.05 under \Normal(0,1) and 0.0758 under t(11). A nominal 95\% interval built with the normal point 1.96 would therefore undercover. import numpy as np from scipy import stats groups = np.repeat([0, 1, 2], [4, 5, 6]) z = np.array([2.1, 3.4, 1.8, 4.0, 2.9, 3.3, 5.1, 2.2, 3.8, 1.5, 4.4, 2.7, 3.9, 5.0, 3.1]) n = len(z) X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), np.eye(3)[groups], z]) # p = 5 columns, rank 4 r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(X) G = np.linalg.pinv(X.T @ X) # one generalized inverse M = X @ G @ X.T lam = np.array([0.0, 1.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # group 1 minus group 2: estimable beta, sigma = np.array([1.0, 0.5, -0.5, 0.0, 0.8]), 2.0 var_lam = sigma ** 2 * lam @ G @ lam # Var(lambda^T beta_hat) print(f"n = {n}, p = {X.shape[1]}, rank = {r}, Var(lambda^T beta_hat) = {var_lam:.4f}") rng = np.random.default_rng(75) reps = 100_000 Y = X @ beta + sigma * rng.normal(size=(reps, n)) # one data set per row est = Y @ (X @ G @ lam) # lambda^T beta_hat = lambda^T G X^T y sse = np.sum((Y - Y @ M) ** 2, axis=1) # y^T (I - M) y s2 = sse / (n - r) t = (est - lam @ beta) / np.sqrt(s2 * (lam @ G @ lam)) print(f"mean {est.mean():.4f}, variance {est.var():.4f}") print(f"E(SSE)/sigma^2 = {np.mean(sse) / sigma**2:.3f} (n - r = {n - r})") print(f"corr(estimate, s^2) = {np.corrcoef(est, s2)[0, 1]:.4f}") print("KS p-value, SSE/sigma^2 vs chi^2(n-r):", round(stats.kstest(sse / sigma**2, "chi2", args=(n - r,)).pvalue, 3)) print("KS p-value, t vs t(n-r): ", round(stats.kstest(t, "t", args=(n - r,)).pvalue, 3)) [Figure 7.5.1. Sampling distributions in a rank-deficient normal linear model (n=15, r=4; 100,000 simulated data sets). (a) 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2 with the \chi^2(11) density. (b) The standardized contrast (binned density, points) with the t(11) and standard normal densities, on a logarithmic scale. (c) The contrast estimate against s^2: no relationship, as independence requires.] Figure 7.5.1. Sampling distributions in a rank-deficient normal linear model (n=15, r=4; 100,000 simulated data sets). (a) 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2 with the \chi^2(11) density. (b) The standardized contrast (binned density, points) with the t(11) and standard normal densities, on a logarithmic scale. (c) The contrast estimate against s^2: no relationship, as independence requires. [Sampling distributions in a rank-deficient normal linear model (n=15, r=4; 100,000 simulated data sets). (a) 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2 with the \chi^2(11) density. (b) The standardized contrast (binned density, points) with the t(11) and standard normal densities, on a logarithmic scale. (c) The contrast estimate against s^2: no relationship, as independence requires.] Sampling distributions in a rank-deficient normal linear model (n=15, r=4; 100,000 simulated data sets). (a) 	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2 with the \chi^2(11) density. (b) The standardized contrast (binned density, points) with the t(11) and standard normal densities, on a logarithmic scale. (c) The contrast estimate against s^2: no relationship, as independence requires. Without normality Which parts of @thm-opt-sampling survive when the errors are merely uncorrelated with common variance? The first two moments of  lambda\T\hbeta do, by @thm-opt-gauss-markov, and so does \E(s^2)=\sigma^2. The normality of  lambda\T\hbeta is lost, but it often returns approximately.  lambda\T\hbeta is a weighted sum of independent errors, and a central limit theorem applies when no single observation dominates the weights. Chapter 19 makes this precise (@thm-dep-nonnormal). The distribution of SSE is less forgiving, because its variance depends on the fourth moment of the errors. [Variance of SSE without normality] Let the errors be independent with mean zero, variance \sigma^2, third moment \mu_3 and fourth moment \mu_4, and let h_{ii} be the leverages. Then \Var(	ext{SSE})=2\sigma^4(n-r)+(\mu_4-3\sigma^4)\sum_{i=1}^n(1-h_{ii})^2 . This is @prp-lm-var-s2 with r in place of p. That proof applies @thm-rv-quadform-variance to 	ext{SSE}=\Y\T(\I-\M)\Y and uses only that \A=\I-\M is idempotent with 	r(\A^2)=	r(\A)=n-r and diagonal entries 1-h_{ii}, and that \A\X beta= zero, which kills the terms carrying  oldsymbol{\uptheta} and \mu_3. None of it needs full column rank. The factor \mu_4-3\sigma^4 is \sigma^4 times the excess kurtosis. For normal errors it vanishes and we recover 2\sigma^4(n-r). For heavy-tailed errors it is positive, and SSE is more variable than the chi-squared theory says. Intervals for \sigma^2 built from @thm-opt-sampling(b) are then too short, and this does not improve with sample size: the ratio of the true variance to the nominal one tends to 1+	frac12(\mu_4/\sigma^4-3) when the leverages are small. The t interval for  lambda\T beta is much less affected, because s^2 enters only through s, and s converges to \sigma whatever the kurtosis. [Laplace errors] Rerun the simulation of @exm-opt-sampling-simulation with Laplace (double-exponential) errors of the same variance \sigma^2=4. For these \mu_4=6\sigma^4. The contrast still has variance 1.9007. For SSE, \sum_i(1-h_{ii})^2=8.138, and @prp-opt-var-sse gives \Var(	ext{SSE})=742.6, more than twice the normal-theory value 352.0. The simulated variance is 741.5. Independence fails too. The contrast and SSE are still uncorrelated, because the errors are symmetric, but the squared error of the contrast has correlation 0.211 with SSE. Samples with a few large errors inflate both. E_lap = rng.laplace(scale=sigma / np.sqrt(2), size=(reps, n)) # variance sigma^2, mu_4 = 6 sigma^4 Y_lap = X @ beta + E_lap est_lap = Y_lap @ (X @ G @ lam) sse_lap = np.sum((Y_lap - Y_lap @ M) ** 2, axis=1) h = np.diag(np.eye(n) - M) var_sse_lap = (6 - 3) * sigma**4 * h @ h + 2 * sigma**4 * (n - r) print(f"Var(SSE): normal theory {2 * sigma**4 * (n - r):.1f}, Laplace formula {var_sse_lap:.1f}, " f"simulated {sse_lap.var():.1f}") print(f"corr(squared error of estimate, SSE) under Laplace errors: " f"{np.corrcoef((est_lap - lam @ beta) ** 2, sse_lap)[0, 1]:.3f}") In the listing, h holds the diagonal of \I-\M, that is, 1-h_{ii}. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Under @eq-opt-normal-model, find the joint distribution of (\hY,\he). Show that \hY and \he are independent, and that \he\sim\Normal_n( zero,\sigma^2(\I-\M)) whatever  beta is. Is \he independent of SSE? [A2] In simple linear regression, write out T of @cor-opt-t for the slope, in terms of S_{xx} and s, and state its distribution. What is r? B. Practice [B1] Let  lambda_1, lambda_2\in\C(\X\T). Show that \Cov( lambda_1\T\hbeta, lambda_2\T\hbeta)=\sigma^2 lambda_1\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda_2, and that under normality the two estimates are independent iff  lambda_1\T(\X\T\X)\ginv lambda_2=0. In a one-way layout with a groups of m observations each and cell-means parameterization \E(Y_{ij})=\mu_i, show that the estimates of \sum_ic_i\mu_i and \sum_id_i\mu_i are independent iff \sum_ic_id_i=0. The covariance is the off-diagonal entry of @thm-opt-sampling(a) with  Lambda=[ lambda_1, lambda_2]. Under normality the pair is bivariate normal, so zero covariance is equivalent to independence (@thm-mvn-independence). In the cell-means model \X\T\X=m\I_a, so  lambda_1\T(\X\T\X)^{-1} lambda_2=\sum_ic_id_i/m, which vanishes iff \sum_ic_id_i=0. [B2] A new observation Y_0=\x_0\T beta+\varepsilon_0 will be taken, with \varepsilon_0\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2) independent of \Y and \x_0\in\C(\X\T). Show that  rac{Y_0-\x_0\T\hbeta}{s\sqrt{1+\x_0\T(\X\T\X)\ginv\x_0}}\sim t(n-r), and deduce a prediction interval for Y_0. Why is the extra 1 in the denominator never negligible? Y_0 is independent of \Y, so Y_0-\x_0\T\hbeta is normal with mean \x_0\T beta-\x_0\T beta=0 and variance \sigma^2+\sigma^2\x_0\T(\X\T\X)\ginv\x_0. It is a function of (Y_0,\M\Y), which is independent of SSE. Dividing by \sigma\sqrt{1+\x_0\T(\X\T\X)\ginv\x_0} gives a standard normal, independent of (n-r)s^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-r), and the ratio is t(n-r) by @def-qf-noncentral-t. The interval is \x_0\T\hbeta\pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{1+\x_0\T(\X\T\X)\ginv\x_0}. The 1 is the variance of the new error itself, which no amount of data about  beta can reduce. The second term tends to zero as the design grows. The first does not. [B3] Use @thm-opt-sampling(b) to construct an exact 1-\alpha confidence interval for \sigma^2. Then, using @prp-opt-var-sse with small leverages, explain why its coverage does not tend to 1-\alpha as n	o\infty when the errors have nonzero excess kurtosis. C. Going deeper [C1] Give a second proof of @thm-opt-sampling(b) and (c) using @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections with the two projections \M and \I-\M. Extend it: if \C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X), show that 
orm{(\M-\Mo)\Y}^2 and SSE are independent, and find the distribution of 
orm{(\M-\Mo)\Y}^2/\sigma^2 when \E(\Y)=\X beta is arbitrary. [C2] For the test that rejects  lambda\T beta=d when \lvert T_dvert>t_{n-r,\alpha/2}, show that the power depends on the parameters only through \lvert\deltavert of @cor-opt-t. For a fixed design, how does the power change when the sample is replicated m times (\X replaced by m stacked copies)?

title: 7.6 Bayesian thread I: the conjugate linear model
content:
Bayesian thread I: the conjugate linear model The previous sections judged estimators by their behaviour over repeated samples, for each fixed value of the parameters. The Bayesian approach treats ( beta,\sigma^2) as uncertain quantities with a probability distribution. It combines a prior distribution, expressing what is known before the data, with the likelihood of Section 7.3, and the result is a posterior distribution. For the normal linear model there is a family of priors for which the posterior is available in closed form, and it connects directly to the rest of the chapter. The posterior mean is a matrix-weighted combination of the prior mean and the least squares estimate. It is biased in the frequentist sense, which is how it escapes the Gauss–Markov bound. And as the prior becomes flat, the posterior reproduces least squares and the t intervals of Section 7.5 exactly. This is the first of several Bayesian threads in the book. Section 12.6 continues it with credible regions and predictive distributions, Chapter 27 with shrinkage priors, and Chapter 39 with generalized linear models. The normal-inverse-gamma family [Inverse gamma and normal-inverse-gamma distributions] 1. A positive random variable V has the inverse gamma distribution 	ext{IG}(a,b), with a,b>0, if 1/V has the gamma distribution with shape a and rate b. Its density is \pi(v)= rac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\,v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v},\qquad v>0 . 2. The pair ( beta,\sigma^2) has the normal-inverse-gamma distribution 	ext{NIG}(\mathbf{m},\V,a,b), with \mathbf{m}\in\Real^p, \V positive definite and a,b>0, if \sigma^2\sim	ext{IG}(a,b) and, given \sigma^2,  beta\sim\Normal_p(\mathbf{m},\sigma^2\V). Its joint density is  egin{aligned} \pi( beta,\sigma^2)&= rac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)(2\pi)^{p/2}\det(\V)^{1/2}}\,(\sigma^2)^{-(a+p/2)-1}\ &\qquad	imes\exp\Bigl\{- rac{2b+( beta-\mathbf{m})\T\V^{-1}( beta-\mathbf{m})}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\}. \end{aligned} {#eq-opt-nig-density} The prior on  beta is scaled by \sigma^2: prior uncertainty about the coefficients is measured in units of the noise level. This is a modelling choice, and it is what makes the family conjugate. It also makes \V dimensionless relative to the likelihood’s (\X\T\X)^{-1}, which is the comparison that matters below. The marginal distribution of  beta is a multivariate t. [Multivariate t] Let \Z\sim\Normal_p( zero, S) and W\sim\chi^2(
u) be independent, with  S positive definite. The law of \mathbf{m}+\Z/\sqrt{W/
u} is the multivariate t distribution t_
u(\mathbf{m}, S). For p=1 and  S=1, this is the t(
u) distribution of @def-qf-noncentral-t shifted by \mathbf{m}. For every \mathbf{c}
e zero, \mathbf{c}\T u with  u\sim t_
u(\mathbf{m}, S) is \mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{m}+\sqrt{\mathbf{c}\T S\mathbf{c}}\,T with T\sim t(
u), because \mathbf{c}\T\Z/\sqrt{\mathbf{c}\T S\mathbf{c}}\sim\Normal(0,1) is independent of W. [Marginals of the normal-inverse-gamma] If ( beta,\sigma^2)\sim	ext{NIG}(\mathbf{m},\V,a,b), then 2b/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(2a), \E(\sigma^2)=b/(a-1) for a>1, and  beta\sim t_{2a} igl(\mathbf{m},\ (b/a)\V igr). In particular, for every  lambda
e zero, ( lambda\T beta- lambda\T\mathbf{m})/\sqrt{(b/a) lambda\T\V lambda}\sim t(2a). Put W=2b/\sigma^2. Changing variables v=2b/w in the inverse gamma density, with \lvert dv/dwvert=2b/w^2, gives the density of W:  rac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\Bigl( rac{2b}{w}\Bigr)^{-a-1}e^{-w/2} rac{2b}{w^2} = rac{w^{a-1}e^{-w/2}}{2^a\Gamma(a)},\qquad w>0, which is the \chi^2(2a) density (@eq-qf-chisq-density). Then \E\sigma^2=2b\,\E(1/W)=2b/(2a-2), since \E(1/W)=1/(
u-2) for W\sim\chi^2(
u), 
u>2. Next let \Z_0=( beta-\mathbf{m})/\sigma. Given \sigma^2, \Z_0\sim\Normal_p( zero,\V), a law that does not depend on \sigma^2. So \Z_0 is independent of \sigma^2, and hence of W, and  beta=\mathbf{m}+\sigma\Z_0=\mathbf{m}+\sqrt{ rac{2b}W}\,\Z_0=\mathbf{m}+ rac{\sqrt{b/a}\,\Z_0}{\sqrt{W/(2a)}} . Since \sqrt{b/a}\,\Z_0\sim\Normal_p( zero,(b/a)\V), this is t_{2a}(\mathbf{m},(b/a)\V) by @def-opt-mvt. The last statement is the remark after @def-opt-mvt. The conjugate update [Conjugate posterior] Let \y follow the normal linear model @eq-opt-normal-model, with \X of any rank, and let the prior be ( beta,\sigma^2)\sim	ext{NIG}(\mathbf{m}_0,\V_0,a_0,b_0). Then the posterior is 	ext{NIG}(\mathbf{m}_n,\V_n,a_n,b_n), where  egin{aligned} \V_n&=(\V_0^{-1}+\X\T\X)^{-1},\qquad \mathbf{m}_n=\V_n(\V_0^{-1}\mathbf{m}_0+\X\T\y),\ a_n&=a_0+ rac n2, \end{aligned} {#eq-opt-posterior-params}  egin{aligned} b_n&=b_0+	frac12 igl(\y\T\y+\mathbf{m}_0\T\V_0^{-1}\mathbf{m}_0-\mathbf{m}_n\T\V_n^{-1}\mathbf{m}_n igr)\ &=b_0+	frac12 igl\{
orm{\y-\X\mathbf{m}_n}^2+(\mathbf{m}_n-\mathbf{m}_0)\T\V_0^{-1}(\mathbf{m}_n-\mathbf{m}_0) igr\}. \end{aligned} {#eq-opt-posterior-b} Consequently  beta\mid\y\sim t_{2a_n} igl(\mathbf{m}_n,(b_n/a_n)\V_n igr), \sigma^2\mid\y\sim	ext{IG}(a_n,b_n), and \E( beta\mid\y)=\mathbf{m}_n. Write \mathbf{P}_0=\V_0^{-1} and \mathbf{P}_n=\mathbf{P}_0+\X\T\X. The matrix \mathbf{P}_n is positive definite, because \mathbf{P}_0 is and \X\T\X is nonnegative definite. This holds whatever the rank of \X. Expanding both sides and using \mathbf{P}_n\mathbf{m}_n=\mathbf{P}_0\mathbf{m}_0+\X\T\y gives the completion of the square 
orm{\y-\X beta}^2+( beta-\mathbf{m}_0)\T\mathbf{P}_0( beta-\mathbf{m}_0)=( beta-\mathbf{m}_n)\T\mathbf{P}_n( beta-\mathbf{m}_n)+C, with C=\y\T\y+\mathbf{m}_0\T\mathbf{P}_0\mathbf{m}_0-\mathbf{m}_n\T\mathbf{P}_n\mathbf{m}_n. Indeed, the left side is  beta\T\mathbf{P}_n beta-2 beta\T(\X\T\y+\mathbf{P}_0\mathbf{m}_0)+\y\T\y+\mathbf{m}_0\T\mathbf{P}_0\mathbf{m}_0, and ( beta-\mathbf{m}_n)\T\mathbf{P}_n( beta-\mathbf{m}_n)= beta\T\mathbf{P}_n beta-2 beta\T\mathbf{P}_n\mathbf{m}_n+\mathbf{m}_n\T\mathbf{P}_n\mathbf{m}_n. Putting  beta=\mathbf{m}_n in the identity shows that C=
orm{\y-\X\mathbf{m}_n}^2+(\mathbf{m}_n-\mathbf{m}_0)\T\mathbf{P}_0(\mathbf{m}_n-\mathbf{m}_0)\ge0, which is the second form of @eq-opt-posterior-b. By Bayes’ theorem the posterior density is proportional, as a function of ( beta,\sigma^2), to prior times likelihood. Using @eq-opt-nig-density and dropping factors free of the parameters,  egin{aligned} \pi( beta,\sigma^2\mid\y)&\propto(\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+p/2)-1} e^{-\{2b_0+( beta-\mathbf{m}_0)\T\mathbf{P}_0( beta-\mathbf{m}_0)\}/(2\sigma^2)}\ &\qquad	imes(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}e^{-
orm{\y-\X beta}^2/(2\sigma^2)} . \end{aligned} By the completion of the square, the exponent is -\{2b_0+C+( beta-\mathbf{m}_n)\T\mathbf{P}_n( beta-\mathbf{m}_n)\}/(2\sigma^2), and 2b_0+C=2b_n. The power of \sigma^2 is -(a_0+n/2+p/2)-1=-(a_n+p/2)-1. So the posterior is proportional to the 	ext{NIG}(\mathbf{m}_n,\V_n,a_n,b_n) density @eq-opt-nig-density. Two densities that are proportional are equal, since both integrate to one. The marginals follow from @lem-opt-nig-marginal. The posterior mean of  beta is \mathbf{m}_n: by the tower property, \E( beta\mid\y)=\E\{\E( beta\mid\sigma^2,\y)\mid\y\}=\mathbf{m}_n. The update has a simple structure. Precisions add: the posterior precision (per unit \sigma^2) is the prior precision \V_0^{-1} plus the data precision \X\T\X. Shape parameters count observations: each observation adds 1/2 to a. Scale parameters accumulate squared discrepancies: b_n adds half of the residual sum of squares at the posterior mean and half of the prior-weighted distance between the posterior and prior means. Because \mathbf{P}_n is positive definite even when \X is rank deficient, the posterior is proper for every design. The prior supplies information about the directions of \Null(\X) that the data cannot, and there the posterior equals the prior (@exr-opt-bayes-nonidentified). The posterior mean as shrinkage [Posterior mean as a combination] In @thm-opt-bayes-conjugate, let \X have full column rank and put \W=\V_n\V_0^{-1}. Then: 1. \mathbf{m}_n=\W\mathbf{m}_0+(\I-\W)\hbeta, with \I-\W=\V_n\X\T\X. Equivalently \V_n^{-1}\mathbf{m}_n=\V_0^{-1}\mathbf{m}_0+(\X\T\X)\hbeta: the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the least squares estimate. 2. b_n=b_0+	frac12 igl\{	ext{SSE}+(\hbeta-\mathbf{m}_0)\T igl(\V_0+(\X\T\X)^{-1} igr)^{-1}(\hbeta-\mathbf{m}_0) igr\}. 3. (g-prior.) If \V_0=g(\X\T\X)^{-1} with g>0, then \W=\I/(1+g) and \mathbf{m}_n=(\mathbf{m}_0+g\hbeta)/(1+g). 4. (Ridge.) If \mathbf{m}_0= zero and \V_0=k^{-1}\I with k>0, then \mathbf{m}_n=(\X\T\X+k\I)^{-1}\X\T\y. (a) \X\T\y=\X\T\X\hbeta by the normal equations (@thm-proj-normal-equations), so \mathbf{m}_n=\V_n\V_0^{-1}\mathbf{m}_0+\V_n\X\T\X\hbeta, and \V_n\V_0^{-1}+\V_n\X\T\X=\V_n\V_n^{-1}=\I. (b) Write \mathbf{P}_0=\V_0^{-1} and \mathbf{K}=\X\T\X. The completion of the square in the proof of @thm-opt-bayes-conjugate shows that 2(b_n-b_0) is the minimum over  beta of 
orm{\y-\X beta}^2+( beta-\mathbf{m}_0)\T\mathbf{P}_0( beta-\mathbf{m}_0), because the remaining term ( beta-\mathbf{m}_n)\T\mathbf{P}_n( beta-\mathbf{m}_n) is nonnegative and vanishes at \mathbf{m}_n. By @eq-proj-distance-split, 
orm{\y-\X beta}^2=	ext{SSE}+( beta-\hbeta)\T\mathbf{K}( beta-\hbeta). Put \mathbf{d}=\hbeta-\mathbf{m}_0 and  beta=\mathbf{m}_0+ u. The quantity to minimize becomes 	ext{SSE}+( u-\mathbf{d})\T\mathbf{K}( u-\mathbf{d})+ u\T\mathbf{P}_0 u, whose minimum over  u, attained at  u=(\mathbf{K}+\mathbf{P}_0)^{-1}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d}, is 	ext{SSE}+\mathbf{d}\T\{\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{K}+\mathbf{P}_0)^{-1}\mathbf{K}\}\mathbf{d}. By @thm-mat-woodbury, \mathbf{K}-\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{K}+\mathbf{P}_0)^{-1}\mathbf{K}=(\mathbf{K}^{-1}+\mathbf{P}_0^{-1})^{-1}=(\V_0+(\X\T\X)^{-1})^{-1}. (c) With \V_0^{-1}=\X\T\X/g, \V_n^{-1}=(1+1/g)\X\T\X, so \W=\V_n\V_0^{-1}=\{g/(1+g)\}(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\X/g=\I/(1+g). (d) Substitute into @eq-opt-posterior-params. Part (a) is the Bayesian counterpart of Gauss–Markov. The posterior mean is linear in \y, and it is biased unless \mathbf{m}_0= beta: \E(\mathbf{m}_n)=\W\mathbf{m}_0+(\I-\W) beta. So the Gauss–Markov theorem does not apply to it, and it can have smaller mean squared error than least squares when the prior mean is close to the truth. Part (d) identifies ridge regression, whose mean squared error was studied in @exr-opt-ridge, as a posterior mean. Chapter 27 develops the connection in @thm-shr-ridge. When the prior is weak relative to the data, \W is close to \mathbf{0} and the posterior mean is close to \hbeta. When it is strong, \W is close to \I and the data barely move it. In general \W is a full matrix, not a multiple of the identity. Shrinkage then happens along the eigenvectors of the problem, not coordinate by coordinate. A single coefficient’s posterior mean need not lie between its prior mean and its least squares estimate, as the next example shows. Only the g-prior of part (c) shrinks every coordinate by the same factor. Its prior covariance copies the shape of the sampling covariance of \hbeta, and that makes it convenient for model comparison. Zellner (1986) introduced it. The flat-prior limit What happens when the prior carries no information? Letting \V_0^{-1}	o\mathbf{0} in @eq-opt-posterior-params gives \mathbf{m}_n	o\hbeta when \X has full rank. The shape parameter needs more care. The NIG density @eq-opt-nig-density carries the factor (\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+p/2)-1}, so letting only a_0,b_0	o0 leads to the prior (\sigma^2)^{-p/2-1}, with a_n=n/2 and t marginals on n degrees of freedom rather than n-p. The improper prior \pi( beta,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2, uniform in  beta and in \log\sigma, is the limit \V_0^{-1}	o\mathbf{0}, a_0	o-p/2, b_0	o0. A negative shape a_0=-p/2 lies outside the proper NIG family, so this prior cannot be reached inside @thm-opt-bayes-conjugate and has to be handled directly. The result is clean. [The flat prior reproduces least squares] Let ank(\X)=p<n, let 	ext{SSE}>0, and take the improper prior \pi( beta,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2. Then the posterior is proper and equals 	ext{NIG} igl(\hbeta,(\X\T\X)^{-1},(n-p)/2,	ext{SSE}/2 igr). In particular, for every  lambda
e zero,  rac{ lambda\T beta- lambda\T\hbeta}{s\sqrt{ lambda\T(\X\T\X)^{-1} lambda}}\ \Big|\ \y\ \sim\ t(n-p), so the 1-\alpha equal-tailed credible interval for  lambda\T beta is the t interval @eq-opt-t-interval. By @eq-proj-distance-split, 
orm{\y-\X beta}^2=	ext{SSE}+( beta-\hbeta)\T\X\T\X( beta-\hbeta). So prior times likelihood is proportional to  egin{aligned} &(\sigma^2)^{-1-n/2}\exp\Bigl\{- rac{	ext{SSE}+( beta-\hbeta)\T\X\T\X( beta-\hbeta)}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\}\ &\qquad=(\sigma^2)^{-(a+p/2)-1}\exp\Bigl\{- rac{2b+( beta-\hbeta)\T\X\T\X( beta-\hbeta)}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\}, \end{aligned} with a=(n-p)/2>0 and b=	ext{SSE}/2>0. This is proportional to the density @eq-opt-nig-density of 	ext{NIG}(\hbeta,(\X\T\X)^{-1},a,b), which is integrable. So the posterior is proper and equal to it. By @lem-opt-nig-marginal with 2a=n-p and b/a=	ext{SSE}/(n-p)=s^2, the stated ratio has the t(n-p) distribution. The frequentist and Bayesian statements now read alike, but they say different things. The t interval of Section 7.5 has probability 1-\alpha of covering the fixed  lambda\T beta before the data are seen. The credible interval has posterior probability 1-\alpha of containing the random  lambda\T beta given the observed data. That the two coincide is a special property of this model and this prior. It is one reason why 1/\sigma^2 is regarded as the natural “noninformative” prior for the normal linear model. A worked example [A prior for the stack loss plant] Return to the stack loss regression of @exm-opt-stackloss-mle. Suppose an engineer, before seeing these 21 days, believed from the chemistry of the process that stack loss should rise roughly one for one with air flow and with cooling water temperature, and should not depend on acid concentration. This belief is hypothetical and is used only for illustration. We encode it as \mathbf{m}_0=(0,\ 1,\ 1,\ 0)\T,\qquad \V_0=\diag(100^2,\ 0.1^2,\ 0.2^2,\ 0.1^2),\qquad a_0=3,\ b_0=18 . So the prior standard deviations of the slopes are 0.1\sigma, 0.2\sigma and 0.1\sigma, the intercept is left essentially free, and the prior mean of \sigma^2 is b_0/(a_0-1)=9. The posterior has a_n=13.5, so the marginal posteriors are t with 27 degrees of freedom, and b_n=112.523. The posterior means of the coefficients are \mathbf{m}_n=(-41.1490,\ 0.7616,\ 1.1606,\ {-}0.1371)\T, against the least squares estimates (-39.9197,\ 0.7156,\ 1.2953,\ {-}0.1521). Each slope has moved toward its prior mean. The intercept has moved too, though its prior is vague, because it is strongly correlated with the slopes when the regressors are not centred. The 95\% credible interval for the air-flow coefficient, using the t(27) quantile 2.052, is (0.550,\ 0.973), narrower than the least squares t interval (0.431,\ 1.000), because the prior adds information. For water temperature and acid concentration the intervals are (0.594,\ 1.727) and (-0.392,\ 0.118). The posterior mean of \sigma^2 is 9.002, almost exactly the prior mean 9, although s^2=10.519. The two parts of @eq-opt-posterior-b explain why. The lack of fit at the posterior mean is
