The successive differences show that the largest step in ideology, 0.903, falls between pure independents and independents leaning Republican, and the step between weak and strong Republicans is 0.658. The reference coding cannot show this directly. The two deviation codings nearly agree here because the groups are of similar size, apart from the small group of pure independents. [Figure 8.5.1. Mean self-placement by party identification in the 1996 ANES (point area proportional to group size), with the three baselines used by the codings of @exm-est-party-coding: the reference level, the unweighted mean of the seven means, and the overall mean.] Figure 8.5.1. Mean self-placement by party identification in the 1996 ANES (point area proportional to group size), with the three baselines used by the codings of @exm-est-party-coding: the reference level, the unweighted mean of the seven means, and the overall mean. [Mean self-placement by party identification in the 1996 ANES (point area proportional to group size), with the three baselines used by the codings of @exm-est-party-coding: the reference level, the unweighted mean of the seven means, and the overall mean.] Mean self-placement by party identification in the 1996 ANES (point area proportional to group size), with the three baselines used by the codings of @exm-est-party-coding: the reference level, the unweighted mean of the seven means, and the overall mean. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm anes = sm.datasets.anes96.load_pandas().data y = anes["selfLR"].to_numpy() # 1 = very liberal ... 7 = very conservative level = anes["PID"].to_numpy().astype(int) # 0 = strong Dem. ... 6 = strong Rep. g = 7 Z = np.eye(g)[level] # n x 7 indicator (cell-means) matrix n_k = Z.sum(axis=0) cell_means = (Z.T @ y) / n_k print("group sizes:", n_k.astype(int)) print("cell means: ", np.round(cell_means, 3)) def coding_matrices(n_k): """Each coding is X = Z K for a nonsingular g x g K; the coefficients are K^{-1} mu.""" g = len(n_k) one = np.ones((g, 1)) reference = np.vstack([np.zeros(g - 1), np.eye(g - 1)]) # level 0 is baseline deviation = np.vstack([np.eye(g - 1), -np.ones(g - 1)]) # sum-to-zero weighted = np.vstack([np.eye(g - 1), -n_k[:-1] / n_k[-1]]) # sum n_k * effect = 0 successive = np.array([[(j + 1 - g if i <= j else j + 1) / g for j in range(g - 1)] for i in range(g)]) # backward differences return {"cell means": np.eye(g), "reference": np.hstack([one, reference]), "sum to zero": np.hstack([one, deviation]), "weighted effect": np.hstack([one, weighted]), "successive differences": np.hstack([one, successive])} for name, K in coding_matrices(n_k).items(): Xc = Z @ K gamma = np.linalg.lstsq(Xc, y, rcond=None)[0] print(f"{name:23s}", np.round(gamma, 3)) Choosing a coding Since every coding gives the same fit, the choice is about communication and, to a lesser extent, precision. Four points are worth keeping in mind. Anything that depends on the fit is invariant. This includes fitted values, residuals, R^2, \hat{\sigma}^2, and the F test that all levels have the same mean. That test compares \C(\Z) with \C( one), and the coding does not enter it (@thm-glh-f-test). Coefficient tests answer different questions. The t test for a reference-coded coefficient tests whether level k differs from the reference level. The t test for a sum-coded coefficient tests whether level k differs from the average of all levels, a question that changes if a level is added. Neither question is wrong, but they are different questions. A table of coefficients from an unfamiliar coding should never be read as if it came from the familiar one. Precision depends on the reference. In reference coding \Var(\hat{\gamma}_j)=\sigma^2(1/n_{j+1}+1/n_1). A small reference group inflates the variance of every coefficient. In @exm-est-party-coding, comparing each of the other five levels with the 37 pure independents instead of the 200 strong Democrats would multiply the standard errors by factors between 1.55 and 1.76. A common default is to use the largest group, or a natural control condition, as the reference. With other regressors, coefficients are adjusted comparisons. When the model also contains other variables, a reference-coded coefficient compares level k with the reference level at equal values of those variables. That is the “holding the others fixed” reading of @def-lm-coefficient-interpretation, with all its caveats. Section 8.6 gives an example in which adjustment changes the answer a great deal. A coding is a choice of coordinates for the g-dimensional space of level means. The coefficients are \mathbf{K}^{-1}\hat{ mu}. To get the comparisons you want, write them down first as the rows of a nonsingular matrix \mathbf{L}, then code with \mathbf{K}=\mathbf{L}^{-1}. For an ordered factor, a useful instance of this principle is the cumulative coding, with columns \mathbf{1}\{	ext{level}\ge k\} for k=2,\dots,g. Then \mathbf{K} is lower triangular with ones on and below the diagonal. Its inverse takes successive differences, so the intercept is \mu_1 and the coefficient of the kth column is \mu_k-\mu_{k-1} (@exr-est-cumulative). An observation’s mean is built up as a sum of steps, which is often how an ordered factor is best described. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] In the model \E(y_i)= eta_0+ eta_1d_i, with n_0 observations in group 0 (level 1) and n_1 in group 1 (level 2), write down the coding matrix \mathbf{K} with  mu=\mathbf{K} beta. Use @prp-est-coding(b), not an inverse of \X\T\X, to find \hbeta. Then show that \Var(\hat{ eta}_1)=\sigma^2(1/n_0+1/n_1) and that \hat{ eta}_1/\operatorname{se}(\hat{ eta}_1) is the pooled two-sample t statistic, where s^2=	ext{SSE}/(n-2) replaces \sigma^2. The two means are \mu_0= eta_0 and \mu_1= eta_0+ eta_1, so \mathbf{K}= egin{psmallmatrix}1&0\1&1\end{psmallmatrix} and \mathbf{K}^{-1}= egin{psmallmatrix}1&0\-1&1\end{psmallmatrix}. By @prp-est-coding(b), \hbeta=\mathbf{K}^{-1}\hat{ mu}=( ar{y}_0,\, ar{y}_1- ar{y}_0)\T. The level means are the estimates of the full-rank cell-means model, with \Cov(\hat{ mu})=\sigma^2 D^{-1}=\sigma^2\diag(1/n_0,1/n_1) (@thm-lm-moments), so \Var(\hat{ eta}_1)=(-1,1)\,\sigma^2 D^{-1}(-1,1)\T=\sigma^2(1/n_0+1/n_1). The residuals are deviations from the group means (@prp-est-coding(a)), so s^2 is the pooled variance, and the ratio is ( ar{y}_1- ar{y}_0)/\{s\sqrt{1/n_0+1/n_1}\}. [A2] For a factor with three levels, write down the null space of [ one, z_1, z_2, z_3]. Show that adding a second factor’s full set of indicators, [ one,\Z_A,\Z_B], creates a null space of dimension at least two, and give two independent null vectors. B. Practice [B1] Let \X have full column rank, let \mathbf{e}_i be the ith coordinate vector with \mathbf{e}_i
otin\C(\X), and fit [\X,\mathbf{e}_i] with coefficients ( beta,\delta). Write \hat{e}_i and h_{ii} for the residual and the leverage (@def-proj-leverage) of observation i in the fit of \X alone. 1. Use @thm-proj-fwl, with \mathbf{e}_i as the regressor of interest and \X as the one partialled out, to show that \hat{\delta}=\hat{e}_i/(1-h_{ii}), and explain why h_{ii}<1. 2. Show that the enlarged fit reproduces y_i exactly, and that its \hbeta is the estimate \hbeta_{(i)} without observation i. 3. Deduce the deletion identity y_i-\x_{(i)}\T\hbeta_{(i)}=\hat{e}_i/(1-h_{ii}): the error in predicting y_i from the other observations is the ordinary residual inflated by 1/(1-h_{ii}). (a) Apply @thm-proj-fwl(a) with \X_1=\mathbf{e}_i and \X_2=\X, and let \M project onto \C(\X). Then \hat{\delta} is the coefficient in the regression of \y on (\I-\M)\mathbf{e}_i: \hat{\delta}=\mathbf{e}_i\T(\I-\M)\y/\mathbf{e}_i\T(\I-\M)\mathbf{e}_i=\hat{e}_i/(1-h_{ii}). The denominator is 
orm{(\I-\M)\mathbf{e}_i}^2, which is positive because \mathbf{e}_i
otin\C(\X). (b) The residual vector of the enlarged fit is orthogonal to every column, in particular to \mathbf{e}_i, so its ith entry is zero. For fixed  beta, the residual sum of squares \sum_{j
e i}(y_j-\x_{(j)}\T beta)^2+(y_i-\x_{(i)}\T beta-\delta)^2 is minimized over \delta by making the last term zero. What remains is the deletion criterion, and its minimizer \hbeta_{(i)} is unique: if \X\mathbf{b}=c\mathbf{e}_i with \mathbf{b}
e zero, then c
e0 by full rank, and \mathbf{e}_i\in\C(\X). So \hbeta=\hbeta_{(i)}. (c) By (b), \hat{\delta}=y_i-\x_{(i)}\T\hbeta_{(i)}; compare with (a). The t statistic for \delta is the externally studentized residual of Chapter 20. [B2] For an ordered factor with g levels, let the coded columns be the indicators of \{	ext{level}\ge k\}, k=2,\dots,g, together with an intercept. Show that \mathbf{K} is lower triangular with ones on and below the diagonal, that \mathbf{K}^{-1} is the first-difference matrix, and hence that the coefficients are \mu_1 and \mu_k-\mu_{k-1}. [B3] On each of m days a warehouse runs N_{1i} machines of type 1 and N_{2i} of type 2, and meters its total energy use V_i. Suppose each running machine of type k uses an amount of energy with mean 	heta_k and variance 	au_k^2, independently of the other machines and the same on every day. Show that \E(V_i)=	heta_1N_{1i}+	heta_2N_{2i}, a linear model without intercept, and that (	heta_1,	heta_2) is identifiable iff the vectors (N_{1i}) and (N_{2i}) are not proportional. Find \Cov(\mathbf{V}); why is it not a multiple of \I? Why is it essential that 	heta_k does not vary by day? C. Going deeper [C1] Show that fitting the reference-coded model is the same as solving the normal equations of the overparameterized one-way model under the side condition \alpha_1=0, with \gamma_0=\mu and \gamma_j=\alpha_{j+1}. State and prove the corresponding facts for the sum-to-zero and weighted effect codings.

title: 8.6 Several factors, interactions and covariates
8.7 Contrasts
content:
Contrasts In the one-way model the individual effects \alpha_k are not estimable, but their differences are. The general form of such a difference is a contrast. Contrasts are the natural targets of inference about a factor. They are estimable, they do not depend on the side condition or coding, and they are what a scientific question about a factor usually asks: does treatment beat control, is there a trend across doses, do two groups of levels differ? This section characterizes them, shows how an orthogonal set of contrasts splits the factor’s sum of squares, and constructs the Helmert and polynomial families. Definition and estimability Throughout, the one-way model is \E(y_{kj})=\mu+\alpha_k for observation j at level k, with n_k\ge1 observations at level k=1,\dots,g, level means \mu_k=\mu+\alpha_k and sample means  ar{y}_k. [Contrast] In a factor model, a contrast in the effects of a factor is a linear function \sum_kc_k\alpha_k whose coefficients satisfy \sum_kc_k=0, not all zero. In the one-way model it equals \sum_kc_k\mu_k, and we call either form a contrast in the level means. Two contrasts are orthogonal (for the given design) if \sum_kc_kd_k/n_k=0. The two forms agree because \sum_kc_k\mu_k=\mu\sum_kc_k+\sum_kc_k\alpha_k. This is where the condition \sum_kc_k=0 comes from: it makes the unidentified \mu drop out. Simple differences \alpha_k-\alpha_l, comparisons of one level with the average of others such as \alpha_1-	frac12(\alpha_2+\alpha_3), and trend coefficients are all contrasts. [Estimable functions in the one-way model] In the one-way model with every n_k\ge1, the function \lambda_0\mu+\sum_k\lambda_k\alpha_k is estimable iff \lambda_0=\sum_k\lambda_k. In particular, a linear function of the effects alone, \sum_kc_k\alpha_k, is estimable iff it is a contrast (or zero). For a contrast, the least squares estimator and its variance under \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I are \hat{\psi}=\sum_kc_k ar{y}_k,\qquad \Var(\hat{\psi})=\sigma^2\sum_k rac{c_k^2}{n_k}. {#eq-est-contrast-var} The null space of \X=[ one,\Z] is spanned by  v=(1,-1,\dots,-1)\T (@exm-proj-oneway-rank). By @thm-est-characterization(c), the function is estimable iff \lambda_0-\sum_k\lambda_k=0. For an estimable function, \lambda_0\mu+\sum_k\lambda_k\alpha_k=\sum_k\lambda_k(\mu+\alpha_k). Every least squares solution has \hat{\mu}+\hat{\alpha}_k= ar{y}_k, since the fitted values are the level means (@exm-proj-oneway-M). So the estimate is \sum_k\lambda_k ar{y}_k. The level means are uncorrelated with variances \sigma^2/n_k, by @thm-rv-linear, which gives the variance. The estimator in @eq-est-contrast-var is the same whatever coding or side condition was used to fit the model. @prp-est-ls-estimator guarantees this, and it is the reason contrasts, rather than coefficients, should be reported. Sums of squares and orthogonal contrasts Each contrast defines a direction in the observation space, and its estimate is the component of \y along that direction. With  D=\diag(n_1,\dots,n_g) and \Z the indicator matrix, put  u_{\mathbf{c}}=\Z D^{-1}\mathbf{c} , {#eq-est-contrast-vector} the vector whose entries equal c_k/n_k for the observations at level k. [Contrasts as projections] Let \mathbf{c} and \mathbf{d} be contrasts, and write \hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{c}}=\mathbf{c}\T\hat{ mu}. Then: 1. \hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{c}}= u_{\mathbf{c}}\T\y, and  u_{\mathbf{c}} is a nonzero vector in \C(\Z)\cap one\perpc; 2. the sum of squares for the contrast, \operatorname{SS}(\mathbf{c})= rac{\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{c}}^2}{\sum_kc_k^2/n_k}, equals 
orm{ P\y}^2, where  P is the orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by  u_{\mathbf{c}}; 3. \Cov(\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{c}},\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{d}})=\sigma^2\sum_kc_kd_k/n_k=\sigma^2 u_{\mathbf{c}}\T u_{\mathbf{d}} when \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I, so orthogonal contrasts have uncorrelated estimates and orthogonal vectors  u; 4. if \mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_{g-1} are pairwise orthogonal contrasts, then \sum_{j=1}^{g-1}\operatorname{SS}(\mathbf{c}_j)=\sum_{k=1}^gn_k( ar{y}_k- ar{y})^2 , the sum of squares between levels. (a) \hat{ mu}= D^{-1}\Z\T\y (@eq-est-indicator-facts), so \mathbf{c}\T\hat{ mu}=(\Z D^{-1}\mathbf{c})\T\y. Clearly  u_{\mathbf{c}}\in\C(\Z), and  one\T u_{\mathbf{c}}= one\T\Z D^{-1}\mathbf{c}=(n_1,\dots,n_g) D^{-1}\mathbf{c}=\sum_kc_k=0. It is nonzero because \Z D^{-1} has full column rank and \mathbf{c}
e zero. (b) By @exm-proj-line, 
orm{ P\y}^2=( u_{\mathbf{c}}\T\y)^2/
orm{ u_{\mathbf{c}}}^2, and 
orm{ u_{\mathbf{c}}}^2=\mathbf{c}\T D^{-1}\Z\T\Z D^{-1}\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c}\T D^{-1}\mathbf{c}=\sum_kc_k^2/n_k. (c) @thm-rv-linear gives \Cov( u_{\mathbf{c}}\T\Y, u_{\mathbf{d}}\T\Y)=\sigma^2 u_{\mathbf{c}}\T u_{\mathbf{d}}, and the same computation as in (b) gives  u_{\mathbf{c}}\T u_{\mathbf{d}}=\mathbf{c}\T D^{-1}\mathbf{d}. (d) The space \C(\Z)\cap one\perpc has dimension g-1 (@thm-proj-nested(c), with \C( one)\subseteq\C(\Z)). By (a) and (c) the vectors  u_{\mathbf{c}_1},\dots, u_{\mathbf{c}_{g-1}} are g-1 nonzero, mutually orthogonal vectors in it, so they form an orthogonal basis. By @thm-proj-sum the sum of the projections onto the lines they span is the projection onto that space, which is \M-n^{-1} one one\T (@thm-proj-nested(b)). Applying it to \y and using Pythagoras gives \sum_j\operatorname{SS}(\mathbf{c}_j)=
orm{(\M-n^{-1} one one\T)\y}^2. The vector (\M-n^{-1} one one\T)\y has entry  ar{y}_k- ar{y} at every observation of level k. So a complete set of orthogonal contrasts decomposes the between-level sum of squares into g-1 one-dimensional pieces. Under normality the pieces are independent, each is \sigma^2 times a noncentral \chi^2 with one degree of freedom, and each is independent of the residual sum of squares (@thm-qf-orthogonal-projections). Each contrast can therefore be tested on its own. Chapter 9 places this decomposition in the general theory of orthogonal sums of squares, and Chapter 15 uses it for the one-way analysis of variance (@thm-aov-orthogonal-contrasts). In a balanced design, with all n_k equal, orthogonality reduces to the ordinary \sum_kc_kd_k=0. In an unbalanced design, contrasts that look orthogonal on paper need not be orthogonal for the data. Helmert contrasts The Helmert matrix of @exm-mat-helmert has rows proportional to \mathbf{h}_k=(\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-1},\,-(k-1),\,0,\dots,0),\qquad k=2,\dots,g . The contrast \mathbf{h}_k\T mu compares level k with the average of the levels before it, since it is (k-1) times 	frac1{k-1}\sum_{l<k}\mu_l-\mu_k. The \mathbf{h}_k are mutually orthogonal in the ordinary sense, so in a balanced design they are orthogonal contrasts. They suit factors whose levels are added in a meaningful order, such as successive refinements of a treatment, where each new level is compared with everything before it. Polynomial contrasts When the levels of a factor are ordered and equally spaced, such as doses 0,10,20,30 or the seven points of a party scale, the natural questions are about the shape of the sequence of means. Is there a linear trend? Curvature? Give the levels scores s_k=k. Apply Gram–Schmidt (@prp-proj-gram-schmidt) to the vectors  one,\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{2},\dots,\mathbf{s}^{g-1} in \Real^g, where \mathbf{s}^{j} has entries s_k^j. This gives orthogonal vectors \mathbf{p}_0,\dots,\mathbf{p}_{g-1}, and \mathbf{p}_j is a polynomial of degree j in the score. For j\ge1, \mathbf{p}_j\perp one, so \mathbf{p}_j is a contrast. Rescaled to integers, the first three for g=7 are 	ext{linear }(-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3),\quad 	ext{quadratic }(5,0,-3,-4,-3,0,5),\quad 	ext{cubic }(-1,1,1,0,-1,-1,1). By construction \mathbf{p}_j is orthogonal to every polynomial of degree less than j. So if the level means follow a polynomial of degree d in the score, every contrast of degree above d is zero. The linear contrast measures the trend, the quadratic the curvature beyond it, and so on. This is the reason for their use. With unequal group sizes the classical integer contrasts are no longer orthogonal for the design. The fix follows @prp-est-contrast-ss(c). Orthogonality is needed in the inner product \sum_kc_kd_k/n_k, which suggests setting \mathbf{c}_j= D\mathbf{p}_j, where now the \mathbf{p}_j are orthogonal polynomials in the weighted inner product \sum_kn_kp_kq_k. Then \sum_kc_{jk}=\sum_kn_kp_{jk}=0, and \sum_kc_{jk}c_{lk}/n_k=\sum_kn_kp_{jk}p_{lk}=0 for j
e l. In observation space,  u_{\mathbf{c}_j}=\Z\mathbf{p}_j is the polynomial of degree j in each observation’s score, orthogonalized over the observations. The weighted linear contrast gives exactly the regression sum of squares of \y on the score (@exr-est-linear-trend). [Trend in ideology across party identification] Return to the seven party-identification groups of @exm-est-party-coding. The between-group sum of squares is 772.87. The classical linear contrast has estimate \hat{\psi}=\sum_k(k-4) ar{y}_k=11.175, variance 0.1652\,\sigma^2 by @eq-est-contrast-var, and sum of squares 755.85, which is 97.8 percent of the between-group sum of squares. The quadratic and cubic contrasts have sums of squares 10.15 and 2.58. Ideology rises almost linearly across the seven-point party scale, with some upward curvature (Figure 8.7.1). The group sizes range from 37 to 200, so the six classical contrasts are not orthogonal for this design. Their sums of squares add to 784.02, which exceeds the between-group total. Part of the variation is counted twice. The weighted orthogonal polynomial contrasts decompose the total exactly: 746.57 for the linear trend and 26.30 for the five higher-degree contrasts together. [Figure 8.7.1. Mean ideological self-placement by party identification (point area proportional to group size), with the weighted least squares linear and quadratic trends in the score. The linear contrast accounts for almost all of the variation between groups.] Figure 8.7.1. Mean ideological self-placement by party identification (point area proportional to group size), with the weighted least squares linear and quadratic trends in the score. The linear contrast accounts for almost all of the variation between groups. [Mean ideological self-placement by party identification (point area proportional to group size), with the weighted least squares linear and quadratic trends in the score. The linear contrast accounts for almost all of the variation between groups.] Mean ideological self-placement by party identification (point area proportional to group size), with the weighted least squares linear and quadratic trends in the score. The linear contrast accounts for almost all of the variation between groups. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm anes = sm.datasets.anes96.load_pandas().data y = anes["selfLR"].to_numpy() level = anes["PID"].to_numpy().astype(int) # 0 = strong Dem. ... 6 = strong Rep. g = 7 n_k = np.bincount(level).astype(float) means = np.bincount(level, weights=y) / n_k def orthogonal_polynomials(scores, weights): """Columns 1..g-1: polynomials in the scores, orthogonal in sum_k w_k u_k v_k.""" V = np.vander(scores, len(scores), increasing=True) # 1, s, s^2, ... W = np.sqrt(weights)[:, None] Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(W * V) # weighted Gram-Schmidt P = Q / W # back to the original scale P = P / np.abs(P).max(axis=0) # cosmetic rescaling return P[:, 1:] # drop the constant column def contrast_ss(c, means, n_k): """Estimate c'mu-hat and its sum of squares (c'mu-hat)^2 / sum(c_k^2 / n_k).""" psi = c @ means return psi, psi ** 2 / np.sum(c ** 2 / n_k) scores = np.arange(g, dtype=float) C_unw = orthogonal_polynomials(scores, np.ones(g)) # the classical table (equal n) C_wtd = n_k[:, None] * orthogonal_polynomials(scores, n_k) # c_k = n_k p(k) ss_between = np.sum(n_k * (means - y.mean()) ** 2) for name, C in [("unweighted", C_unw), ("weighted", C_wtd)]: ss = [contrast_ss(C[:, j], means, n_k)[1] for j in range(g - 1)] print(f"{name:10s} SS by degree: {np.round(ss, 2)} total {sum(ss):.2f}", f"(between groups {ss_between:.2f})") Coding matrices are not contrast matrices Section 8.5 coded a factor by an intercept and the columns \Z\mathbf{C}. When the columns of \mathbf{C} are contrasts, as for Helmert or polynomial coding, it is tempting to read the coefficient of column j as the estimate of the contrast \mathbf{c}_j\T mu. That reading is wrong in general. By @prp-est-coding(b) the coefficients are the rows of \mathbf{K}^{-1}, with \mathbf{K}=[ one,\mathbf{C}], applied to \hat{ mu}. The rows of \mathbf{K}^{-1} and the columns of \mathbf{K} are related simply only when the columns are orthogonal. [Orthogonal codings] If the columns of \mathbf{K}=[ one_g,\mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_{g-1}] are mutually orthogonal, then the coefficients of the coded model are \hat{\gamma}_0= rac1g\sum_k ar{y}_k,\qquad \hat{\gamma}_j= rac{\mathbf{c}_j\T\hat{ mu}}{\mathbf{c}_j\T\mathbf{c}_j},\quad j=1,\dots,g-1 , whatever the group sizes. With orthogonal columns, \mathbf{K}\T\mathbf{K}=\diag(g,\mathbf{c}_1\T\mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_{g-1}\T\mathbf{c}_{g-1}), so \mathbf{K}^{-1}=(\mathbf{K}\T\mathbf{K})^{-1}\mathbf{K}\T. Apply @prp-est-coding(b). The orthogonality required here is the plain one, \mathbf{c}_j\T\mathbf{c}_l=0, not the design orthogonality of @def-est-contrast, because \hat{ gamma}=\mathbf{K}^{-1}\hat{ mu} is pure algebra and does not involve the n_k. Helmert coding, in the usual software convention, uses the columns \mathbf{c}_j=-\mathbf{h}_{j+1}, which compare level j+1 with the levels before it, and \mathbf{c}_j\T\mathbf{c}_j=j(j+1). In the party data the first three Helmert coefficients are 0.1408, 0.0698 and 0.1271, while the contrasts themselves are 0.2817, 0.4187 and 1.5253, larger by the factors 2, 6 and 12. For a non-orthogonal coding there is no such shortcut. Reference coding has \mathbf{c}_j=\mathbf{e}_{j+1}, yet its coefficients are \mu_{j+1}-\mu_1, not \mu_{j+1}. def helmert(g): """Coding matrix whose column k compares level k+1 with the mean of levels 1..k.""" C = np.zeros((g, g - 1)) for k in range(1, g): C[:k, k - 1] = -1.0 C[k, k - 1] = k return C H = helmert(g) K = np.column_stack([np.ones(g), H]) gamma = np.linalg.solve(K, means) # Helmert-coded coefficients psi = H.T @ means # the contrasts c_k' mu-hat print("coefficients:", np.round(gamma[1:], 4)) print("contrasts: ", np.round(psi, 4)) print("ratio: ", np.round(psi / gamma[1:], 1)) # = c_k' c_k = k(k+1) A coefficient from a contrast-coded regression estimates a contrast only up to a scale factor, and only when the coding columns are orthogonal. To test or report a contrast, compute \mathbf{c}\T\hat{ mu} and its variance @eq-est-contrast-var directly, or read it from the coded fit using \mathbf{K}^{-1}. Do not read it off the coefficient table. Contrasts in the two-way additive model In the additive model \mu+\alpha_i+ eta_j of Section 8.6, a row contrast is \sum_ic_i\alpha_i with \sum_ic_i=0. It is a combination of the differences \alpha_i-\alpha_1, so in a connected design it is estimable (@thm-est-connected). In a balanced design, with m\ge1 observations in every one of the ab cells, the least squares fit is  ar{y}_{i\cdot\cdot}+ ar{y}_{\cdot j\cdot}- ar{y}_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}. This is shown in @exm-proj-two-factor for m=1, and the averaging argument there is unchanged for m>1. Hence \widehat{	extstyle\sum_ic_i\alpha_i}=\sum_ic_i igl( ar{y}_{i\cdot\cdot}+ ar{y}_{\cdot j\cdot}- ar{y}_{\cdot\cdot\cdot} igr)=\sum_ic_i ar{y}_{i\cdot\cdot}, \qquad \Var= rac{\sigma^2}{bm}\sum_ic_i^2 , since the terms not depending on i are multiplied by \sum_ic_i=0. The row contrast is estimated from the row means alone, as if factor B were absent. In an unbalanced design this is false. The row means are then contaminated by the column effects (@exr-est-unbalanced-rows), and the least squares estimate has to adjust for them. That adjustment is the subject of Chapter 17. Interaction contrasts, and their estimability when cells are empty, were treated in @prp-est-interaction. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Find the linear, quadratic and cubic orthogonal polynomial contrasts for g=4 equally spaced levels, scaled to integers. Check that they are mutually orthogonal and that the quadratic contrast vanishes when \mu_k=a+bk. [A2] Show that the Helmert contrasts \mathbf{h}_2,\dots,\mathbf{h}_g are orthogonal for the design iff n_1=n_2=\dots=n_{g-1}, whatever n_g is. Hint: compute \sum_kh_{jk}h_{lk}/n_k for j<l. B. Practice [B1] Show that for every contrast \mathbf{c}, \operatorname{SS}(\mathbf{c})\le\sum_kn_k( ar{y}_k- ar{y})^2, with equality when c_k=n_k( ar{y}_k- ar{y}). This fact is the basis of Scheffé’s method in Chapter 13 (@thm-mc-scheffe). By @prp-est-contrast-ss(b), \operatorname{SS}(\mathbf{c})=
orm{ P\y}^2 with  P projecting onto a line inside \mathcal S=\C(\Z)\cap one\perpc. Let  P_{\mathcal S}=\M-n^{-1} one one\T. Because the line lies in \mathcal S,  P\y= P P_{\mathcal S}\y (@thm-proj-nested(a)), and so 
orm{ P\y}^2\le
orm{ P_{\mathcal S}\y}^2=\sum_kn_k( ar{y}_k- ar{y})^2. Equality holds when the line contains  P_{\mathcal S}\y, whose entries are  ar{y}_k- ar{y} at level k. That vector is  u_{\mathbf{c}} for c_k=n_k( ar{y}_k- ar{y}), and this \mathbf{c} is a contrast because \sum_kn_k( ar{y}_k- ar{y})=0. [B2] In the additive two-way model with n_{ij} observations in cell (i,j), show that \E( ar{y}_{i\cdot\cdot})=\mu+\alpha_i+\sum_jn_{ij} eta_j/n_{i\cdot}. Deduce that \sum_ic_i ar{y}_{i\cdot\cdot} is unbiased for every row contrast and every  beta iff the proportions n_{ij}/n_{i\cdot} do not depend on i, that is, iff the cell counts are proportional, n_{ij}=n_{i\cdot}n_{\cdot j}/n. C. Going deeper [C1] Let \x be the n-vector giving each observation’s score s_k. Show that the sum of squares of the weighted linear contrast \mathbf{c}_1= D\mathbf{p}_1 equals the regression sum of squares 
orm{(\M_1-n^{-1} one one\T)\y}^2 of the simple regression of \y on \x with intercept, where \M_1 projects onto \C([ one,\x]). Conclude that the remaining weighted contrasts together measure the lack of fit of the straight line to the level means. In the weighted inner product, \mathbf{p}_1 is \mathbf{s} minus its weighted mean, \mathbf{s}- ar{s}_w one with  ar{s}_w=\sum_kn_ks_k/n, up to scale. Then  u_{\mathbf{c}_1}=\Z D^{-1} D\mathbf{p}_1=\Z\mathbf{p}_1, whose entries are s_k- ar{s}_w. That is \x- ar{x} one, the centred score vector. By @prp-est-contrast-ss(b), \operatorname{SS}(\mathbf{c}_1) is the squared length of the projection of \y onto the line spanned by \x- ar{x} one. By @exm-proj-simple-nested this line is \C([ one,\x])\cap one\perpc, and the projection onto it is \M_1-n^{-1} one one\T. The remaining weighted contrasts span the orthogonal complement of that line in \C(\Z)\cap one\perpc, which is \C(\Z)\cap\C([ one,\x])\perpc. Their total sum of squares is 
orm{(\M-\M_1)\y}^2, the reduction in residual sum of squares from the straight-line model to the model with a separate mean for each level.

title: 8.8 Summary and Notes
content: Summary and Notes Summary 1. The data determine the mean vector \X\bbeta and nothing more. A function of \bbeta is identifiable iff it is a function of \X\bbeta, and \bbeta itself is identifiable iff \rank(\X)=p (@def-est-identifiable, @thm-est-identifiable-mean and @prp-est-identifiable-rank). 2. A single coefficient is identifiable iff its column is not a combination of the others (@prp-est-coordinate). Rank deficiency comes from construction, from identities among variables (age, period and cohort), or from the design (@exm-est-apc). 3. A linear function \blambda\T\bbeta has a linear unbiased estimator iff it is identifiable iff \blambda\in\C(\X\T) (@def-est-estimable and @thm-est-estimable-identifiable). The estimable functions form a space of dimension \rank(\X) (@cor-est-estimable-space). 4. Eight equivalent tests of estimability, including \blambda\perp\Null(\X), \blambda\T\G\X\T\X=\blambda\T, and invariance over least squares solutions (@thm-est-characterization). The estimate is \blambda\T\hbeta for any solution, with variance \sigma^2\blambda\T\G\blambda for any generalized inverse (@prp-est-ls-estimator). 5. For a nonestimable \blambda, a generalized-inverse solution estimates a different, estimable function \blambda\T\G\X\T\X\bbeta, and the reported variance can be any number (@prp-est-H and @exr-est-any-variance). Decide estimability with the SVD of \X, and treat near-nonestimable functions as unestimated (@exm-est-near-estimable). 6. Full-rank reparameterizations are choices of basis for the estimable space (@thm-est-reparameterization). Side conditions \bT\bb=\bzero select a unique solution iff \rank(\bT)=p-r and no combination of them is estimable (@thm-est-side-conditions). The constrained coefficients are then particular estimable functions (@prp-est-side-meaning). The minimum-norm solution is itself a side condition (@prp-est-min-norm-side). 7. A coding of a factor is a nonsingular matrix \mathbf{K}, and its coefficients estimate \mathbf{K}^{-1}\bmu, the rows of \mathbf{K}^{-1} applied to the level means (@def-est-coding and @prp-est-coding). 8. In the additive two-way model the rank is a+b minus the number of connected components of the design, and a difference of levels is estimable iff the levels are connected (@thm-est-connected). In the interaction model, exactly the combinations of occupied cell means are estimable (@prp-est-interaction). 9. With a covariate, adjusted differences between levels subtract the slope times the difference in covariate means, the slope being estimated within levels (@prp-est-adjusted). 10. Contrasts are the estimable functions of a factor’s effects (@def-est-contrast and @thm-est-oneway-contrasts). Orthogonal contrasts, in the design inner product \sum_kc_kd_k/n_k, decompose the between-level sum of squares (@prp-est-contrast-ss). Coding coefficients equal scaled contrasts only for orthogonal codings (@prp-est-coding-dual). Notes and sources Identifiability and estimability. Christensen (2020, §2.1) develops estimability from identifiability, as this chapter does, and stresses that the estimable functions are exactly the identifiable linear ones. Agresti (2015, §1.4) gives a short treatment aimed at generalized linear models, where the same definitions apply to the linear predictor. Rencher and Schaalje (2008, ch. 12) is a detailed textbook account of the non-full-rank model: estimable functions and their tests, the estimators \mathbf{r}\T\X\T\y and \blambda\T\hbeta, reparameterization and side conditions, with small worked layouts. The notion of an estimable function goes back to R. C. Bose’s work on the design of experiments in the 1940s. Scheffé (1959) and Searle (1971) made it standard, and Rao (1973) treats it through generalized inverses. The characterization @thm-est-characterization collects conditions that are scattered through these sources. That a generalized-inverse solution estimates the estimable function \blambda\T\G\X\T\X\bbeta (@prp-est-H) follows at once from \E(\G\X\T\Y)=\G\X\T\X\bbeta, but its consequence for software output deserves more emphasis than it usually gets. Side conditions and software. The exact conditions of @thm-est-side-conditions, and the formula (\X\T\X+\bT\T\bT)^{-1}\X\T\y, are standard (see Rencher and Schaalje 2008, §12.6, and Searle 1971). The coding matrices, called “contrasts”, that S and R use for factors are described by Chambers and Hastie (1992), and Venables and Ripley (2002) discuss the treatment, sum, Helmert and polynomial codings of R. The minimum-norm solution rests on the Moore–Penrose inverse (Penrose 1955), and column-pivoted QR is described in Golub and Van Loan (2013). Indicator variables. Sen and Srivastava (1990, ch. 4) is a practical account of indicator variables: the two-sample comparison as a regression, polychotomous factors, hierarchical codings, factors with continuous covariates, broken-line regression and aggregated indicators as responses. Where this chapter meets those themes it takes its own route: the two-sample comparison through the coding proposition (@exr-est-two-sample), the indicator of a single observation through the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem (@exr-est-single-dummy), and count regressors without intercept in a new setting (@exr-est-counts). Connectedness, empty cells and cohorts. Connectedness of two-way designs, and its role in estimability, is treated at length by Searle (1971, 1987). Searle (1987) is also the standard reference for unbalanced data and empty cells, which Chapter 17 takes up. The age–period–cohort problem of @exm-est-apc is a well-known instance of a dependency among variables. Holford (1983) showed which functions of the age, period and cohort effects are estimable, among them the second differences of @exr-est-apc-factors. Data. The survey examples use the extract of the 1996 American National Election Study distributed with statsmodels (Seabold and Perktold 2010) as a public-domain data set. The other examples use simulated data, generated by the scripts in code/ch08/. References - Agresti, Alan (2015). Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. - Chambers, John M. and Hastie, Trevor, eds. (1992). Statistical Models in S. Pacific Grove, CA: Wadsworth & Brooks/Cole. - Christensen, Ronald (2020). Plane Answers to Complex Questions: The Theory of Linear Models. 5th edition. Cham: Springer. - Golub, Gene H. and Van Loan, Charles F. (2013). Matrix Computations. 4th edition. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. - Holford, Theodore R. (1983). The Estimation of Age, Period and Cohort Effects for Vital Rates. Biometrics 39(2), 311–324. - Penrose, Roger (1955). A Generalized Inverse for Matrices. Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 51(3), 406–413. - Rao, C. Radhakrishna (1973). Linear Statistical Inference and Its Applications. 2nd edition. New York: Wiley. - Rencher, Alvin C. and Schaalje, G. Bruce (2008). Linear Models in Statistics. 2nd edition. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. - Scheffé, Henry (1959). The Analysis of Variance. New York: Wiley. - Seabold, Skipper and Perktold, Josef (2010). Statsmodels: Econometric and Statistical Modeling with Python. Proceedings of the 9th Python in Science Conference, 92–96. - Searle, Shayle R. (1971). Linear Models. New York: Wiley. - Searle, Shayle R. (1987). Linear Models for Unbalanced Data. New York: Wiley. - Sen, Ashish and Srivastava, Muni (1990). Regression Analysis: Theory, Methods, and Applications. New York: Springer. - Venables, William N. and Ripley, Brian D. (2002). Modern Applied Statistics with S. 4th edition. New York: Springer.

title: Sums of Squares and Orthogonal Decomposition
content: Sums of Squares and Orthogonal Decomposition An analysis of variance table looks like bookkeeping. Behind every row there is a subspace, and behind the whole table an orthogonal decomposition of the space in which the data live: sums of squares are squared lengths of projections, and degrees of freedom are dimensions. Sequential and partial sums of squares, and the Type I, II and III sums of squares printed by software, differ only in which subspaces they project onto, and so in which hypotheses they address. When the subspaces are orthogonal, as in balanced designs and with orthogonal polynomials, the distinctions disappear. The coefficient of determination is a ratio of two of these squared lengths, and we mark what it does not measure. Finally, the expectation of each sum of squares shows what an F ratio compares, preparing the tests of Part III. What you need. Chapter 6 throughout, especially projections and their ranks (@thm-proj-sum, @prp-proj-trace-rank), nested models (@thm-proj-nested, @thm-proj-constraint-space), the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem (@thm-proj-fwl) and R^2 as a squared cosine (@thm-proj-r2-cosine). The linear model and the moments of least squares estimates from Chapter 5 (@def-lm-linear-model, @thm-lm-moments). The mean of a quadratic form (@thm-rv-quadform-mean) and the distribution theory of Chapter 4 (@thm-qf-orthogonal-projections, @thm-qf-cochran-algebra). Estimable functions and contrasts from Chapter 8 appear in Sections 9.2 to 9.4. Roadmap - Decomposing the total sum of squares - Extra sums of squares - Sequential and partial sums of squares - Orthogonal designs - The coefficient of determination and its limits - Expected mean squares - Summary and notes

title: 9.1 Decomposing the total sum of squares
content:
Decomposing the total sum of squares Every sum of squares in a linear model is the squared length of a projection of the data. Chapter 6 showed this for the residual sum of squares, 
orm{(\I-\M)\y}^2, and for the drop in residual sum of squares between nested models, 
orm{(\M-\Mo)\y}^2 (@eq-proj-extra-ss). This section turns these observations into a general framework. An analysis of variance is a choice of mutually orthogonal subspaces that together fill the model space. Once that choice is made, the whole table follows from Pythagoras: the sums of squares add up because the pieces are orthogonal, and the degrees of freedom add up because dimensions of orthogonal subspaces add. Throughout the chapter the model is \E(\Y)=\X beta with \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I (@def-lm-linear-model). \X is n	imes p of rank r, which may be less than p, and \M is the orthogonal projection onto \C(\X). The identities of the chapter hold for every data vector \y. Probability enters only where a covariance, an expectation or a distribution is stated, and systematically in Section 9.6. Orthogonal decompositions of the model space [Analysis of variance decomposition] An analysis of variance decomposition of the model space is a list of subspaces \mathcal V_1,\dots,\mathcal V_k of \C(\X) that are mutually orthogonal and whose sum is \C(\X): \C(\X)=\mathcal V_1\dirsum\mathcal V_2\dirsum\dots\dirsum\mathcal V_k, \qquad \mathcal V_i\perp\mathcal V_j\ (i
eq j). The subspace \mathcal V_{k+1}=\C(\X)\perpc is the error space. Writing  P_i for the orthogonal projection onto \mathcal V_i, the sum of squares for \mathcal V_i is 
orm{ P_i\y}^2=\y\T P_i\y, its degrees of freedom are r_i=\dim\mathcal V_i, and its mean square is 
orm{ P_i\y}^2/r_i. The same space can be decomposed in many ways, and the choice is the statistician’s: the constants, a regressor of interest, a block of nuisance regressors, the linear and quadratic parts of a trend. The theorem collects what is true of all decompositions. [The analysis of variance identity] Let \mathcal V_1,\dots,\mathcal V_k be an analysis of variance decomposition of \C(\X), with projections  P_1,\dots, P_k and dimensions r_1,\dots,r_k. Then: 1.  P_i P_j= zero for i
eq j,  P_1+\dots+ P_k=\M, and \I= P_1+ P_2+\dots+ P_k+(\I-\M), a sum of k+1 mutually orthogonal projections; 2. for every \y\in\Real^n the vectors  P_1\y,\dots, P_k\y,(\I-\M)\y are mutually orthogonal and 
orm{\y}^2=
orm{ P_1\y}^2+\dots+
orm{ P_k\y}^2+
orm{(\I-\M)\y}^2 ; {#eq-ss-anova-identity} 3. r_i=ank( P_i)=	r( P_i), r_1+\dots+r_k=r, and the error space has dimension 	r(\I-\M)=n-r; 4. if the columns of \Q_i (n	imes r_i) form an orthonormal basis of \mathcal V_i, then 
orm{ P_i\y}^2=
orm{\Q_i\T\y}^2 is a sum of r_i squares, and together with an orthonormal basis \Q_{k+1} of the error space the matrix  U=[\Q_1,\dots,\Q_{k+1}] is orthogonal; 5. the subspaces \mathcal W_j=\mathcal V_1\dirsum\dots\dirsum\mathcal V_j form a chain \mathcal W_1\subseteq\dots\subseteq\mathcal W_k=\C(\X) with projections \mathbf{N}_j= P_1+\dots+ P_j, and  P_j=\mathbf{N}_j-\mathbf{N}_{j-1} (with \mathbf{N}_0= zero). Conversely, every chain \{ zero\}=\mathcal W_0\subseteq\mathcal W_1\subseteq\dots\subseteq\mathcal W_k=\C(\X) gives an analysis of variance decomposition with \mathcal V_j=\mathcal W_{j-1}\perpc\cap\mathcal W_j. (a) For any  u,  P_j u\in\mathcal V_j\subseteq\mathcal V_i\perpc, so  P_i P_j u= zero by @prp-proj-trace-rank(c). Applying @thm-proj-sum repeatedly, the sum  P_1+\dots+ P_k is the orthogonal projection onto \mathcal V_1\dirsum\dots\dirsum\mathcal V_k=\C(\X), and a projection is determined by its range, so the sum is \M. Each  P_i satisfies \M P_i= P_i, because its columns lie in \C(\X), and therefore (\I-\M) P_i= zero. The projection \I-\M onto \C(\X)\perpc (@thm-proj-sym-idem) is thus orthogonal to every  P_i. (b) Multiply \I=\sum_i P_i+(\I-\M) by \y. For two different pieces, ( P_i\y)\T( P_j\y)=\y\T P_i P_j\y=0, using symmetry and (a). Pythagoras gives the identity. (c) Rank equals trace for projections (@prp-proj-trace-rank(b)), and the trace is additive, so \sum_ir_i=	r(\M)=r by @thm-proj-M-formula, and 	r(\I-\M)=n-r. (d) By @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula,  P_i=\Q_i\Q_i\T, so \y\T P_i\y=
orm{\Q_i\T\y}^2. Columns taken from different \Q_i are orthogonal because the subspaces are, so  U has orthonormal columns. It has r_1+\dots+r_k+(n-r)=n of them, so it is square and hence orthogonal. (e) The \mathbf{N}_j are projections onto \mathcal W_j by @thm-proj-sum, and the chain is nested by construction. Conversely, given a chain, @thm-proj-nested(b) shows that \mathbf{N}_j-\mathbf{N}_{j-1} is the projection onto \mathcal V_j=\mathcal W_{j-1}\perpc\cap\mathcal W_j. For i<j we have \mathcal V_i\subseteq\mathcal W_i\subseteq\mathcal W_{j-1}, which is orthogonal to \mathcal V_j. The projections telescope to \mathbf{N}_k=\M, so by @thm-proj-sum the orthogonal sum of the \mathcal V_j is \C(\M)=\C(\X). Part (e) says that decompositions and chains are the same thing. Listing the rows of an analysis of variance table from the top is the same as fitting a sequence of ever larger models and recording what each step adds. Section 9.3 builds on this. Degrees of freedom are dimensions “Degrees of freedom” can seem like a rule of thumb (“subtract one for every parameter estimated”). Part (d) of @thm-ss-decomposition gives the phrase an exact meaning. Rotate the data into the orthonormal coordinates  z= U\T\y. The rotation preserves length, and it splits  z into consecutive blocks \Q_1\T\y,\dots,\Q_{k+1}\T\y of sizes r_1,\dots,r_k,n-r. The sum of squares for \mathcal V_i is the sum of the squares of the r_i coordinates in its block. A sum of squares has r_i degrees of freedom because it is a sum of r_i squares of orthonormal linear combinations of the data, and it cannot be written with fewer. The rotation also explains why degrees of freedom govern the size of a sum of squares. If \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I, the coordinates  U\T\Y are uncorrelated with variance \sigma^2 (@thm-rv-linear), so a block of r_i of them has expected sum of squares r_i\sigma^2 plus the squared length of its mean (Section 9.6). The divisor n-1 of the sample variance is the case \Real^n=\spn( one)\dirsum one\perpc: the n deviations y_i- ar{y} lie in an (n-1)-dimensional subspace, and the Helmert matrix of @exm-mat-helmert writes their sum of squares as n-1 squared orthonormal contrasts. The regression analysis of variance table The most common decomposition comes from the chain \spn( one)\subseteq\C(\X), available whenever  one\in\C(\X), which is the case for every model with an intercept. Write  P_1=n^{-1} one one\T for the projection onto the constant vectors (@exm-proj-line). The chain gives the three-way decomposition of @eq-proj-three-way, \I= P_1+(\M- P_1)+(\I-\M), with ranks 1, r-1 and n-r. The squared lengths are 
orm{ P_1\y}^2=n ar{y}^2,\qquad 	ext{SSR}=
orm{(\M- P_1)\y}^2=\sum_i(\hat{y}_i- ar{y})^2,\qquad 	ext{SSE}=
orm{(\I-\M)\y}^2=\sum_i(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 . They are usually arranged as follows. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Source df Sum of squares Mean square ----------------------------- ----------------- ----------------- ---------------------- Mean 1 n ar{y}^2 n ar{y}^2 Regression (after the mean) r-1 	ext{SSR} 	ext{SSR}/(r-1) Residual n-r 	ext{SSE} s^2=	ext{SSE}/(n-r) Total n \y\T\y ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- This is the uncorrected table. Its total is the raw sum of squares \sum_iy_i^2, with n degrees of freedom. The row for the mean is rarely of interest, because it records only that the average response is not zero. Deleting it gives the corrected table, whose total is 	ext{SST}=\sum_i(y_i- ar{y})^2=
orm{(\I- P_1)\y}^2 on n-1 degrees of freedom. The corrected identity 	ext{SST}=	ext{SSR}+	ext{SSE} is @eq-proj-corrected-decomposition. “Correcting for the mean” is thus a projection. We first project the data onto  one\perpc and then decompose what is left. The ratio of the two mean squares, F= rac{	ext{SSR}/(r-1)}{	ext{SSE}/(n-r)} , compares the variation along the regression directions with the variation in the error space. Under normality and when no regressor matters, it has the F(r-1,n-r) distribution (@thm-qf-nested-f). Section 9.6 explains why this ratio is the right comparison, and Chapter 11 develops the test. A few formulas make the table easy to compute from any least squares solution. [Computing the sums of squares] Let \hbeta be any least squares estimate. Then: 1. 
orm{\M\y}^2=\hbeta\T\X\T\y and 	ext{SSE}=\y\T\y-\hbeta\T\X\T\y; 2. if  one\in\C(\X), then 	ext{SSR}=\hbeta\T\X\T\y-n ar{y}^2; 3. if \X=[ one,\X_1] has full column rank and 	ilde{\X}_1=(\I- P_1)\X_1 is the matrix of centred regressors, then 	ext{SSR}=\hbeta_1\T	ilde{\X}_1\T	ilde{\X}_1\hbeta_1=\hbeta_1\T	ilde{\X}_1\T\y, where \hbeta_1 holds the slopes. (a) \X\hbeta=\M\y (@thm-proj-ls-projection), so 
orm{\M\y}^2=\y\T\M\y=\y\T\X\hbeta=\hbeta\T\X\T\y. The second formula follows from 	ext{SSE}=\y\T\y-\y\T\M\y (@prp-proj-fit-residual). (b) \M- P_1 is a projection (@thm-proj-nested), so 	ext{SSR}=\y\T\M\y-\y\T P_1\y=
orm{\M\y}^2-n ar{y}^2; now use (a). (c) By @lem-proj-fwl-split with \X_2= one, \M- P_1 is the projection onto \C(	ilde{\X}_1), and by @thm-proj-fwl the slopes are the coefficients of (\M- P_1)\y in terms of the columns of 	ilde{\X}_1. So (\M- P_1)\y=	ilde{\X}_1\hbeta_1 and 	ext{SSR}=
orm{	ilde{\X}_1\hbeta_1}^2. The last equality uses 	ilde{\X}_1\T\y=	ilde{\X}_1\T(\M- P_1)\y=	ilde{\X}_1\T	ilde{\X}_1\hbeta_1. In (a), \hbeta\T\X\T\y is the same for every solution of the normal equations, even though \hbeta is not unique when r<p. That is no accident. It equals 
orm{\M\y}^2, which depends only on the model space. [An analysis of variance table for murder rates] Return to the regression of the 2009 murder rate of the 50 US states on poverty, single parenthood and urbanization, with an intercept (@exm-proj-fwl-crime). Here r=4 and  ar{y}=4.514. The listing computes every sum of squares from the coordinates of \y in an orthonormal basis of \C(\X), as in @thm-ss-decomposition(d): the first coordinate gives the mean, the next three the regression. Source df Sum of squares Mean square --------------------- ---- ---------------- ------------- Mean 1 1018.81 1018.81 Regression 3 182.80 60.93 Residual 46 101.96 2.217 Total (uncorrected) 50 1303.57 Total (corrected) 49 284.76 The regression mean square is 27.49 times the residual mean square. If none of the three regressors were related to the murder rate and the errors were normal, a ratio this large would occur with probability about 2.5	imes 10^{-10}. The proportion of the corrected total that the regression accounts for is 182.80/284.76=0.6419, the R^2 of @thm-proj-r2-cosine. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy import stats data = sm.datasets.statecrime.load_pandas().data.drop(index="District of Columbia") y = data["murder"].to_numpy() n = len(y) X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), data["poverty"], data["single"], data["urban"]]) r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(X) Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(X) # orthonormal basis of C(X); first column spans 1 z = Q.T @ y # coordinates of My in that basis ss_mean = z[0] ** 2 # n * ybar^2 ss_reg = np.sum(z[1:] ** 2) # ||(M - P1) y||^2, r - 1 squared coordinates ss_res = y @ y - np.sum(z ** 2) # ||(I - M) y||^2 rows = [("mean", 1, ss_mean), ("regression", r - 1, ss_reg), ("residual", n - r, ss_res), ("total", n, y @ y)] for name, df, ss in rows: print(f"{name:11s} df = {df:3d} SS = {ss:9.2f} MS = {ss / df:8.3f}") F = (ss_reg / (r - 1)) / (ss_res / (n - r)) print(f"corrected total = {ss_reg + ss_res:.2f}, F = {F:.2f}") The QR factorization supplies the orthonormal basis of @thm-ss-decomposition(d); its first column is \pm one/\sqrt n because Gram–Schmidt starts with the intercept (@prp-proj-gram-schmidt). No n	imes n projection matrix is formed. Models without an intercept The corrected table depends on  one\in\C(\X). Without it, the chain \spn( one)\subseteq\C(\X) is not available, and the corrected “identity” fails. For any model matrix \X, with \hY=\M\y and \he=(\I-\M)\y, \sum_i(y_i- ar{y})^2=\sum_i(\hat{y}_i- ar{y})^2+\sum_i\hat{\varepsilon}_i^2-2 ar{y}\sum_i\hat{\varepsilon}_i . The last term vanishes for every \y iff  one\in\C(\X). Write \y- ar{y} one=(\hY- ar{y} one)+\he and expand the squared length. The cross term is 2(\hY- ar{y} one)\T\he=2\hY\T\he-2 ar{y} one\T\he=-2 ar{y}\, one\T\he, since \hY\perp\he. If  one\in\C(\X), then  one\T\he=0 (@prp-proj-fit-residual(b)). If  one
otin\C(\X), take \y= one. Then  ar{y}=1 and  one\T\he= one\T(\I-\M) one=
orm{(\I-\M) one}^2>0, so the last term is not zero. Without an intercept the valid decomposition is the uncorrected one, 
orm{\y}^2=
orm{\M\y}^2+	ext{SSE}, whose regression row has r degrees of freedom. That is appropriate only when the mean response is known to vanish when every regressor is zero. [Forcing the murder regression through the origin] Refit the model of @exm-ss-crime-anova without the intercept. The residual sum of squares rises from 101.96 to 177.73, so the fit is much worse. Yet the residuals now sum to -8.332, and the would-be corrected identity is off by -2 ar{y}\sum_i\hat{\varepsilon}_i=75.22: the corrected total 284.76 is not 31.81+177.73=209.54. The uncentred ratio 
orm{\hY}^2/
orm{\y}^2, which some software reports as R^2 for such models, is 0.8637, much larger than the 0.6419 of the better model with an intercept (@exr-proj-uncentred-r2). X0 = X[:, 1:] # drop the intercept column b0, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X0, y, rcond=None) e0 = y - X0 @ b0 ybar = y.mean() sst = np.sum((y - ybar) ** 2) ssr_star = np.sum((X0 @ b0 - ybar) ** 2) sse0 = e0 @ e0 print(f"SST = {sst:.2f} but SSR* + SSE = {ssr_star + sse0:.2f}") print(f"sum of residuals = {e0.sum():.3f}, -2 ybar * sum = {-2 * ybar * e0.sum():.2f}") Coarsening and refining Coarsening merges rows: replacing \mathcal V_1 and \mathcal V_2 by \mathcal V_1\dirsum\mathcal V_2 gives another decomposition, whose sums of squares and degrees of freedom are sums of the old ones. The regression row is a coarsening of the table that gives each regressor its own row (Section 9.3). Refining splits a row: any subspace of dimension r_i can be cut into r_i orthogonal lines, each carrying one degree of freedom. A refinement is useful only when its lines answer questions of interest. Section 9.4 chooses them with orthogonal contrasts and orthogonal polynomials. An analysis of variance table is a list of mutually orthogonal subspaces that fill \Real^n. Its sums of squares are the squared lengths of the projections of \y, its degrees of freedom are the dimensions, and both columns add up because of Pythagoras. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] For simple regression, \X=[ one,\x] with \x not constant, show that 	ext{SSR}=\hat{ eta}_1^2S_{xx}=S_{xy}^2/S_{xx} and that the F ratio of the corrected table equals t^2, where t=\hat{ eta}_1\sqrt{S_{xx}}/s. [A2] A regression with an intercept has a corrected table in which the regression row has 3 degrees of freedom and sum of squares 120, the residual mean square is 2.5, and the corrected total sum of squares is 172.5. Find n, the residual degrees of freedom, the F ratio and R^2. B. Practice [B1] Let  U=[\Q_1,\dots,\Q_{k+1}] be the orthogonal matrix of @thm-ss-decomposition(d) and  z= U\T\Y. Suppose \E(\Y)= mu\in\C(\X) and \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I. Show that the coordinates of  z are uncorrelated with variance \sigma^2, that the last n-r of them have mean zero, and deduce \E(	ext{SSE})=(n-r)\sigma^2. Show that if in addition \Y is normal, the coordinates are independent. By @thm-rv-linear, \Cov( z)= U\T(\sigma^2\I) U=\sigma^2\I and \E( z)= U\T mu. The last block is \Q_{k+1}\T mu, and  mu\in\C(\X) is orthogonal to the error space, so it is zero. Then 	ext{SSE}=
orm{\Q_{k+1}\T\Y}^2 is a sum of n-r squares of variables with mean zero and variance \sigma^2, so its expectation is (n-r)\sigma^2. Under normality  z is normal (@thm-mvn-linear) with diagonal covariance, and uncorrelated jointly normal variables are independent (@thm-mvn-independence). [B2] For a model without an intercept, the quantity 1-	ext{SSE}/	ext{SST} is sometimes reported as R^2. Show that it is negative iff the model fits worse than the intercept-only model. Construct a data set with n=4 and one regressor for which it is below -1. C. Going deeper [C1] Let \mathcal V be a subspace with projection  P. Show that 
orm{ P\y}^2=\max_{ v\in\mathcal V,\  v
eq zero} rac{( v\T\y)^2}{ v\T v}, with the maximum attained at  v= P\y when  P\y
eq zero. Interpret: the sum of squares of a row with r_i degrees of freedom is the largest one-degree-of-freedom sum of squares obtainable by refining that row. Chapter 13 uses this fact to build Scheffé’s simultaneous intervals. For  v\in\mathcal V,  v\T\y= v\T P\y, so by Cauchy–Schwarz (@prp-mat-cauchy-schwarz) ( v\T\y)^2\le v\T v\,
orm{ P\y}^2, with equality iff  v is a multiple of  P\y. Taking  v= P\y\in\mathcal V attains the bound. A line \spn( v) inside \mathcal V carries the one-degree-of-freedom sum of squares ( v\T\y)^2/ v\T v (@exm-proj-line), so no refinement of the row gives a line with a larger sum of squares than the whole row.

title: 9.2 Extra sums of squares
content:
Extra sums of squares Most questions asked of a regression compare two models. Each question names a reduced model inside the full one, and the natural measure of what the full model adds is how much it lowers the residual sum of squares. This section develops that measure, its computation when regressors are added to a fitted model, and a closed form when the reduced model is defined by linear constraints. Notation [Extra sum of squares] Let \X_1 and \X_2 be matrices with n rows, let \X=[\X_1,\X_2], and let \M_1 and \M be the projections onto \C(\X_1) and \C(\X). The extra sum of squares of \X_2 given \X_1 is 	ext{SS}(\X_2\mid\X_1)=\y\T(\M-\M_1)\y=	ext{SSE}(\X_1)-	ext{SSE}(\X), with ank(\X)-ank(\X_1) degrees of freedom. Here 	ext{SSE}(\cdot) is the residual sum of squares of the model with the given model matrix. The two expressions agree by @eq-proj-extra-ss. One also writes 	ext{SS}( beta_2\mid beta_1), or 	ext{SS}(B\mid\mu,A) in factor models; some books write R, for “reduction”. Four properties follow from @thm-proj-nested and @thm-proj-reparam. 1. It depends only on the two column spaces. Rescaling, recoding, centring, replacing \X_2 by \X_2+\X_1\B, and rank deficiency change nothing. 2. It is nonnegative, and zero iff \M\y=\M_1\y, that is, iff adding \X_2 leaves the fitted values unchanged. 3. It obeys a chain rule: 	ext{SS}(\X_2,\X_3\mid\X_1)=	ext{SS}(\X_2\mid\X_1)+	ext{SS}(\X_3\mid\X_1,\X_2), because the projections telescope. 4. It is the sum of squares of a residualized regression. The next lemma makes this precise. [Extra sums of squares by residualizing] For any \X_1 and \X_2, let 	ilde{\X}_2=(\I-\M_1)\X_2. Then \C([\X_1,\X_2])=\C(\X_1)\dirsum\C(	ilde{\X}_2) with the two summands orthogonal, so \M=\M_1+ P_{\C(	ilde{\X}_2)} and 	ext{SS}(\X_2\mid\X_1)=
orm{ P_{\C(	ilde{\X}_2)}\y}^2 =\y\T	ilde{\X}_2(	ilde{\X}_2\T	ilde{\X}_2)\ginv	ilde{\X}_2\T\y . The argument for part (a) of @lem-proj-fwl-split uses no rank condition, so it applies here: the columns of 	ilde{\X}_2 lie in \C(\X) and are orthogonal to \C(\X_1), and every \X_1 b_1+\X_2 b_2 equals 	ilde{\X}_2 b_2+(\X_1 b_1+\M_1\X_2 b_2). By @thm-proj-sum, \M=\M_1+ P_{\C(	ilde{\X}_2)}. The formula is @thm-proj-M-formula applied to 	ilde{\X}_2. Adding regressors to a fitted model Suppose \E(\Y)=\X beta has been fitted and we add the columns of an n	imes t matrix \mathbf{Z}, giving \E(\Y)=\X beta+\mathbf{Z} gamma with model matrix \W=[\X,\mathbf{Z}]. Only a t	imes t matrix has to be inverted. [Adding regressors] Let \W=[\X,\mathbf{Z}] have full column rank p+t, let \mathbf{C}=(\X\T\X)^{-1}, \hbeta=\mathbf{C}\X\T\y, and \R=\I-\X\mathbf{C}\X\T. Then: 1. \mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z} is positive definite; 2. the least squares coefficients of the enlarged model are \hat{ gamma}=(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}\mathbf{Z}\T\R\y,\qquad \hbeta_W=\hbeta- L\hat{ gamma},\qquad  L=\mathbf{C}\X\T\mathbf{Z} ; 3. the residual sum of squares falls by 	ext{SS}(\mathbf{Z}\mid\X)=\y\T\R\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}\mathbf{Z}\T\R\y=\hat{ gamma}\T\mathbf{Z}\T\R\y =\hat{ gamma}\T(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})\hat{ gamma} ; 4. if \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I, then \Cov(\hat{ gamma})=\sigma^2(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}, \Cov(\hbeta_W,\hat{ gamma})=- L\Cov(\hat{ gamma}) and \Cov(\hbeta_W)=\sigma^2 igl[\mathbf{C}+ L(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1} L\T igr]. (a) \R is the symmetric idempotent residual projection of the model \X, so \mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{a}=
orm{\R\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{a}}^2\ge0. If \R\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{a}= zero, then \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{a}\in\C(\X), say \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{a}=\X b, so \W(- b\T,\mathbf{a}\T)\T= zero and full column rank forces \mathbf{a}= zero. (b) Apply the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem (@thm-proj-fwl) with \X_1=\mathbf{Z} and \X_2=\X. Then \M_2=\I-\R and 	ilde{\X}_1=\R\mathbf{Z}, so part (a) of that theorem gives \hat{ gamma}=(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}\mathbf{Z}\T\R\y, which is the stated formula because \R is symmetric and idempotent. Part (c) of the theorem gives \hbeta_W=\mathbf{C}\X\T(\y-\mathbf{Z}\hat{ gamma})=\hbeta- L\hat{ gamma}. (c) By @lem-ss-residualized, the extra sum of squares is the squared length of the projection of \y onto \C(\R\mathbf{Z}), which is \y\T\R\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}\mathbf{Z}\T\R\y by @thm-proj-M-formula. Substituting (b) gives the other two forms. (d) Both \hat{ gamma} and \hbeta are linear in \y, and by @thm-rv-linear \Cov(\hat{ gamma})=\sigma^2(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}\mathbf{Z}\T\R\R\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}=\sigma^2(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}, \qquad \Cov(\hbeta,\hat{ gamma})=\sigma^2\mathbf{C}\X\T\R\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1}= zero , since \X\T\R= zero. With \Cov(\hbeta)=\sigma^2\mathbf{C} (@thm-lm-moments), the formula \hbeta_W=\hbeta- L\hat{ gamma} gives \Cov(\hbeta_W,\hat{ gamma})=- L\Cov(\hat{ gamma}) and \Cov(\hbeta_W)=\Cov(\hbeta)+ L\Cov(\hat{ gamma}) L\T. Since  L(\mathbf{Z}\T\R\mathbf{Z})^{-1} L\T is nonnegative definite, part (d) shows that adding regressors never decreases the variances of the coefficients already in the model, when both models are correct (compare @exr-mat-adding-regressors, and see @exr-ss-no-variance-change). Chapter 26 measures this price of adjustment as variance inflation (@def-col-vif). In computation one updates a QR factorization instead of using these formulas (Chapter 10). [Adding poverty and urbanization] In the state data, fit the murder rate on single parenthood first: \hat{y}=-8.2146+0.5147\,x_{	ext{single}}, with residual sum of squares 121.92. Now add \mathbf{Z}=[\x_{	ext{poverty}},\x_{	ext{urban}}]. The listing computes \hat{ gamma}=(0.2538,\,0.0046) from the old residual projection alone, and corrects the old coefficients to -9.0946 and 0.3980. These agree with a fresh fit of the enlarged model. The residual sum of squares falls by 19.96, on 2 degrees of freedom, to 101.96. Single parenthood’s coefficient drops by almost a quarter once poverty is allowed to take its share, the pattern seen in @exm-proj-sequential-order. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm data = sm.datasets.statecrime.load_pandas().data.drop(index="District of Columbia") y = data["murder"].to_numpy() n = len(y) one = np.ones(n) cols = {"poverty": data["poverty"].to_numpy(), "single": data["single"].to_numpy(), "urban": data["urban"].to_numpy()} X = np.column_stack([one, cols["single"]]) # the model already fitted Z = np.column_stack([cols["poverty"], cols["urban"]]) # the regressors to add XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) beta_X = XtX_inv @ X.T @ y R = np.eye(n) - X @ XtX_inv @ X.T # residual projection of the old model gamma = np.linalg.solve(Z.T @ R @ Z, Z.T @ R @ y) # new coefficients beta_new = beta_X - XtX_inv @ X.T @ Z @ gamma # old coefficients, corrected extra_ss = gamma @ Z.T @ R @ y # SS(Z | X) = SSE_X - SSE_W print("gamma =", gamma.round(4), " corrected beta =", beta_new.round(4)) print(f"SSE_X = {y @ R @ y:.2f}, extra SS = {extra_ss:.2f}") One column at a time With t=1, @thm-ss-adding links the extra sum of squares of a single regressor to its coefficient and standard error. [The extra sum of squares of one column] Let \X have full column rank p, write c_{jj} for the jth diagonal entry of (\X\T\X)^{-1}, and let \X_{(j)} be \X without its jth column. Then 	ext{SS}(\x_j\mid\X_{(j)})= rac{\hat{ eta}_j^2}{c_{jj}}=t_j^2\,s^2, \qquad t_j= rac{\hat{ eta}_j}{s\sqrt{c_{jj}}},\quad s^2= rac{	ext{SSE}}{n-p}. Consequently, the ratio of this one-degree-of-freedom sum of squares to the residual mean square is t_j^2. Permute the columns so that \x_j comes last; this carries c_{jj} to the last diagonal entry of the inverse. Write \X=[\X_{(j)},\x_j] and \R=\I-\X_{(j)}(\X_{(j)}\T\X_{(j)})^{-1}\X_{(j)}\T for the residual projection of \X_{(j)}. By @thm-mat-partitioned-inverse the last diagonal entry of (\X\T\X)^{-1} is the inverse of the Schur complement \x_j\T\x_j-\x_j\T\X_{(j)}(\X_{(j)}\T\X_{(j)})^{-1}\X_{(j)}\T\x_j=\x_j\T\R\x_j, so \x_j\T\R\x_j=1/c_{jj}. Now apply @thm-ss-adding with \X_{(j)} as the old model and \mathbf{Z}=\x_j: then \hat{\gamma}=\hat{ eta}_j, and part (c) gives 	ext{SS}(\x_j\mid\X_{(j)})=\hat{ eta}_j^2\,\x_j\T\R\x_j=\hat{ eta}_j^2/c_{jj}. The definition of t_j gives the last form. For poverty in the three-regressor model, \hat{ eta}=0.2538 and c_{jj}=0.003935, so the extra sum of squares is 0.2538^2/0.003935=16.37. This is exactly the last entry for poverty in Order B of @exm-proj-sequential-order. The t statistic is 2.718, and t^2s^2=7.386	imes2.217=16.37. Xf = np.column_stack([one, cols["poverty"], cols["single"], cols["urban"]]) fit = sm.OLS(y, Xf).fit() C = np.linalg.inv(Xf.T @ Xf) j = 1 # poverty partial_ss = fit.params[j] ** 2 / C[j, j] print(f"beta = {fit.params[j]:.4f}, c_jj = {C[j, j]:.6f}, beta^2/c_jj = {partial_ss:.2f}") print(f"t = {fit.tvalues[j]:.3f}, t^2 * s^2 = {fit.tvalues[j] ** 2 * fit.scale:.2f}") Sums of squares for linear hypotheses Reduced models often come as constraints: two coefficients are equal, a set of coefficients vanishes, a contrast among group means is zero. Section 6.5 identified the test space of such a constraint (@thm-proj-constraint-space). The next theorem gives its sum of squares in terms of the least squares estimate, with no reduced model fitted. [Sum of squares of a linear hypothesis] Let  Lambda be a p	imes q matrix of rank q such that each entry of  Lambda\T beta is estimable, so that  Lambda=\X\T T for some n	imes q matrix  T=[ oldsymbol{\uprho}_1,\dots, oldsymbol{\uprho}_q] (@def-est-estimable, @thm-proj-invariant-functions). Let \G be any generalized inverse of \X\T\X, let \hbeta be any least squares estimate, and let \mathbf{d}\in\Real^q. Then: 1.  Lambda\T\hbeta and  Lambda\T\G Lambda do not depend on the choices of \hbeta and \G, and  Lambda\T\G Lambda is positive definite; 2. the subspace \mathcal S_0=\{\X b: Lambda\T b= zero\} of \C(\X) has orthogonal complement in \C(\X) equal to \C(\M T), of dimension q, and the projection onto \C(\M T) is \M T( Lambda\T\G Lambda)^{-1} T\T\M; 3. the minimum of 
orm{\y-\X b}^2 over \{ b: Lambda\T b=\mathbf{d}\} exceeds 	ext{SSE} by 	ext{SS}_H=( Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d})\T( Lambda\T\G Lambda)^{-1}( Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d}). {#eq-ss-hypothesis} (a)  Lambda\T\hbeta= T\T\X\hbeta= T\T\M\y and  Lambda\T\G Lambda= T\T\X\G\X\T T= T\T\M T by @thm-proj-M-formula, and neither expression involves the choices. Since \X\T\M=\X\T, we have \X\T(\M T)= Lambda, which has rank q, so the q columns of \M T are linearly independent. Hence  T\T\M T=(\M T)\T(\M T) is positive definite. (b)  Lambda\T b= T\T\X b, so \mathcal S_0=\C(\X)\cap\Null( T\T). @thm-proj-constraint-space identifies its orthogonal complement in \C(\X) as \C(\M T). The columns of \M T are independent, so @thm-proj-M-formula gives the projection \M T( T\T\M T)^{-1} T\T\M, and  T\T\M T= Lambda\T\G Lambda by (a). (c) First let \mathbf{d}= zero. Minimizing over  Lambda\T b= zero is minimizing 
orm{\y- mu}^2 over  mu\in\mathcal S_0, so by @eq-proj-extra-ss the excess over 	ext{SSE} is the squared length of the projection of \y onto \C(\X)\ominus\mathcal S_0=\C(\M T), where \ominus denotes the orthogonal complement within \C(\X). By (b) this is \y\T\M T( Lambda\T\G Lambda)^{-1} T\T\M\y, and  T\T\M\y= Lambda\T\hbeta. For general \mathbf{d}, the rows of  Lambda\T are independent, so there is a  b_0 with  Lambda\T b_0=\mathbf{d}. Substituting  b= b_0+ b_* turns the problem into minimizing 
orm{\y_*-\X b_*}^2 subject to  Lambda\T b_*= zero, with \y_*=\y-\X b_0. The data \y_* have the same residual sum of squares as \y, and \hbeta- b_0 is a least squares estimate for them, since \X(\hbeta- b_0)=\M\y_*. Applying the case \mathbf{d}= zero to \y_* gives @eq-ss-hypothesis, because  Lambda\T(\hbeta- b_0)= Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d}. In @eq-ss-hypothesis,  Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d} measures how far the estimate is from the hypothesis, and \sigma^2 Lambda\T\G Lambda is the covariance of  Lambda\T\hbeta (Chapter 7), so 	ext{SS}_H/\sigma^2 is the squared Mahalanobis length of the discrepancy (@prp-mvn-mahalanobis). No reduced model has to be fitted. In the full-rank case the constrained minimizer itself has a closed form, which recovers the classical restricted least squares estimator. [Restricted least squares] Let \X have full column rank, \mathbf{C}=(\X\T\X)^{-1}, and let  Lambda (p	imes q) have rank q. For any \mathbf{d}\in\Real^q, the unique minimizer of 
orm{\y-\X b}^2 subject to  Lambda\T b=\mathbf{d} is \hbeta_H=\hbeta-\mathbf{C} Lambda( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1}( Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d}), and 
orm{\y-\X\hbeta_H}^2=	ext{SSE}+
orm{\X(\hbeta-\hbeta_H)}^2, where the last term equals 	ext{SS}_H of @eq-ss-hypothesis with \G=\mathbf{C}.  Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda is positive definite because \mathbf{C} is and  Lambda has full column rank, and  Lambda\T\hbeta_H= Lambda\T\hbeta-( Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d})=\mathbf{d}. For any  b, @eq-proj-distance-split with  u=\X b gives 
orm{\y-\X b}^2=	ext{SSE}+
orm{\X(\hbeta- b)}^2. Every feasible  b has the form \hbeta_H+ v with  Lambda\T v= zero, and then 
orm{\X(\hbeta- b)}^2=
orm{\X(\hbeta-\hbeta_H)}^2-2(\hbeta-\hbeta_H)\T\X\T\X v+
orm{\X v}^2 . The cross term vanishes: (\hbeta-\hbeta_H)\T\X\T\X v=( Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d})\T( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1} Lambda\T\mathbf{C}\X\T\X v =( Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d})\T( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1} Lambda\T v=0. So the objective is 	ext{SSE}+
orm{\X(\hbeta-\hbeta_H)}^2+
orm{\X v}^2, minimized exactly when \X v= zero, that is,  v= zero. Finally 
orm{\X(\hbeta-\hbeta_H)}^2=( Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d})\T( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1} Lambda\T\mathbf{C}\X\T\X\mathbf{C} Lambda( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1}( Lambda\T\hbeta-\mathbf{d}), which simplifies to 	ext{SS}_H. The same estimator comes out of Lagrange multipliers (@prp-mat-lagrange with \A=\X\T\X). The proof above shows instead that the constrained fit is the feasible point nearest to \hbeta in the geometry of \X\T\X. [Equal effects of poverty and single parenthood] Both poverty and single parenthood are percentages of the population. Is one percentage point of either associated with the same change in the murder rate? The hypothesis is  lambda\T beta=0 with  lambda=(0,1,-1,0)\T. Formula @eq-ss-hypothesis gives 	ext{SS}_H=1.807 on one degree of freedom, identical to the drop in residual sum of squares when the two regressors are replaced by their sum. Its ratio to the residual mean square is 0.815, so the data are entirely compatible with equal effects. For a hypothesis with a nonzero right-hand side,  eta_{	ext{single}}=0.5, @thm-ss-restricted gives the constrained coefficients 0.1803 for poverty and -0.0044 for urbanization, and a sum of squares of 3.357, both confirmed by a direct fit of the reduced model. def hypothesis_ss(X, y, Lam, d=None): """(L'b - d)' [L' (X'X)^- L]^{-1} (L'b - d) for estimable L'beta = d.""" G = np.linalg.pinv(X.T @ X) b = G @ X.T @ y u = Lam.T @ b - (0 if d is None else d) return u @ np.linalg.solve(Lam.T @ G @ Lam, u) def sse(Z): b, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Z, y, rcond=None) e = y - Z @ b return e @ e Lam_equal = np.array([[0.0, 1.0, -1.0, 0.0]]).T # beta_poverty = beta_single ss_equal = hypothesis_ss(Xf, y, Lam_equal) X_equal = np.column_stack([one, cols["poverty"] + cols["single"], cols["urban"]]) print(f"H: equal slopes formula {ss_equal:.3f} SSE_0 - SSE {sse(X_equal) - sse(Xf):.3f}") Constraints that are not estimable Without estimability, the reduced model \mathcal S_0=\{\X b: Lambda\T b= zero\} is still defined, but it may be larger than the number of constraints suggests. [How much a constraint restricts] For any p	imes q matrix  Lambda, the subspace \mathcal S_0=\{\X b: Lambda\T b= zero\} has dimension r-\dim igl(\C( Lambda)\cap\C(\X\T) igr). So the extra sum of squares for the constraint has \dim igl(\C( Lambda)\cap\C(\X\T) igr) degrees of freedom. It is identically zero iff no nonzero linear combination of the constrained functions is estimable. \mathcal S_0 is the image of \Null( Lambda\T) under  b\mapsto\X b, and the kernel of this map restricted to \Null( Lambda\T) is \Null( Lambda\T)\cap\Null(\X), the null space of the stacked matrix [ Lambda,\X\T]\T. By rank–nullity (@thm-mat-rank-nullity), \dim\mathcal S_0=\dim\Null( Lambda\T)-\dim igl(\Null( Lambda\T)\cap\Null(\X) igr) =(p-ank Lambda)- igl(p-ank[ Lambda,\X\T] igr). The dimension formula for a sum of subspaces (Section 6.2) gives ank[ Lambda,\X\T]=\dim igl(\C( Lambda)+\C(\X\T) igr)=ank Lambda+r-\dim igl(\C( Lambda)\cap\C(\X\T) igr). Substituting, \dim\mathcal S_0=r-\dim igl(\C( Lambda)\cap\C(\X\T) igr). The degrees of freedom of the extra sum of squares are r-\dim\mathcal S_0. A combination  Lambda\mathbf{a} is estimable iff it lies in \C(\X\T) (@thm-proj-invariant-functions), which gives the last statement. In the one-way layout \E(Y_{ij})=\mu+\alpha_i, the constraint \alpha_1=\alpha_2 has one degree of freedom. The constraint \alpha_1=0 has none: it does not restrict the mean vector, and only picks one of the least squares solutions (@thm-est-side-conditions). Software asked to “test” a nonestimable hypothesis either refuses or silently tests its estimable part. Chapter 17 meets this with empty cells (@thm-ub-empty-cells). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] In simple regression, compute 	ext{SS}_H for  eta_1=0 from @eq-ss-hypothesis and show that it equals \hat{ eta}_1^2S_{xx}, in agreement with @exr-ss-simple-anova. B. Practice [B1] Prove the chain rule 	ext{SS}(\X_2,\X_3\mid\X_1)=	ext{SS}(\X_2\mid\X_1)+	ext{SS}(\X_3\mid\X_1,\X_2), and deduce 	ext{SS}(\X_3\mid\X_1,\X_2)\le	ext{SS}(\X_2,\X_3\mid\X_1). Show by an example from @exm-ss-adding-crime or its listing that 	ext{SS}(\X_3\mid\X_1,\X_2)\le	ext{SS}(\X_3\mid\X_1) can fail. Let \M_1, \M_{12} and \M_{123} be the projections onto the nested column spaces. Then \M_{123}-\M_1=(\M_{12}-\M_1)+(\M_{123}-\M_{12}), and the chain rule follows by taking \y\T(\cdot)\y. Both terms are nonnegative, which gives the inequality. For the failure, the listing of Section 9.3 reports 	ext{SS}(\x_{	ext{urban}}\mid one)=6.30 but 	ext{SS}(\x_{	ext{urban}}\mid one,\x_{	ext{poverty}})=29.26. Adjusting for poverty more than quadruples the sum of squares for urbanization. [B2] In @thm-ss-restricted with \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I, show that \Cov(\hbeta_H)=\sigma^2 igl[\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{C} Lambda( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1} Lambda\T\mathbf{C} igr], that \Cov(\hbeta)-\Cov(\hbeta_H) is nonnegative definite, and that \E(\hbeta_H)= beta when the constraint is true. What is \E(\hbeta_H) when it is false? Write \mathbf{K}=\mathbf{C} Lambda( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1}, so \hbeta_H=(\I-\mathbf{K} Lambda\T)\hbeta+\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d}. By @thm-rv-linear and \Cov(\hbeta)=\sigma^2\mathbf{C}, \Cov(\hbeta_H)=\sigma^2(\I-\mathbf{K} Lambda\T)\mathbf{C}(\I- Lambda\mathbf{K}\T). Expanding and using  Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1}=\I, the two cross terms and the last term all equal \mathbf{K} Lambda\T\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C} Lambda( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1} Lambda\T\mathbf{C}, with signs -,-,+, which gives the formula. The difference \sigma^2\mathbf{C} Lambda( Lambda\T\mathbf{C} Lambda)^{-1} Lambda\T\mathbf{C} is of the form \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\T with \mathbf{A} positive definite, hence nonnegative definite. Finally \E(\hbeta_H)= beta-\mathbf{K}( Lambda\T beta-\mathbf{d}), which is  beta iff  Lambda\T beta=\mathbf{d}. A false constraint buys the smaller variance at the price of a bias. [B3] In the one-way layout with model matrix \X=[ one, z_1,\dots, z_g] and group sizes n_1,\dots,n_g, use the generalized inverse \G=\diag(0,1/n_1,\dots,1/n_g) in @eq-ss-hypothesis to show that the sum of squares for \alpha_1=\alpha_2 is ( ar{y}_1- ar{y}_2)^2/(1/n_1+1/n_2). Verify with @prp-ss-effective-df that the constraint \alpha_1=0 has zero degrees of freedom. \G is a generalized inverse because \X\T\X has the block form with first row (n,n_1,\dots,n_g) and lower right block \diag(n_1,\dots,n_g), and a direct multiplication gives \X\T\X\G\X\T\X=\X\T\X. With  lambda=(0,1,-1,0,\dots,0)\T, \G\X\T\y=(0, ar{y}_1,\dots, ar{y}_g)\T, so  lambda\T\hbeta= ar{y}_1- ar{y}_2 and  lambda\T\G lambda=1/n_1+1/n_2. For \alpha_1=0,  lambda=(0,1,0,\dots,0)\T is not in \C(\X\T) (@exm-proj-ginverse-numeric), and \C( lambda) is a line, so \C( lambda)\cap\C(\X\T)=\{ zero\}. C. Going deeper [C1] Using @exr-ss-max-single and @lem-ss-residualized, show that 	ext{SS}(\X_2\mid\X_1)=\max_{\mathbf{a}} rac{(\mathbf{a}\T	ilde{\X}_2\T\y)^2}{\mathbf{a}\T	ilde{\X}_2\T	ilde{\X}_2\mathbf{a}}, the maximum being over \mathbf{a} with 	ilde{\X}_2\mathbf{a}
eq zero. Deduce that the extra sum of squares of a block is at least that of any single column of the block, given \X_1, and that the sum of squares of an estimable hypothesis  Lambda\T beta= zero equals \max_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{a}\T Lambda\T\hbeta)^2/(\mathbf{a}\T Lambda\T\G Lambda\mathbf{a}). [C2] @exr-mat-adding-regressors gives the matrix inequality behind the remark after @thm-ss-adding. Using part (d) of that theorem instead, show that \Var(\hat{ eta}_{W,j})=\Var(\hat{ eta}_j) iff the jth row of  L is zero, and that this holds for every j iff \X\T\mathbf{Z}= zero. Show that when \X\T\mathbf{Z}= zero the estimates \hbeta do not change at all. [C3] In the additive two-way model \E(Y_{ijk})=\mu+\alpha_i+ eta_j with all cells occupied, use @prp-ss-effective-df to find the degrees of freedom of the extra sums of squares for the constraints (i) \sum_i\alpha_i=0 and \sum_j eta_j=0; (ii) \alpha_1=\alpha_2; (iii) \alpha_1=0 and \alpha_1=\alpha_2.

title: 9.3 Sequential and partial sums of squares
content:
Sequential and partial sums of squares How should the variation explained by a model be shared among its terms? A term is a block of columns representing one idea: a regressor, the coding columns of a factor, or an interaction. One answer enters the terms one at a time and credits each with what it adds to those already present. Another credits each term with what it adds when entered last. This section defines both, explains the three “types” of sums of squares that software prints, and identifies the hypothesis that each of them addresses. Sequential sums of squares Write the model matrix as a sequence of terms, \X=[\X_0,\X_1,\dots,\X_k], where \X_0 is usually the intercept column  one. Let \M_j be the projection onto \C(\X_0,\X_1,\dots,\X_j), so that \M_k=\M. Sequential sums of squares The sequential (or Type I) sum of squares of the term \X_j, for the order \X_0,\X_1,\dots,\X_k, is 	ext{SS}(\X_j\mid\X_0,\dots,\X_{j-1})=\y\T(\M_j-\M_{j-1})\y ,\qquad j=1,\dots,k, with d_j=ank(\M_j)-ank(\M_{j-1}) degrees of freedom. The sequential sums of squares are the analysis of variance decomposition of @thm-ss-decomposition(e) for the chain \C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X_0,\X_1)\subseteq\dots\subseteq\C(\X), after the first piece \M_0 has been set aside. They add up to the regression sum of squares 	ext{SS}(\X_1,\dots,\X_k\mid\X_0), their degrees of freedom add up to r-ank(\X_0), and under normality they are independent of each other and of the residual sum of squares (@thm-qf-orthogonal-projections). A term linearly dependent on earlier ones receives zero degrees of freedom. The price is that each piece depends on the order: \X_j is credited only with the part of its span orthogonal to the terms that happen to precede it. For the murder rates of Section 6.5, poverty received 102.49 first and 16.37 last (@exm-proj-sequential-order). The order dependence can be more surprising than “entering first gives more credit”.
