title: 28.4 Support recovery
content:
Support recovery Good prediction does not require the right variables: the bounds of Section 28.3 allow false variables with small coefficients and missed true ones. Often, though, the variables are the object of interest. This section asks when the lasso selects exactly the right variables with the right signs. The answer needs a condition on the design much stronger than those of Section 28.2, and it fails in simple, realistic examples. Uniqueness The question “which variables does the lasso select?” needs an answer that does not depend on which minimizer is reported. [Uniqueness of the lasso fit] 1. All lasso estimates at a given \lambda have the same fitted values \X\hat{ beta}_\lambda and the same \ell_1 norm. Hence they share the vector \hat{ z}=\X\T(\Y-\X\hat{ beta}_\lambda)/(n\lambda) of @eq-hd-optimality. 2. Let \hat{ beta}_\lambda be a lasso estimate with support \hat S. If |\hat z_j|<1 for every j
otin\hat S and \X_{\hat S} has full column rank, then \hat{ beta}_\lambda is the only lasso estimate. (a) The first statement is @thm-shr-lasso-kkt(c). The vector \hat{ z} depends on \hat{ beta}_\lambda only through \X\hat{ beta}_\lambda. (b) Let  b be any lasso estimate. By (a) its optimality conditions @eq-hd-optimality hold with the same \hat{ z}. If b_j
e0 then \hat z_j=\operatorname{sign}(b_j), so |\hat z_j|=1 and j\in\hat S. Thus  b is supported on \hat S, and \X_{\hat S} b_{\hat S}=\X b=\X\hat{ beta}_\lambda=\X_{\hat S}\hat{ beta}_{\lambda,\hat S}. Full column rank of \X_{\hat S} gives  b=\hat{ beta}_\lambda. The irrepresentable condition When will the lasso choose exactly S? Suppose for a moment that it does, with the correct signs  z_S=\operatorname{sign}( beta_S). Then @eq-hd-optimality on S determines the estimate: \X_S\T(\Y-\X_S\hat{ beta}_S)/n=\lambda z_S, so  egin{aligned} \hat{ beta}_S&=(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}(\X_S\T\Y-n\lambda z_S)\ &= beta_S+(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}\X_S\T e-\lambda\hat{ Sigma}_{SS}^{-1} z_S , \end{aligned} {#eq-hd-oracle-lasso} where \hat{ Sigma}_{SS}=\X_S\T\X_S/n. The estimate is least squares on the true support, shifted towards zero by \lambda\hat{ Sigma}_{SS}^{-1} z_S. For each k
otin S, the optimality conditions also require |\x_k\T(\Y-\X_S\hat{ beta}_S)|\le n\lambda. Since \Y-\X_S\hat{ beta}_S=(\I-\M_S) e+n\lambda\X_S(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1} z_S, where \M_S projects onto \C(\X_S), this reads \Bigl|\,\underbrace{\x_k\T\X_S(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1} z_S}_{a_k}+ rac{\x_k\T(\I-\M_S) e}{n\lambda}\,\Bigr|\le1 . {#eq-hd-dual-feasibility} The first term does not involve the noise at all. The vector (\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}\X_S\T\x_k holds the least squares coefficients of \x_k on the active columns, and a_k is their sum weighted by the true signs. If an inactive column is well explained by the active ones, with coefficients that line up with the signs of  beta_S, then |a_k| is large and the condition is hard to meet. [Irrepresentable and beta-min conditions] Let \X_S have full column rank. The design satisfies the irrepresentable condition for  beta with margin \eta\in(0,1] if \max_{k
otin S}\  igl|\x_k\T\X_S(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}\operatorname{sign}( beta_S) igr|\le1-\eta . A beta-min condition is a lower bound on  eta_{\min}=\min_{j\in S}| eta_j|. The condition depends on the design and on the signs of the true coefficients, but not on their sizes. It holds with \eta=1 when the inactive columns are orthogonal to the active ones. It is much stronger than the compatibility condition. van de Geer and Bühlmann (2009) compare the two and show that a uniform version of the irrepresentable condition implies compatibility; the example below shows that the converse fails. Sufficient conditions [Sign recovery by the lasso] Suppose \lambda_{\min}(\hat{ Sigma}_{SS})\ge C_{\min}>0 and the irrepresentable condition holds with margin \eta. Let \lambda>0, put g=\lambda
orm{\hat{ Sigma}_{SS}^{-1}\operatorname{sign}( beta_S)}_\infty, and suppose  eta_{\min}>g. Consider the events \mathcal{A}=\Bigl\{\max_{k
otin S} rac{|\x_k\T(\I-\M_S) e|}{n}<\eta\lambda\Bigr\}, \mathcal{B}=\Bigl\{ igl\|(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}\X_S\T e igr\|_\infty< eta_{\min}-g\Bigr\}. 1. On \mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{B} the lasso estimate is unique and \operatorname{sign}(\hat{ beta}_\lambda)=\operatorname{sign}( beta). In particular its support is exactly S. 2. The probabilities of the complements satisfy \Pr(\mathcal{A}^c)\le2(p-s)\exp\Bigl\{- rac{n\eta^2\lambda^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\},\qquad \Pr(\mathcal{B}^c)\le2s\exp\Bigl\{- rac{nC_{\min}( eta_{\min}-g)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\}. 3. Consequently, if \lambda= rac{\sigma}{\eta}\sqrt{ rac{2\log\{4(p-s)/\delta\}}{n}}\quad	ext{and}\quad  eta_{\min}\ge g+\sigma\sqrt{ rac{2\log(4s/\delta)}{nC_{\min}}}, the lasso recovers the signs of  beta with probability at least 1-\delta. (a) Construct a candidate and check that it is optimal. This is the primal–dual witness argument. Let  z_S=\operatorname{sign}( beta_S), let \check{ beta} be zero off S with \check{ beta}_S given by the right side of @eq-hd-oracle-lasso, and let \check{ z}=\X\T(\Y-\X\check{ beta})/(n\lambda). On S. By construction \X_S\T(\Y-\X_S\check{ beta}_S)=n\lambda z_S, so \check{ z}_S= z_S. By @eq-hd-oracle-lasso, for j\in S, |\check eta_j- eta_j|\le\|(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}\X_S\T e\|_\infty+g< eta_{\min}\le| eta_j| on \mathcal{B}. So \check eta_j is nonzero with the sign of  eta_j, and \check z_j=\operatorname{sign}(\check eta_j). Off S. Since \X beta=\X_S beta_S\in\C(\X_S), (\I-\M_S)\Y=(\I-\M_S) e, and \Y-\X_S\check{ beta}_S=\Y-\M_S\Y+n\lambda\X_S(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1} z_S =(\I-\M_S) e+n\lambda\X_S(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1} z_S . So for k
otin S, \check z_k=a_k+\x_k\T(\I-\M_S) e/(n\lambda), with |a_k|\le1-\eta by the irrepresentable condition. On \mathcal{A}, |\check z_k|<1-\eta+\eta=1. So \check{ beta} and \check{ z} satisfy @eq-hd-optimality, and \check{ beta} is a lasso estimate, because the conditions are sufficient (@thm-shr-lasso-kkt(b)). Its support is S, \X_S has full column rank because C_{\min}>0, and |\check z_k|<1 off S. By @lem-hd-lasso-unique(b) it is the only lasso estimate. (b) \x_k\T(\I-\M_S) e/n is normal with mean zero and variance \sigma^2
orm{(\I-\M_S)\x_k}^2/n^2\le\sigma^2
orm{\x_k}^2/n^2=\sigma^2/n. The jth entry of (\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}\X_S\T e is normal with mean zero and variance \sigma^2[(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}]_{jj}\le\sigma^2/(nC_{\min}), by @thm-mat-extremal-rayleigh applied to (\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}, whose largest eigenvalue is 1/(nC_{\min}) at most. Apply @lem-hd-gaussian-max with t=\eta\lambda and t= eta_{\min}-g. The events in the lemma use >, and the events here use \ge, which have the same probability for normal variables with positive variance (and probability zero for those with zero variance). (c) With the stated \lambda, the first bound in (b) equals \delta/2. With the stated  eta_{\min}, the second is at most \delta/2. The three hypotheses ask that the active columns be well conditioned (C_{\min}), that the inactive ones not be representable by them (\eta), and that the coefficients stand out from noise and shrinkage ( eta_{\min}). Since g\le\lambda\sqrt s/C_{\min}, the last asks in the worst case for every nonzero coefficient to exceed a multiple of \sigma\sqrt{s\log p/n}. The theorem in this form is due to Wainwright (2009). The condition is also necessary [Failure of the irrepresentable condition] Let \X_S have full column rank, and suppose that for some k
otin S |a_k|= igl|\x_k\T\X_S(\X_S\T\X_S)^{-1}\operatorname{sign}( beta_S) igr|>1 . Then the probability that for some \lambda>0 some lasso estimate has \operatorname{sign}(\hat{ beta}_\lambda)=\operatorname{sign}( beta) is at most 	frac12. Suppose a lasso estimate at some \lambda>0 has the signs of  beta. Its support is S, so by the calculation leading to @eq-hd-dual-feasibility, |a_k+W_k/(n\lambda)|\le1, where W_k=\x_k\T(\I-\M_S) e. Since |a_k|>1, this forces \operatorname{sign}(a_k)\,W_k/(n\lambda)\le1-|a_k|<0, so \operatorname{sign}(a_k)W_k<0. The event in question is therefore contained in \{\operatorname{sign}(a_k)W_k<0\}, which does not depend on \lambda. W_k is normal with mean zero, so this event has probability  rac12 if (\I-\M_S)\x_k
e zero, and probability zero otherwise. The argument is due to Zhao and Yu (2006), who showed in addition that the condition with \le1 is necessary for sign consistency. The bound  rac12 does not improve with more data. Sampling more observations cannot repair a design in which an inactive variable imitates the active ones with coefficients aligned with their signs. In the noiseless limit the lasso never recovers the signs (@exr-hd-noiseless). [An inactive variable that looks active] Let x_1,x_2 be independent standard normal regressors, let x_3 have correlation r with each of them, and let x_4,\dots,x_{500} be independent noise variables, with Y=0.5x_1+0.5x_2+\varepsilon and \sigma=1. The population coefficients of x_3 on (x_1,x_2) are (r,r), so a_3=2r (@exr-hd-irrepresentable-example). With r=0.3 the condition holds with margin 0.4; with the moderate correlation r=0.6 it fails. Both population designs have \lambda_{\min}( Sigma)>0, so both are benign for prediction. Figure 28.4.1(a) shows, for each sample size, the fraction of 200 data sets (fixed design, new errors) for which some penalty on a fine grid gives exactly the right signs. When the condition holds, this rises from 0.12 at n=50 to 0.66 at n=100 and 1.000 at n=800. When it fails, it rises only slowly, from 0.03 at n=100 to 0.155 at n=800, and it can never exceed the bound  rac12 of @prp-hd-irrepresentable-necessary, however large n is. The sample irrepresentable quantities at n=800 are 0.66 and 1.21. Panel (b) shows why. Along the lasso path for one data set with r=0.6 and n=800, the inactive x_3 is the first variable to enter, because its inner product \x_3\T\X beta/n with the signal (the mean of the \x_3\T\Y/n that decides which variable enters first) is 0.62 in this sample (0.6 in the population) and exceeds that of x_1 and x_2 (0.5 each). It never leaves. The lasso finds x_1 and x_2 later, but always together with x_3. [Figure 28.4.1. Support recovery with p=500, two active regressors and an inactive regressor correlated r with both. (a) Fraction of data sets in which some penalty gives exactly the right signs, against n. (b) The lasso path of one data set with r=0.6, n=800: the inactive x_3 enters first and stays; grey lines are the noise variables.] Figure 28.4.1. Support recovery with p=500, two active regressors and an inactive regressor correlated r with both. (a) Fraction of data sets in which some penalty gives exactly the right signs, against n. (b) The lasso path of one data set with r=0.6, n=800: the inactive x_3 enters first and stays; grey lines are the noise variables. [Support recovery with p=500, two active regressors and an inactive regressor correlated r with both. (a) Fraction of data sets in which some penalty gives exactly the right signs, against n. (b) The lasso path of one data set with r=0.6, n=800: the inactive x_3 enters first and stays; grey lines are the noise variables.] Support recovery with p=500, two active regressors and an inactive regressor correlated r with both. (a) Fraction of data sets in which some penalty gives exactly the right signs, against n. (b) The lasso path of one data set with r=0.6, n=800: the inactive x_3 enters first and stays; grey lines are the noise variables. import numpy as np def soft(z, t): """Soft thresholding S(z, t) = sign(z) max(|z| - t, 0).""" return np.sign(z) * np.maximum(np.abs(z) - t, 0.0) def lasso_cd(X, Y, lam, B=None, tol=1e-9, max_sweeps=2000): """Minimize ||y - X b||^2 / (2n) + lam ||b||_1 for every column y of Y, by coordinate descent.""" n, p = X.shape Y = Y.reshape(n, -1) B = np.zeros((p, Y.shape[1])) if B is None else B.copy() R = Y - X @ B # residuals, one column per response scale = np.sum(X ** 2, axis=0) / n active = np.arange(p) for sweep in range(max_sweeps): change = 0.0 for j in active: z = X[:, j] @ R / n + scale[j] * B[j] new = soft(z, lam) / scale[j] d = new - B[j] if np.any(d != 0): R -= np.outer(X[:, j], d) B[j] = new change = max(change, np.max(np.abs(d))) if change < tol: if len(active) == p: # converged over all coordinates break active = np.arange(p) # check every coordinate once more else: active = np.flatnonzero(np.any(B != 0, axis=1)) if sweep % 5 else np.arange(p) return B def make_design(rng, n, p, r): """x_1, x_2 independent; x_3 correlated r with each; x_4, ..., x_p independent noise.""" Z = rng.normal(size=(n, p)) Z[:, 2] = r * Z[:, 0] + r * Z[:, 1] + np.sqrt(1 - 2 * r ** 2) * Z[:, 2] return Z / np.sqrt(np.sum(Z ** 2, axis=0) / n) # ||x_j||^2 = n def irrepresentable(X, S, signs): """max over j outside S of |x_j^T X_S (X_S^T X_S)^{-1} sign(beta_S)|.""" A = X[:, S] w = A @ np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, signs) out = np.delete(X.T @ w, S) return np.max(np.abs(out)) def recovers_signs(X, Y, beta, lams): """For each column of Y: does some penalty in lams give exactly sign(beta)?""" ok = np.zeros(Y.shape[1], dtype=bool) B = None for lam in lams: # from large to small, warm starts B = lasso_cd(X, Y, lam, B) ok |= np.all(np.sign(B) == np.sign(beta)[:, None], axis=0) return ok rng = np.random.default_rng(2840) n, p, sigma = 100, 200, 1.0 beta = np.zeros(p) beta[:2] = 0.5 S = np.array([0, 1]) lams = np.geomspace(1.0, 0.1, 30) for r in [0.3, 0.6]: X = make_design(rng, n, p, r) Y = (X @ beta)[:, None] + sigma * rng.normal(size=(n, 100)) print(f"r = {r}: irrepresentable quantity {irrepresentable(X, S, np.ones(2)):.2f}," f" sign recovery in {recovers_signs(X, Y, beta, lams).mean():.2f} of 100 data sets") Screening instead of selection A weaker goal, often enough in practice, is screening: the selected set should contain S, with false variables left for a second stage to remove. It needs only the restricted eigenvalue and a beta-min condition. [Variable screening] Suppose \lambda\ge2\lambda_0, the event \mathcal{T} of @eq-hd-lambda0 occurs, \kappa^2(S)>0, and  eta_{\min}>3\lambda\sqrt s/\kappa^2(S). Then every lasso estimate has \hat S\supseteq S. If j\in S and \hat eta_{\lambda,j}=0, then |\hat eta_{\lambda,j}- eta_j|=| eta_j|\ge eta_{\min}. By @thm-hd-lasso-estimation(b), |\hat eta_{\lambda,j}- eta_j|\le
orm{\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta}\le3\lambda\sqrt s/\kappa^2(S)< eta_{\min}, a contradiction. In @exm-hd-irrepresentable with r=0.6, screening succeeds where selection fails: x_1 and x_2 are found, together with x_3. Second stages build on this. The thresholded lasso discards small coefficients and needs no irrepresentable condition (@exr-hd-thresholded). The adaptive lasso of Zou (2006) refits with penalty weights 1/|\hat eta_j| from a first stage, and stability selection (Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2010) keeps the variables selected in most subsamples. All need beta-min conditions; none can find a coefficient below the noise level. The lasso’s selected set is a random set that depends on small features of the data, especially among correlated regressors. Reporting it as “the important variables” without an assessment of its stability invites overinterpretation. Section 28.5 shows what goes wrong if the selected set is then treated as fixed. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] In the population version of @exm-hd-irrepresentable, with  Sigma_{SS}=\I_2 and  Sigma_{3S}=(r,r), compute  Sigma_{3S} Sigma_{SS}^{-1}\operatorname{sign}( beta_S) for  beta_S=(0.5,0.5) and for  beta_S=(0.5,-0.5). For which signs does the irrepresentable condition fail?  Sigma_{3S} Sigma_{SS}^{-1}=(r,r). With signs (1,1) the quantity is 2r, which exceeds 1 for r> rac12. With signs (1,-1) it is 0, so the condition holds with \eta=1. The trouble arises only when x_3 imitates the combination x_1+x_2 that appears in the signal. B. Practice [B1] Let  Sigma=(1-ho)\I+ho one one\T with 0\leho<1. Show that  Sigma_{kS} Sigma_{SS}^{-1} z_S=ho\,( one\T z_S)/\{1+(s-1)ho\} for k
otin S, and conclude that the population irrepresentable condition holds for every sign pattern, with margin at least (1-ho)/\{1+(s-1)ho\}. [B2] (Thresholded lasso.) Under the assumptions of @thm-hd-lasso-estimation(b), let B=3\lambda\sqrt s/\kappa^2(S) and suppose  eta_{\min}>2B. Show that \{j:|\hat eta_{\lambda,j}|>B\}=S, and that the signs of the retained coefficients are correct. No irrepresentable condition is needed. Every coordinate satisfies |\hat eta_{\lambda,j}- eta_j|\le
orm{\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta}\le B. For j
otin S, |\hat eta_{\lambda,j}|\le B, so j is discarded. For j\in S, |\hat eta_{\lambda,j}|\ge| eta_j|-B>2B-B=B, so j is kept, and \hat eta_{\lambda,j} lies within B<| eta_j| of  eta_j, so it has the same sign. The price is the stronger beta-min condition  eta_{\min}>6\lambda\sqrt s/\kappa^2(S) and a threshold that depends on the unknown \kappa and s. C. Going deeper [C1] Let \sigma=0, so \Y=\X beta, and let \X_S have full column rank. Show that if \max_{k
otin S}|a_k|<1, then every \lambda with 0<\lambda< eta_{\min}/
orm{\hat{ Sigma}_{SS}^{-1}\operatorname{sign}( beta_S)}_\infty gives a unique lasso estimate with the correct signs, and that if |a_k|>1 for some k
otin S, then no \lambda>0 does. With  e= zero, the events \mathcal{A} and \mathcal{B} of @thm-hd-support hold whenever \eta>0 and  eta_{\min}>g, which is the stated range of \lambda, with \eta=1-\max_k|a_k|. Part (a) of the theorem applies, and its proof uses no probability. Conversely, if some lasso estimate had the correct signs, @eq-hd-dual-feasibility with  e= zero would require |a_k|\le1 for all k
otin S. So with perfect data, the irrepresentable condition (in its weak form) is necessary and, with strict inequality, sufficient.

title: 28.5 Post-selection and debiased inference
content:
Post-selection and debiased inference This section turns to confidence intervals and tests for a single coefficient  eta_j when p>n. Two tempting approaches fail: least squares intervals for the model the lasso selected, as if it had been fixed in advance, and intervals around the lasso estimate itself, whose shrinkage bias is at least as large as its standard error. The fix is a one-step correction of the lasso, which turns out to be the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem with a lasso in place of a projection. Why intervals after selection fail The least squares interval of @thm-ci-estimable-interval has coverage 1-\alpha for a model fixed before the data are seen. After selection, the interval for  eta_j is computed only in the samples where x_j was selected, which are those in which its estimated effect happened to be large. Conditional on selection the estimate is biased away from zero, and the interval is centred in the wrong place. This is the winner’s curse of Chapter 29 (@prp-sel-selection-bias), and the multiplicity problem of Chapter 13 in another form. With the lasso and p>n it is severe, because the selection is among hundreds or thousands of candidates. Leeb and Pötscher (2006) proved that this cannot be repaired by estimating the distribution of the post-selection estimator, which depends on the unknown coefficients in a way that no estimator can track uniformly. One can change the target (the selected model’s coefficients, conditional on the selection) or the estimator. This section changes the estimator. The lasso estimate itself is no better as a centre for an interval. On the event of @thm-hd-support, @eq-hd-oracle-lasso shows that it equals least squares on S minus \lambda\hat{ Sigma}_{SS}^{-1}\operatorname{sign}( beta_S). The shift is of order \lambda\asymp\sigma\sqrt{\log p/n}, which is larger than the standard error \sigma/\sqrt n of the oracle estimate by the factor \sqrt{\log p}. An interval of the usual width centred at the lasso estimate misses the truth more and more often as p grows. The debiased lasso Write \hat{ Sigma}=\X\T\X/n, and let \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}} be a p	imes p matrix computed from \X alone, meant to act like an inverse of \hat{ Sigma} (which does not exist when p>n). Its rows are \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_1\T,\dots,\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_p\T. [Debiased lasso] Given a lasso estimate \hat{ beta}_\lambda and \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}, the debiased (or desparsified) lasso is \hat{\mathbf{b}}=\hat{ beta}_\lambda+ rac1n\,\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\X\T(\Y-\X\hat{ beta}_\lambda). {#eq-hd-debiased} Its jth entry uses only the row \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j. The quantity \mu_j=
orm{\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j-\mathbf{e}_j}_\infty measures how far \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j is from being the jth row of an inverse of \hat{ Sigma}. The correction adds to the lasso a multiple of the residual correlations \X\T(\Y-\X\hat{ beta}_\lambda)/n. If \hat{ Sigma} were invertible and \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}=\hat{ Sigma}^{-1}, \hat{\mathbf{b}} would be the least squares estimate (@exr-hd-debias-low-dim). [Debiased lasso] In the setting of Section 28.3, let \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}} depend on \X only, and let \hat{\mathbf{b}} be the debiased lasso. 1. (Decomposition.) \sqrt n(\hat{\mathbf{b}}- beta)=\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{r}, where \mathbf{w}=\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\X\T e/\sqrt n\sim\Normal_p( zero,\sigma^2\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\T) exactly, and \mathbf{r}=-\sqrt n(\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\hat{ Sigma}-\I)(\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta). 2. (Remainder.) |r_j|\le\sqrt n\,\mu_j
orm{\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta}_1. If \lambda\ge2\lambda_0, \phi^2(S)>0 and \mathcal{T} occurs, then |r_j|\le4\sqrt n\,\mu_j\lambda s/\phi^2(S). 3. (Variance.) If \mu_j<1, then \omega_j^2=\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j\T\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j\ge(1-\mu_j)^2. 4. (Asymptotic normality.) Consider a sequence of such problems with n	o\infty, in which p, s, \X,  beta and \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}} may change with n and \sigma is fixed. Suppose \lambda=2\lambda_0 with \delta=\delta_n	o0 and \log(1/\delta_n)=O(\log p); \phi^2(S)\ge\phi_0^2>0; \mu_j\le C\sqrt{\log p/n} for a constant C; s\log p/\sqrt n	o0; and \hat\sigma/\sigma	o1 in probability. Then T_j= rac{\sqrt n\,(\hat b_j- eta_j)}{\hat\sigma\,\omega_j}\ 	o\ \Normal(0,1)\quad	ext{in distribution}, {#eq-hd-debiased-t} and the interval \hat b_j\pm z_{\alpha/2}\hat\sigma\omega_j/\sqrt n has coverage tending to 1-\alpha. (a) Substitute \Y=\X beta+ e in @eq-hd-debiased and write  oldsymbol{\Delta}=\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta: \hat{\mathbf{b}}- beta= oldsymbol{\Delta}+ rac1n\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\X\T( e-\X oldsymbol{\Delta}) = rac1n\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\X\T e-(\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\hat{ Sigma}-\I) oldsymbol{\Delta} . Multiply by \sqrt n. Since \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}} is a fixed matrix, \mathbf{w} is a linear function of  e, hence normal with mean zero and covariance \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\X\T(\sigma^2\I)\X\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\T/n=\sigma^2\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\T (@thm-mvn-linear). (b) The jth row of \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\hat{ Sigma}-\I is (\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j-\mathbf{e}_j)\T, because \hat{ Sigma} is symmetric. By Hölder’s inequality |r_j|\le\sqrt n\,\mu_j
orm{ oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1. The second bound follows from @thm-hd-lasso-estimation(a). (c) The columns of \X have 
orm{\x_j}^2=n, so \mathbf{e}_j\T\hat{ Sigma}\mathbf{e}_j=1. The jth entry of \hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j differs from 1 by at most \mu_j, so \mathbf{e}_j\T\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j\ge1-\mu_j>0. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the nonnegative definite form \hat{ Sigma} (@prp-mat-cauchy-schwarz applied to \hat{ Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{e}_j and \hat{ Sigma}^{1/2}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j) gives (1-\mu_j)^2\le(\mathbf{e}_j\T\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j)^2\le(\mathbf{e}_j\T\hat{ Sigma}\mathbf{e}_j)\,\omega_j^2=\omega_j^2. (d) Write T_j=(\sigma/\hat\sigma)\{w_j/(\sigma\omega_j)+r_j/(\sigma\omega_j)\}. By (a), w_j/(\sigma\omega_j) has exactly the \Normal(0,1) law. For the remainder, \log(2p/\delta_n)=\log2+\log p+\log(1/\delta_n)\le C'\log p for a constant C' and large n, so \lambda=2\lambda_0\le2\sigma\sqrt{2C'\log p/n}. On \mathcal{T}, which has probability at least 1-\delta_n	o1, part (b) gives  egin{aligned} |r_j|&\le4\sqrt n\cdot C\sqrt{ rac{\log p}n}\cdot2\sigma\sqrt{ rac{2C'\log p}n}\cdot rac{s}{\phi_0^2}\ &= rac{8\sqrt{2C'}\,C\sigma}{\phi_0^2}\cdot rac{s\log p}{\sqrt n}\ 	o\ 0 . \end{aligned} By (c) and \mu_j	o0, \omega_j\ge rac12 for large n. Hence r_j/(\sigma\omega_j)	o0 in probability, and Slutsky’s lemma (with \sigma/\hat\sigma	o1) gives @eq-hd-debiased-t. The coverage statement is \Pr(|T_j|\le z_{\alpha/2})	o1-\alpha. The theorem separates what the design must deliver (a \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}} with small \mu_j, and \phi^2(S) bounded below) from what the lasso delivers (an \ell_1 error of order s\sqrt{\log p/n}). The condition s\log p/\sqrt n	o0 is stronger than the s\log p/n	o0 that suffices for prediction: the remainder must be small compared with the standard error 1/\sqrt n. Constructing the approximate inverse The remaining question is how to find a \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}} with small \mu_j when \hat{ Sigma} is singular. The node-wise lasso regresses each column on all the others. [Node-wise lasso] For a fixed j, let \hat{ gamma}_j\in\Real^{p-1} be a lasso estimate, with penalty \lambda_j, for the regression of \x_j on the other columns \X_{-j}. Put \hat{ z}_j=\x_j-\X_{-j}\hat{ gamma}_j and \hat	au_j^2=\x_j\T\hat{ z}_j/n, and let \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j have entry 1/\hat	au_j^2 in position j and -\hat{ gamma}_j/\hat	au_j^2 elsewhere. Then: 1. \hat	au_j^2=
orm{\hat{ z}_j}^2/n+\lambda_j
orm{\hat{ gamma}_j}_1\ge0; 2. if \hat	au_j^2>0, then (\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j)_j=1 and \mu_j=
orm{\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j-\mathbf{e}_j}_\infty\le\lambda_j/\hat	au_j^2; 3. the jth debiased estimate is \hat b_j= rac{\hat{ z}_j\T(\Y-\X_{-j}\hat{ beta}_{\lambda,-j})}{\hat{ z}_j\T\x_j}. {#eq-hd-debiased-fwl} The optimality conditions @eq-hd-optimality for the node-wise regression say that \X_{-j}\T\hat{ z}_j/n=\lambda_j\hat{ oldsymbol{\upkappa}}, where \hat{ oldsymbol{\upkappa}} has entries of size at most 1 and equal to \operatorname{sign}(\hat\gamma_{j,k}) where \hat\gamma_{j,k}
e0. Hence \hat{ gamma}_j\T\X_{-j}\T\hat{ z}_j/n=\lambda_j
orm{\hat{ gamma}_j}_1, and since \x_j=\hat{ z}_j+\X_{-j}\hat{ gamma}_j, \hat	au_j^2= rac{\x_j\T\hat{ z}_j}{n}= rac{
orm{\hat{ z}_j}^2}n+\lambda_j
orm{\hat{ gamma}_j}_1 , which is (a). For (b), \X\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j=(\x_j-\X_{-j}\hat{ gamma}_j)/\hat	au_j^2=\hat{ z}_j/\hat	au_j^2, so the kth entry of \hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j is \x_k\T\hat{ z}_j/(n\hat	au_j^2). For k=j this is 1 by the definition of \hat	au_j^2. For k
e j it is \lambda_j\hat\kappa_k/\hat	au_j^2, of size at most \lambda_j/\hat	au_j^2. For (c), \hat b_j is \hat eta_{\lambda,j}+\hat{ z}_j\T(\Y-\X\hat{ beta}_\lambda)/(n\hat	au_j^2). Put n\hat	au_j^2=\hat{ z}_j\T\x_j and \X\hat{ beta}_\lambda=\x_j\hat eta_{\lambda,j}+\X_{-j}\hat{ beta}_{\lambda,-j}; the terms in \hat eta_{\lambda,j} cancel. Part (c) shows what the debiased lasso is. By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem (@thm-proj-fwl), the least squares coefficient of \x_j comes from regressing \Y on the part of \x_j orthogonal to the other columns, which is zero when p>n. The node-wise lasso replaces it by a lasso residual \hat{ z}_j, nearly orthogonal to every other column by (b), and removes the other regressors’ effect approximately through \X_{-j}\hat{ beta}_{\lambda,-j}. Javanmard and Montanari (2014) instead choose \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j to minimize \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\T\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}} subject to 
orm{\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}-\mathbf{e}_j}_\infty\le\mu. [Sketch: when the assumptions of part (d) hold] This is a sketch; the full arguments are in van de Geer, Bühlmann, Ritov and Dezeure (2014) and Javanmard and Montanari (2014). Suppose the rows of \X are independent \Normal_p( zero, Sigma), the eigenvalues of  Sigma are bounded away from 0 and \infty, and row j of  Sigma^{-1} has at most s_j nonzero entries. The population regression of x_j on the others then has s_j nonzero coefficients and residual variance 	au_j^2=1/( Sigma^{-1})_{jj}. By the lemma \mu_j\le\lambda_j/\hat	au_j^2 deterministically, so with \lambda_j\asymp\sqrt{\log p/n} it remains to show \hat	au_j^2\approx	au_j^2. This follows from Section 28.3 applied to the node-wise regression, with the random-design bound of Section 28.2, when s_j\log p/n	o0; the scaled lasso (Sun and Zhang 2012) supplies \hat\sigma. Then \omega_j^2	o( Sigma^{-1})_{jj}, which van de Geer and coauthors show to be the smallest asymptotic variance of a regular estimator. The theorem covers one prespecified coefficient, or a fixed finite set. Coefficients chosen because they look large bring back the selection problem, and simultaneous intervals need a multiplicity correction such as Bonferroni (@thm-mc-bonferroni). With moderate n and a truth that is not very sparse, the remainder r_j can be comparable to the noise, and coverage suffers. A simulation [Coverage of three intervals] Take n=200, p=400, a fixed Gaussian design with correlations 0.5^{|j-k|}, \sigma=1, and  eta_1=1,  eta_6=0.15,  eta_{11}=-1,  eta_{16}=0.15, all other coefficients zero. The targets are a strong coefficient  eta_1, a weak one  eta_6, and  eta_2=0, whose regressor is correlated 0.5 with x_1. In each of 1000 data sets we fit the lasso with \lambda=\sigma\sqrt{2\log p/n}=0.245, below 2\lambda_0 for the reason seen in @exm-hd-lasso-bounds, and compute three 95% intervals: - the naive interval: least squares on the selected variables and its t interval, reported only when the target was selected; - the debiased interval \hat b_j\pm1.96\,\hat\sigma\omega_j/\sqrt n, with node-wise lasso rows (\lambda_j=0.024) and \hat\sigma^2 the lasso residual sum of squares divided by n minus the number of selected variables; - the oracle t interval from least squares on the true support plus the target. The results are in Figure 28.5.1. For the null coefficient  eta_2, the lasso selected x_2 in a fraction 0.069 of the data sets, and in those the naive interval covered zero only in a fraction 0.174. For the weak coefficient, selected in a fraction 0.329, the naive coverage was 0.903, and for the strong one 0.915. The debiased intervals covered  eta_1,  eta_6 and  eta_2 in fractions 0.960, 0.946 and 0.940 respectively, close to the oracle’s 0.943, 0.956 and 0.958 for the same three coefficients. On the strong coefficient the lasso’s average error is -0.210, close to -\lambda, and the debiased estimate’s is 0.014. The standardized estimates T_1 have mean 0.14 and standard deviation 0.95 (panel (a)). Two costs remain. The debiased intervals are wider than the oracle’s (0.393 against 0.288 for  eta_1): part of this is the price of not knowing the support, and part is tuning. The node-wise penalty \lambda_j=0.024, a tenth of \sqrt{2\log p/n}, keeps the bound \mu_j\le\lambda_j/\hat	au_j^2 of @lem-hd-nodewise, and so the remainder, small. But it lets the node-wise fits explain much of each column: \hat	au_j^2 (0.28, 0.25 and 0.27 for  eta_1,  eta_6 and  eta_2) is well below the population value 1/( Sigma^{-1})_{jj}, which is  rac34 for j=1 and  rac35 otherwise, and that allows a larger \omega_j (@exr-hd-nodewise-bound). The second cost is a remainder bias: 0.049 for  eta_2 and 0.046 for the weak  eta_6, about a third of its value. This is the term r_j/\sqrt n of @thm-hd-debiased, at most \mu_j
orm{\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta}_1, with \mu_j between 0.088 and 0.099 and an average lasso \ell_1 error of 0.74. At n=200 that product is not negligible. [Figure 28.5.1. Inference for single coefficients with n=200, p=400, 1000 data sets. (a) Histogram of the standardized debiased estimates of  eta_1 and the \Normal(0,1) density. (b) Coverage of nominal 95% intervals: naive least squares after lasso selection (computed only when the target is selected), the debiased lasso, and the oracle.] Figure 28.5.1. Inference for single coefficients with n=200, p=400, 1000 data sets. (a) Histogram of the standardized debiased estimates of  eta_1 and the \Normal(0,1) density. (b) Coverage of nominal 95% intervals: naive least squares after lasso selection (computed only when the target is selected), the debiased lasso, and the oracle. [Inference for single coefficients with n=200, p=400, 1000 data sets. (a) Histogram of the standardized debiased estimates of  eta_1 and the \Normal(0,1) density. (b) Coverage of nominal 95% intervals: naive least squares after lasso selection (computed only when the target is selected), the debiased lasso, and the oracle.] Inference for single coefficients with n=200, p=400, 1000 data sets. (a) Histogram of the standardized debiased estimates of  eta_1 and the \Normal(0,1) density. (b) Coverage of nominal 95% intervals: naive least squares after lasso selection (computed only when the target is selected), the debiased lasso, and the oracle. import numpy as np from scipy import stats def soft(z, t): """Soft thresholding S(z, t) = sign(z) max(|z| - t, 0).""" return np.sign(z) * np.maximum(np.abs(z) - t, 0.0) def lasso_cd(X, Y, lam, B=None, tol=1e-9, max_sweeps=2000): """Minimize ||y - X b||^2 / (2n) + lam ||b||_1 for every column y of Y, by coordinate descent.""" n, p = X.shape Y = Y.reshape(n, -1) B = np.zeros((p, Y.shape[1])) if B is None else B.copy() R = Y - X @ B # residuals, one column per response scale = np.sum(X ** 2, axis=0) / n active = np.arange(p) for sweep in range(max_sweeps): change = 0.0 for j in active: z = X[:, j] @ R / n + scale[j] * B[j] new = soft(z, lam) / scale[j] d = new - B[j] if np.any(d != 0): R -= np.outer(X[:, j], d) B[j] = new change = max(change, np.max(np.abs(d))) if change < tol: if len(active) == p: # converged over all coordinates break active = np.arange(p) # check every coordinate once more else: active = np.flatnonzero(np.any(B != 0, axis=1)) if sweep % 5 else np.arange(p) return B def nodewise_row(X, j, lam_j): """Row theta_j of Theta from the lasso of x_j on the other columns, and tau_j^2.""" n, p = X.shape others = np.delete(np.arange(p), j) gamma = lasso_cd(X[:, others], X[:, j], lam_j)[:, 0] z = X[:, j] - X[:, others] @ gamma # lasso residual of x_j on the rest tau2 = X[:, j] @ z / n theta = np.zeros(p) theta[j] = 1.0 theta[others] = -gamma return theta / tau2, tau2 def debiased_interval(X, Y, B, j, theta, level=0.95): """Debiased estimate of beta_j and its normal-theory interval, one per column of Y.""" n = X.shape[0] R = Y - X @ B b = B[j] + theta @ X.T @ R / n # one-step correction sigma_hat = np.sqrt(np.sum(R ** 2, axis=0) / (n - np.sum(B != 0, axis=0))) G = X.T @ X / n se = sigma_hat * np.sqrt(theta @ G @ theta / n) z = stats.norm.ppf((1 + level) / 2) return b, b - z * se, b + z * se def toeplitz_design(rng, n, p, rho): idx = np.arange(p) L = np.linalg.cholesky(rho ** np.abs(idx[:, None] - idx[None, :])) X = rng.normal(size=(n, p)) @ L.T return X / np.sqrt(np.sum(X ** 2, axis=0) / n) rng = np.random.default_rng(2850) n, p, sigma = 200, 400, 1.0 X = toeplitz_design(rng, n, p, rho=0.5) beta = np.zeros(p) beta[[0, 5, 10, 15]] = [1.0, 0.15, -1.0, 0.15] lam = sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.log(p) / n) targets = {"strong": 0, "weak": 5, "null": 1} Ys = (X @ beta)[:, None] + sigma * rng.normal(size=(n, 200)) Bs = lasso_cd(X, Ys, lam) for name, j in targets.items(): theta, tau2 = nodewise_row(X, j, 0.1 * np.sqrt(2 * np.log(p) / n)) b, lo, hi = debiased_interval(X, Ys, Bs, j, theta) print(f"{name:6s}: lasso bias {Bs[j].mean() - beta[j]:+.3f}, debiased bias {b.mean() - beta[j]:+.3f}," f" coverage {np.mean((lo <= beta[j]) & (beta[j] <= hi)):.3f}") Other routes to valid inference Other approaches answer different questions. Sample splitting (Wasserman and Roeder 2009) selects on one half of the data and fits on the other (@exr-hd-sample-splitting). Selective inference (Lee, Sun, Sun and Taylor 2016) conditions on the lasso having chosen the reported model, a union of polyhedra in \Y. Simultaneous inference over all models (Berk, Brown, Buja, Zhang and Zhao 2013) widens the intervals, as Scheffé’s method does. These target the coefficients of the selected model, which generally differ from  eta_j. Double selection (Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen 2014) targets  eta_j: it keeps the controls that predict the response or x_j and refits least squares, the idea of @eq-hd-debiased-fwl. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Suppose p<n, \X has full column rank and \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}=\hat{ Sigma}^{-1}. Show that the debiased lasso @eq-hd-debiased equals the least squares estimate, whatever \hat{ beta}_\lambda is, and that \mu_j=0 and \mathbf{r}= zero in @thm-hd-debiased. \hat{\mathbf{b}}=\hat{ beta}_\lambda+(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T(\Y-\X\hat{ beta}_\lambda)=\hat{ beta}_\lambda+\hbeta-\hat{ beta}_\lambda=\hbeta, where \hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\Y. Then \hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}=\I, so every \mu_j=0 and \mathbf{r}= zero, and part (a) of the theorem reduces to \sqrt n(\hbeta- beta)\sim\Normal_p( zero,\sigma^2\hat{ Sigma}^{-1}) (@thm-opt-sampling). [A2] On the event of @thm-hd-support, with \hat{ Sigma}_{SS}=\I, show that the interval \hat eta_{\lambda,j}\pm1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n for j\in S covers  eta_j iff |\x_j\T e/\sqrt n\,\sigma^{-1}-\sqrt n\lambda\operatorname{sign}( eta_j)/\sigma|\le1.96. If \lambda=2\lambda_0, what happens to its coverage as p	o\infty? B. Practice [B1] (Sample splitting.) Split the observations into halves I_1 and I_2 chosen independently of the data. Select a set \hat S of columns using only the data in I_1, and suppose \X_{I_2,\hat S} has full column rank and |\hat S|<|I_2|. Show that if \hat S\supseteq S, then conditionally on the data in I_1, the usual t interval for  eta_j (j\in\hat S) from the least squares fit of \Y_{I_2} on \X_{I_2,\hat S} has exact coverage 1-\alpha. What does the fit estimate when \hat S misses an active variable? The errors in I_2 are independent of those in I_1, so conditionally on the data in I_1 the set \hat S is fixed and \Y_{I_2}\sim\Normal(\X_{I_2} beta,\sigma^2\I). If \hat S\supseteq S, then \X_{I_2} beta=\X_{I_2,\hat S} beta_{\hat S}, so the fit on \X_{I_2,\hat S} is a correctly specified normal linear model with coefficients  beta_{\hat S}, and the t interval of @thm-ci-estimable-interval has exact conditional coverage. Averaging over the data in I_1, coverage is exact on the event \hat S\supseteq S. If \hat S misses an active variable, the fit estimates the projected coefficients (\X_{I_2,\hat S}\T\X_{I_2,\hat S})^{-1}\X_{I_2,\hat S}\T\X_{I_2} beta (@prp-lm-misspecified), which differ from  beta_{\hat S} when the missed variables are correlated with the selected ones, and the residual mean square overestimates \sigma^2. [B2] In @lem-hd-nodewise, show that \omega_j^2=\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j\T\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j=
orm{\hat{ z}_j}^2/(n\hat	au_j^4), and hence \omega_j^2\le1/\hat	au_j^2. Interpret: a small \hat	au_j^2 (a column that the others explain well) means a large variance for \hat b_j. Compare with the variance inflation factor (@def-col-vif). \X\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j=\hat{ z}_j/\hat	au_j^2, so \omega_j^2=
orm{\X\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j}^2/n=

orm{(\I-\M_{(j)})\x_j}^2/n, and \omega_j^2=1/\hat	au_j^2 is the variance factor n/\{S_{jj}(1-R_j^2)\} of @eq-proj-vif-preview for a column with 
orm{\x_j}^2=n (and an intercept among the other columns). The node-wise lasso residual plays the role of the FWL residual, and 1/\hat	au_j^2 the role of the variance inflation. C. Going deeper [C1] The two quantities in @thm-hd-debiased pull against each other: \mu_j controls the remainder and \omega_j the standard error, and a \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_j that makes one small makes the other large. This exercise computes the trade-off exactly. 1. Suppose p<n and \hat{ Sigma} is invertible. Show that the only  oldsymbol{\uptheta} with \mu_j=0, that is with \hat{ Sigma} oldsymbol{\uptheta}=\mathbf{e}_j, gives \omega_j^2=(\hat{ Sigma}^{-1})_{jj}, the least squares variance factor of @exr-hd-nodewise-bound. 2. Let p=2, \hat{ Sigma}= egin{pmatrix}1&ho\ho&1\end{pmatrix} with 0<ho<1, and j=1. Substituting (a,b)\T=\hat{ Sigma} oldsymbol{\uptheta}, show that  oldsymbol{\uptheta}\T\hat{ Sigma} oldsymbol{\uptheta}=(a^2-2ho ab+b^2)/(1-ho^2) while the constraint 
orm{\hat{ Sigma} oldsymbol{\uptheta}-\mathbf{e}_1}_\infty\le\mu reads |a-1|\le\mu and |b|\le\mu. 3. Show that for 0<\mu\leho/(1+ho) the minimum is at (a,b)=(1-\mu,\mu), with value \omega_1^2(\mu)= rac{1-2(1+ho)\mu(1-\mu)}{1-ho^2}, so that \omega_1^2(0)=(\hat{ Sigma}^{-1})_{11} and  rac{d}{d\mu}\omega_1^2(0)=-2/(1-ho). 4. Read the result against @thm-hd-debiased(b) and (c), and against the tuning reported in 1. (a) \hat{ Sigma} oldsymbol{\uptheta}=\mathbf{e}_j has the unique solution  oldsymbol{\uptheta}=\hat{ Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}_j, and  oldsymbol{\uptheta}\T\hat{ Sigma} oldsymbol{\uptheta} =\mathbf{e}_j\T\hat{ Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}_j=(\hat{ Sigma}^{-1})_{jj}. By @exr-hd-debias-low-dim the debiased estimate is then least squares, with exactly that variance factor. (b)  oldsymbol{\uptheta}=\hat{ Sigma}^{-1}(a,b)\T, so  oldsymbol{\uptheta}\T\hat{ Sigma} oldsymbol{\uptheta}=(a,b)\hat{ Sigma}^{-1}(a,b)\T, and \hat{ Sigma}^{-1}=(1-ho^2)^{-1} egin{pmatrix}1&-ho\-ho&1\end{pmatrix} gives the stated form. The constraint is a constraint on (a,b) directly. (c) Write f(a,b)=(a^2-2ho ab+b^2)/(1-ho^2) on the box [1-\mu,1+\mu]	imes[-\mu,\mu]. Then \partial f/\partial a=2(a-ho b)/(1-ho^2), and on the box a-ho b\ge(1-\mu)-ho\mu>0 because \mu\leho/(1+ho)<1/(1+ho); so f increases in a and a=1-\mu. Next \partial f/\partial b=2(b-ho a)/(1-ho^2) vanishes at b=ho(1-\mu), which exceeds \mu exactly when \mu<ho/(1+ho); so f decreases in b throughout [-\mu,\mu] and b=\mu. Substituting, (1-\mu)^2-2ho(1-\mu)\mu+\mu^2=1-2(1+ho)\mu+2(1+ho)\mu^2, which is the stated numerator. Setting \mu=0 gives 1/(1-ho^2), and differentiating at \mu=0 gives -2(1+ho)/(1-ho^2)=-2/(1-ho). orm{\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta}_1 grows linearly in \mu at the same time. The theorem’s condition \mu_j\le C\sqrt{\log p/n} is a choice of a point on this curve: it is what makes the remainder vanish beside 1/\sqrt n, at the price of the variance the exact inverse would have delivered. Part (c) of the theorem gives the floor \omega_j^2\ge(1-\mu_j)^2, so the variance cannot be driven below about one however \mu is chosen. The simulation of 1 sits at the other end: its node-wise penalty is a tenth of \sqrt{2\log p/n}, which keeps \mu_j near 0.09 and the remainder small, and pays for it with a \hat	au_j^2 far below its population value and hence intervals wider than the oracle’s. [C2] Why one correction and not two? Write T( b)= b+\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\X\T(\Y-\X b)/n, so that \hat{\mathbf{b}}=T(\hat{ beta}_\lambda), and put \mathbf{K}=\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\hat{ Sigma}-\I. 1. Show that T( b)- beta=-\mathbf{K}( b- beta)+\mathbf{w}/\sqrt n with \mathbf{w} as in @thm-hd-debiased(a), and deduce that the k-fold iterate satisfies \sqrt n igl(T^{k}(\hat{ beta}_\lambda)- beta igr) =(-\mathbf{K})^{k}\sqrt n\, oldsymbol{\Delta}+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(-\mathbf{K})^{i}\mathbf{w}, \qquad  oldsymbol{\Delta}=\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta . 2. With \mu=\max_k\mu_k, show that 
orm{\mathbf{K} oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1\le p\,\mu
orm{ oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1, and hence that the bound of @thm-hd-debiased(b) on the jth remainder is multiplied by p\mu for each extra iteration. 3. Show that under the conditions of @thm-hd-debiased(d) with p>n one has p\mu\ge\sqrt{n\log p}\,C^{-1}	o\infty up to the constant, so that the guarantee is lost after one extra step, however small \mu is. 4. Show that when p<n and \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}=\hat{ Sigma}^{-1}, \mathbf{K}= zero and every iterate equals the least squares estimate, so nothing of this happens in low dimension. (a) Substituting \Y=\X beta+ e, \Y-\X b=\X( beta- b)+ e, so T( b)- beta=( b- beta)-\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\hat{ Sigma}( b- beta) +\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\X\T e/n=-\mathbf{K}( b- beta)+\mathbf{w}/\sqrt n , with \mathbf{w}=\hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\X\T e/\sqrt n. The map is affine with linear part -\mathbf{K}; iterating it k times from \hat{ beta}_\lambda and multiplying by \sqrt n gives the display. At k=1 it is @thm-hd-debiased(a). (b) The kth row of \mathbf{K} is (\hat{ Sigma}\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}_k-\mathbf{e}_k)\T, so |(\mathbf{K} oldsymbol{\Delta})_k|\le\mu_k
orm{ oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1\le\mu
orm{ oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1 by Hölder, and summing over the p coordinates, 
orm{\mathbf{K} oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1\le p\mu
orm{ oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1. Applying the jth-row bound once more, |\{(\mathbf{K})^{2} oldsymbol{\Delta}\}_j|\le\mu_j
orm{\mathbf{K} oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1 \le p\mu\cdot\mu_j
orm{ oldsymbol{\Delta}}_1, and by induction each further step costs a factor p\mu. (c) The one-step remainder is controlled by taking \mu of the order \sqrt{\log p/n}, which is what the condition \mu_j\le C\sqrt{\log p/n} asks for and what @lem-hd-nodewise delivers. At that order, and with p>n, p\mu\asymp p\sqrt{ rac{\log p}n}\ \ge\ n\sqrt{ rac{\log p}n}=\sqrt{n\log p}\ 	o\ \infty . The \ell_1 norm of the error is spread over p coordinates, and each application of \mathbf{K} trades a factor \mu against a factor p; with p larger than n, p wins. (d) Then \hat{ oldsymbol{\Theta}}\hat{ Sigma}=\I, so \mathbf{K}= zero and T( b)= beta+\mathbf{w}/\sqrt n=\hbeta for every  b, by @exr-hd-debias-low-dim. The iteration converges in one step because the correction is exact. The moral is that @eq-hd-debiased is not the first step of a convergent scheme. It is the one step whose error the design can be made to control, and the noise term of (a) also changes as soon as k>1, since \sum_i(-\mathbf{K})^{i}\mathbf{w} no longer has the covariance \sigma^2\omega_j^2 that the interval uses.

title: 28.6 Summary and Notes
content:
Summary and Notes Summary 1. When p>n, least squares interpolates and no single coefficient is estimable. The minimum-norm solution \X^+\y is the ridgeless limit of ridge and the limit of gradient descent from zero; its error splits into the invisible null-space part of  beta and the variance \sigma^2\sum_id_i^{-2} (@thm-hd-min-norm). 2. For isotropic Gaussian regressors its risk is exact (@prp-hd-isotropic-risk). Fitting p of D features gives the double descent curve (@cor-hd-double-descent), whose peak at p=n belongs to the estimator and disappears with a tuned ridge penalty. 3. Sparsity restores identifiability (@prp-hd-sparse-identifiable). The compatibility and restricted eigenvalue conditions ask for curvature only on a cone of approximately sparse vectors (@def-hd-re); they transfer from populations to samples with a loss of 16s\delta (@prp-hd-re-basic), and can be small in samples even when they are large in the population. 4. On the event 
orm{\X\T e/n}_\infty\le\lambda_0=\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2p/\delta)/n}, which has probability at least 1-\delta (@lem-hd-gaussian-max), every lasso estimate with \lambda\ge2\lambda_0 has its error in the cone and prediction error at most 3\lambda
orm{ beta}_1 without conditions and 9\lambda^2s/\phi^2(S) under compatibility (@thm-hd-lasso-prediction). Its \ell_1 and \ell_2 errors are of order \lambda s and \lambda\sqrt s (@thm-hd-lasso-estimation). 5. Exact sign recovery holds under the irrepresentable and beta-min conditions (@thm-hd-support). Without the irrepresentable condition it has probability at most  rac12 for every sample size (@prp-hd-irrepresentable-necessary); screening needs only the restricted eigenvalue and beta-min conditions (@prp-hd-screening). 6. Intervals computed after selection under-cover. The debiased lasso adds a one-step correction; its error is exactly normal plus a remainder bounded by \sqrt n\mu_j
orm{\hat{ beta}_\lambda- beta}_1, which vanishes when s\log p/\sqrt n	o0 (@thm-hd-debiased). With node-wise lasso rows it is the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell estimator with a lasso residual (@lem-hd-nodewise). Notes and sources Scope. None of the planning sources treats p>n in depth; Agresti (2015, section 11.2) notes it briefly, through a Bayesian prior. Bühlmann and van de Geer (2011), Hastie, Tibshirani and Wainwright (2015) and Wainwright (2019) develop all the topics of the chapter at length. Interpolation. The term double descent is from Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal (2019). Belkin, Hsu and Xu (2020) give exact risk formulas for Gaussian features, including omitted features as in @cor-hd-double-descent. Hastie, Montanari, Rosset and Tibshirani (2022) treat general covariances and ridge asymptotically, and Bartlett, Long, Lugosi and Tsigler (2020) characterize benign overfitting. Design conditions and the lasso. The lasso is due to Tibshirani (1996); Tibshirani (2013) studies uniqueness. Greenshtein and Ritov (2004) introduced persistence, behind the slow rate. The restricted eigenvalue condition and the fast rates are from Bickel, Ritov and Tsybakov (2009), with the Dantzig selector of Candès and Tao (2007); the basic-inequality presentation follows Bühlmann and van de Geer (2011, chapter 6), and van de Geer and Bühlmann (2009) compare the conditions. Donoho and Huo (2001) used mutual coherence, and Cohen, Dahmen and DeVore (2009) the null space property. Raskutti, Wainwright and Yu (2010, 2011) prove the random-design bound and the minimax lower bound. Belloni, Chernozhukov and Wang (2011) and Sun and Zhang (2012) free \lambda from \sigma. Selection and inference. The irrepresentable condition is due to Zhao and Yu (2006) and Meinshausen and Bühlmann (2006), the primal–dual witness proof to Wainwright (2009); Zou (2006) and Meinshausen and Bühlmann (2010) propose the adaptive lasso and stability selection. Leeb and Pötscher (2005, 2006) analyse post-selection distributions and prove that they cannot be estimated uniformly. The debiased lasso is due to Zhang and Zhang (2014), van de Geer, Bühlmann, Ritov and Dezeure (2014) and Javanmard and Montanari (2014). The alternatives are due to Wasserman and Roeder (2009), Meinshausen, Meier and Bühlmann (2009), Lee, Sun, Sun and Taylor (2016), Berk, Brown, Buja, Zhang and Zhao (2013) and Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014). title: Model Selection and Prediction
content: Model Selection and Prediction A fitted model is judged by how well it predicts responses it has not seen, and its error on the responses it was fitted to flatters it. For any fitting procedure the flattery is twice the covariance between the fit and the data, 2\sigma^2p/n for least squares whether the model is right or wrong. Correcting for it gives Mallows’ C_p and AIC. BIC answers a different question, which model is most probable: it finds a true finite model with probability tending to one, while AIC predicts almost as well as the best candidate when no finite model is true. Cross-validation estimates prediction error with fewer assumptions, and for least squares and ridge it needs no refitting. The search over subsets is unstable, and every estimate and interval computed after it is biased by it, unless the inference is designed to survive the search. What you need. Chapter 6 (projections, @thm-proj-nested, and the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, @thm-proj-fwl), Chapter 7 (the likelihood of the normal model, @thm-opt-mle), Chapter 9 (adjusted R^2, @prp-ss-adjusted-r2), Chapter 11 (the F test, @thm-glh-f-test), Chapter 13 (Scheffé and Bonferroni, @thm-mc-scheffe and @thm-mc-bonferroni), Chapter 14 (prediction error and its optimism, @prp-cor-optimism and @thm-cor-prediction-error), Chapter 19 (omitted and irrelevant regressors, @thm-dep-mse) and Chapter 20 (the deletion formulas and PRESS, @thm-res-deletion). From this part: Chapter 26 (collinearity) and Chapter 27 (ridge regression, thresholding and Stein’s lemma, @lem-shr-stein). Roadmap - Prediction error and optimism - Mallows’ Cp, AIC and BIC - Cross-validation - All subsets and stepwise search - Selection bias and honest inference - Summary and notes

title: 29.1 Prediction error and optimism
content:
Prediction error and optimism Chapter 19 compared a short regression with a long one and found that neither wins everywhere. Leaving out regressors whose coefficients are small buys a drop in variance that can outweigh the bias it causes, and @thm-dep-mse located the break-even point exactly: at the design points the short fit is better iff the noncentrality @eq-dep-gamma of the omitted block is less than the number of columns omitted. The noncentrality is unknown, so the theorem does not choose a model. It does say what a good choice should aim at, namely the error of the fitted values as predictions, and this chapter builds that into procedures. The residual mean square describes how well a fit reproduces the data it was fitted to, and every fitting procedure bends towards those data. This section makes the size of that bend exact for any procedure, and turns it into a definition of the degrees of freedom a procedure spends. In-sample prediction error Throughout the chapter the data follow \Y= mu+ e,\qquad \E( e)= zero,\qquad \Cov( e)=\sigma^2\I_n , {#eq-sel-model} where the mean vector  mu\in\Real^n is unrestricted. A candidate linear model \C(\X) may or may not contain  mu. That is the point of model selection: we want procedures whose properties do not depend on a candidate being right. A fitting procedure is any function \hat{ mu}=\hat{ mu}(\Y) from \Real^n to \Real^n with \E
orm{\hat{ mu}(\Y)}^2<\infty: least squares on a fixed model, least squares on a model chosen from the data, ridge regression, thresholding. [Training error, prediction error, optimism] Let \Y^*= mu+ e^*, where  e^* is independent of  e and has the same distribution: new responses at the same design points. For a fitting procedure \hat{ mu}: 1. the training error is \overline{	ext{err}}=n^{-1}
orm{\Y-\hat{ mu}}^2; 2. the in-sample prediction error is 	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}}=n^{-1}\E igl(
orm{\Y^*-\hat{ mu}}^2 igm|\Y igr); 3. the optimism is 	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}}-\overline{	ext{err}}, and its mean \omega=\E(	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}}-\overline{	ext{err}}) is the expected optimism. Expanding \Y^*-\hat{ mu}= e^*+( mu-\hat{ mu}) and using the independence of  e^* and \Y, 	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}}=\sigma^2+ rac1n
orm{\hat{ mu}- mu}^2 . {#eq-sel-err-in} So the in-sample prediction error is the irreducible \sigma^2 plus the average squared error of the fitted values as estimates of the mean. Ranking procedures by \E(	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}}) is the same as ranking them by the risk \E
orm{\hat{ mu}- mu}^2, which is the criterion of @thm-dep-mse(c). In-sample refers to the design points: the responses are new, the regressor values old. New regressor values are taken up at the end of the section. The covariance penalty [Optimism is a covariance] Under @eq-sel-model, let \hat{ mu} be a fitting procedure. 1. The expected optimism is \omega= rac2n\sum_{i=1}^n\Cov(\hat{\mu}_i,Y_i). 2. If \hat{ mu}= S\Y for a fixed n	imes n matrix  S, then \omega=2\sigma^2	r( S)/n and \E
orm{\hat{ mu}- mu}^2=
orm{(\I- S) mu}^2+\sigma^2	r( S S\T). 3. For least squares on a model matrix \X of rank p, whether or not  mu\in\C(\X),  egin{aligned} \E(\overline{	ext{err}})&=\sigma^2\, rac{n-p}n+ rac{
orm{(\I-\M) mu}^2}n,\ \E(	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}})&=\sigma^2\, rac{n+p}n+ rac{
orm{(\I-\M) mu}^2}n, \end{aligned} and \omega=2\sigma^2p/n. (a) Write \Y-\hat{ mu}=(\Y- mu)-(\hat{ mu}- mu). Then 
orm{\Y-\hat{ mu}}^2=
orm{ e}^2+
orm{\hat{ mu}- mu}^2-2 e\T(\hat{ mu}- mu). Take expectations and compare with @eq-sel-err-in: n\,\E(	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}})=n\sigma^2+\E
orm{\hat{ mu}- mu}^2, so n\omega=2\E igl[ e\T(\hat{ mu}- mu) igr]=2\sum_i\E igl[(Y_i-\mu_i)\hat{\mu}_i igr], since  mu is constant and \E( e)= zero. Because \E(Y_i-\mu_i)=0, the last expectation is \Cov(\hat{\mu}_i,Y_i). The moments exist by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. (b) \Cov( S\Y,\Y)=\sigma^2 S, whose diagonal sums to \sigma^2	r( S). For the risk,  S\Y- mu= S e-(\I- S) mu has mean -(\I- S) mu and covariance \sigma^2 S S\T, and @thm-rv-quadform-mean with \A=\I gives the sum of the squared mean and the trace. (c) Take  S=\M, with 	r(\M)=p and \M\M\T=\M (@prp-proj-trace-rank). Then \E(	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}})=\sigma^2+n^{-1}\{
orm{(\I-\M) mu}^2+\sigma^2p\}, and subtracting \omega gives \E(\overline{	ext{err}}). Part (c) with  mu\in\C(\X) is @prp-cor-optimism(a). What is new is that the optimism of least squares does not depend on  mu: a wrong model has larger training and prediction errors, but both grow by the same squared bias, so a penalty depending only on p is a sensible correction even for wrong models. Part (a) asks nothing of the procedure but finite second moments: a fit is optimistic to the extent that each fitted value follows its own response. The training error of a procedure understates its prediction error by 2/n times the total covariance between fitted values and responses. For least squares on p columns the covariance is \sigma^2p, right model or wrong. [Optimism of a wrong model] Take n=30 equally spaced points t_i on [-1,1], a curved mean \mu_i=1+t_i+1.5t_i^2, \sigma=1, and fit by least squares a straight line in t together with two columns of pure noise, so p=4. The model is wrong: its squared bias per observation is 
orm{(\I-\M) mu}^2/n=0.2054. Over 20000 simulated data sets the average optimism is 0.2688, against 2\sigma^2p/n=0.2667 from @thm-sel-optimism(c). Ridge regression (@thm-shr-ridge) on the same columns with penalty \lambda=5 is a linear smoother with 	r( S)=3.207; its simulated optimism is 0.2163, against 2	imes3.207/30=0.2138 from part (b). import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(2901) n, sigma, reps = 30, 1.0, 20_000 t = np.linspace(-1, 1, n) X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), t, rng.normal(size=(n, 2))]) # line + 2 irrelevant columns mu = 1 + t + 1.5 * t**2 # the true mean is curved p = X.shape[1] M = X @ np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T) # projection onto C(X) Y = mu + sigma * rng.normal(size=(reps, n)) # one data set per row fit = Y @ M # M is symmetric train = np.mean((Y - fit) ** 2, axis=1) # training error err_in = sigma**2 + np.mean((fit - mu) ** 2, axis=1) # in-sample prediction error print(f"average optimism {np.mean(err_in - train):.4f}, 2 sigma^2 p / n = {2 * sigma**2 * p / n:.4f}") lam = 5.0 S = X @ np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * np.eye(p), X.T) # ridge smoother fit_r = Y @ S.T train_r = np.mean((Y - fit_r) ** 2, axis=1) err_in_r = sigma**2 + np.mean((fit_r - mu) ** 2, axis=1) omega_r = np.mean(err_in_r - train_r) print(f"ridge: optimism {omega_r:.4f}, 2 sigma^2 tr(S) / n = {2 * np.trace(S) / n:.4f}") Degrees of freedom of a procedure @thm-sel-optimism suggests measuring the complexity of any procedure by the covariance it creates. [Degrees of freedom] The degrees of freedom of a fitting procedure \hat{ mu} under @eq-sel-model is 	ext{df}(\hat{ mu})= rac1{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\Cov(\hat{\mu}_i,Y_i), so that \omega=2\sigma^2\,	ext{df}(\hat{ mu})/n. For least squares on a fixed model 	ext{df}=p, the number of free coefficients, and for a linear smoother 	ext{df}=	r( S). For ridge regression with singular values d_j of \X this is \sum_jd_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda), the effective degrees of freedom of @thm-shr-ridge, which falls from ank(\X) to 0 as \lambda grows. If 	ext{df} is known, \widehat{	ext{Err}}_{	ext{in}}=\overline{	ext{err}}+ rac{2\sigma^2}n\,	ext{df}(\hat{ mu}) {#eq-sel-covariance-penalty} is an unbiased estimate of \E(	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}}) by @thm-sel-optimism(a). Section 29.2 turns this into Mallows’ C_p. For a procedure that searches, the covariance is not a count and has to be computed. Under normal errors it is computed by Stein’s lemma, @lem-shr-stein(b), proved in Section 27.5 for the James–Stein theorem: if \Z\sim\Normal_p( oldsymbol{\uptheta},\sigma^2\I) and each g_i is absolutely continuous in z_i with the integrability stated there, then \E[(\Z- oldsymbol{\uptheta})\T\mathbf{g}(\Z)]=\sigma^2\E\sum_i\partial g_i(\Z)/\partial z_i. [Degrees of freedom as a divergence] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I). Suppose that for each i, for almost every value of the other coordinates, y_i\mapsto\hat{\mu}_i(\y) is absolutely continuous, and that \E\lvert\partial\hat{\mu}_i/\partial y_ivert and \E\hat{\mu}_i^2 are finite. Then 	ext{df}(\hat{ mu})=\E\sum_{i=1}^n rac{\partial\hat{\mu}_i}{\partial y_i}(\Y), and \overline{	ext{err}}+2\sigma^2n^{-1}\sum_i\partial\hat{\mu}_i/\partial y_i is an unbiased estimate of \E(	ext{Err}_{	ext{in}}) that does not involve  mu. Since \E(Y_i-\mu_i)=0, \sum_i\Cov(\hat{\mu}_i,Y_i)=\E[(\Y- mu)\T\hat{ mu}(\Y)], and each term is integrable by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. @lem-shr-stein(b) with \mathbf{g}=\hat{ mu} turns this into \sigma^2\E\sum_i\partial\hat{\mu}_i/\partial y_i. The unbiasedness statement is then @thm-sel-optimism(a). The estimate in the proposition is Stein’s unbiased risk estimate (Stein 1981). For a linear smoother the divergence is 	r( S), and nothing is new. The interesting cases are adaptive. Soft thresholding. Take an orthonormal design, \X\T\X=\I_p, and put \Z=\X\T\Y\sim\Normal_p(\X\T mu,\sigma^2\I). For a fit \hat{ mu}=\X\hat{ beta}(\Z), \sum_i\Cov(\hat{\mu}_i,Y_i)=	r\Cov(\X\hat{ beta},\Y)=	r\Cov(\hat{ beta},\X\T\Y)=\sum_j\Cov(\hat{ eta}_j,Z_j), so the degrees of freedom can be computed coordinate by coordinate in the sequence model Z_j\sim\Normal(	heta_j,\sigma^2). The lasso in this design is soft thresholding, \hat{ eta}_j=\operatorname{sign}(Z_j)(\lvert Z_jvert-\lambda)_+ (@thm-shr-lasso-orthonormal). It is Lipschitz, with derivative 1\{\lvert Z_jvert>\lambda\} except at \pm\lambda, so by @prp-sel-divergence its degrees of freedom are the expected number of nonzero coefficients, as an exercise of Section 27.4 found by direct integration. The shrinkage exactly pays for the search. Hard thresholding. Subset selection in the same design keeps or drops each coordinate whole, \hat{ eta}_j=Z_j1\{\lvert Z_jvert>\lambda\} (@thm-shr-lasso-orthonormal again). This jumps by \lambda at \pm\lambda, so Stein’s lemma does not apply, and the degrees of freedom exceed the expected count. [Degrees of freedom of hard thresholding] Let Z\sim\Normal(	heta,\sigma^2) and \lambda>0. Then  egin{aligned}  rac{\Cov igl(Z1\{\lvert Zvert>\lambda\},Z igr)}{\sigma^2} &=\Pr(\lvert Zvert>\lambda)\ &\quad+ rac\lambda\sigma\Bigl[\phi\Bigl( rac{\lambda-	heta}\sigma\Bigr)+\phi\Bigl( rac{\lambda+	heta}\sigma\Bigr)\Bigr], \end{aligned} where \phi is the standard normal density. Write Z=	heta+\sigma W with W\sim\Normal(0,1), and put a=(\lambda-	heta)/\sigma, b=(-\lambda-	heta)/\sigma, so that \lvert Zvert>\lambda iff W>a or W<b. The covariance is \E[\sigma W(	heta+\sigma W)1\{W>a	ext{ or }W<b\}]. The truncated moments of the standard normal are \E[W1\{W>a\}]=\phi(a), \E[W1\{W<b\}]=-\phi(b), \E[W^21\{W>a\}]=1-\Phi(a)+a\phi(a) and \E[W^21\{W<b\}]=\Phi(b)-b\phi(b), each by one integration by parts. Collecting terms, \sigma	heta igl(\phi(a)-\phi(b) igr)+\sigma^2 igl(1-\Phi(a)+\Phi(b)+a\phi(a)-b\phi(b) igr). Since \sigma	heta+\sigma^2a=\sigma\lambda and -\sigma	heta-\sigma^2b=\sigma\lambda, this is \sigma^2\Pr(\lvert Zvert>\lambda)+\sigma\lambda igl(\phi(a)+\phi(b) igr), and \phi(b)=\phi((\lambda+	heta)/\sigma). The first term is the expected number of coefficients kept. The second is the price of the search: the fit follows Z most closely just where Z decides whether to keep the coordinate. At the threshold \lambda=\sigma\sqrt2 (which Section 29.2 shows is where C_p and AIC put it) and 	heta=0, the expected count is 0.157 but the degrees of freedom are 0.572: the search term 0.415 is more than twice the count. At 	heta=\sigma the degrees of freedom are 0.896, and at 	heta=3\sigma they are 1.104, more than one full parameter for a single coordinate. [Best subset of a given size] Keep the k largest of m=20 values \lvert Z_jvert and set the rest to zero, with Z_j\sim\Normal(	heta_j,1) independent. For a subset fixed in advance the degrees of freedom would be k. Figure 29.1.1 shows them by simulation. When all 	heta_j=0, the best single coordinate already costs 4.91 degrees of freedom, the best five cost 13.94 and the best ten 18.27. When five means equal 6 and the rest are zero, choosing the best five is almost free (5.06), because the five are obvious; choosing a sixth means choosing among fifteen pure-noise coordinates, and the degrees of freedom jump to 9.47. Searching among many candidates of equal merit is expensive, and choosing between clear winners and clear losers is cheap. [Figure 29.1.1. Degrees of freedom of the best subset of size k among 20 orthonormal coordinates, by simulation (20000 data sets). The dashed line is 	ext{df}=k, correct only when the subset is fixed in advance.] Figure 29.1.1. Degrees of freedom of the best subset of size k among 20 orthonormal coordinates, by simulation (20000 data sets). The dashed line is 	ext{df}=k, correct only when the subset is fixed in advance. [Degrees of freedom of the best subset of size k among 20 orthonormal coordinates, by simulation (20000 data sets). The dashed line is 	ext{df}=k, correct only when the subset is fixed in advance.] Degrees of freedom of the best subset of size k among 20 orthonormal coordinates, by simulation (20000 data sets). The dashed line is 	ext{df}=k, correct only when the subset is fixed in advance. m, reps_s = 20, 20_000 Zs = rng.normal(size=(reps_s, m)) def subset_df(theta, k): """Monte Carlo df of 'keep the k largest |Y_j|' when Y ~ N(theta, I).""" Yb = theta + Zs keep = np.argsort(-np.abs(Yb), axis=1)[:, :k] fit = np.zeros_like(Yb) np.put_along_axis(fit, keep, np.take_along_axis(Yb, keep, axis=1), axis=1) return np.mean(np.sum(fit * Zs, axis=1)) # sum_j Cov(fit_j, Y_j) null = np.zeros(m) sparse = np.r_[np.full(5, 6.0), np.zeros(m - 5)] # five large means for k in (1, 5, 10): print(f"k = {k:2d}: df null {subset_df(null, k):5.2f}, df sparse {subset_df(sparse, k):5.2f}") So a penalty of 2\sigma^2p/n is right for a model chosen in advance and too small for a model chosen by search, a point Section 29.5 returns to. New regressor values The in-sample error keeps the design fixed. For a new case with its own regressors the error is larger, and for least squares with k normal regressors and a correct model @thm-cor-prediction-error gives it exactly; since \E(s^2)=\sigma^2, s^2(1+1/n)(n-2)/(n-k-2) estimates it without bias. Breiman and Spector (1992) found that fixed-design estimates understate the error when the design is random, and recommended five- or ten-fold cross-validation. Cross-validation (Section 29.3) estimates the random-design error directly. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] The procedure \hat{ mu}(\Y)=\Y interpolates the data. Compute its training error, its in-sample prediction error and its degrees of freedom, and check @thm-sel-optimism(a). B. Practice [B1] Let  S_\lambda=\X(\X\T\X+\lambda\I)^{-1}\X\T be the ridge smoother, whose trace \sum_jd_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda) was found in @thm-shr-ridge. Show that 	r( S_\lambda S_\lambda\T)<	r( S_\lambda) for every \lambda>0 with \X
e\mathbf{0}, and that for a symmetric smoother  S with eigenvalues in [0,1], 	r( S S\T)=	r( S) iff  S is an orthogonal projection. A symmetric  S with eigenvalues s_j\in[0,1] has 	r( S S\T)=	r( S^2)=\sum_js_j^2\le\sum_js_j=	r( S), with equality iff every s_j\in\{0,1\}, that is, iff  S is idempotent, an orthogonal projection (@thm-proj-sym-idem). The ridge smoother is symmetric with eigenvalues d_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda), which lie in (0,1) for d_j>0, and at least one d_j is positive. So the variance term of @thm-sel-optimism(b), \sigma^2	r( S S\T), is strictly smaller than the optimism term \sigma^2	r( S). [B2] Arrange n observations on a circle, and let \hat{\mu}_i be the average of Y_{i-q},\dots,Y_{i+q} (indices modulo n, 2q+1\le n). Find the degrees of freedom and the expected optimism, and explain why a wider window is “simpler”. C. Going deeper [C1] In the sequence model Z_j\sim\Normal(	heta_j,\sigma^2), j=1,\dots,p, independent, soft thresholding at \lambda has Stein’s unbiased risk estimate 	ext{SURE}(\lambda)=\sum_{j=1}^p\min(Z_j^2,\lambda^2)-p\sigma^2+2\sigma^2\#\{j:\lvert Z_jvert>\lambda\} by @prp-sel-divergence, because Z_j-\hat{	heta}_j is Z_j when \lvert Z_jvert\le\lambda and \pm\lambda otherwise. Let 0=a_0\le a_1\le\dots\le a_p be 0 and the ordered \lvert Z_jvert. Show that 	ext{SURE} is nondecreasing on each interval [a_k,a_{k+1}), so it is minimized over \lambda\ge0 at one of a_0,\dots,a_p. Compute 	ext{SURE}(0), and explain why the minimized value is biased downwards. (Minimizing SURE is the SureShrink rule of Donoho and Johnstone 1995.) On [a_k,a_{k+1}) exactly p-k of the \lvert Z_jvert exceed \lambda (for distinct values), so 	ext{SURE}(\lambda)=\sum_{\lvert Z_jvert\le a_k}Z_j^2+(p-k)\lambda^2-p\sigma^2+2\sigma^2(p-k), which is nondecreasing in \lambda and smallest at a_k. At \lambda=0 nothing is shrunk and 	ext{SURE}(0)=p\sigma^2, the exact risk of \Z. Each 	ext{SURE}(a_k) is unbiased for its own risk, so their minimum has expectation at most the smallest risk: the optimism of a minimized estimate studied in Section 29.5. [C2] In @exm-sel-subset-df with all 	heta_j=0 and k=1, show that the degrees of freedom equal \E\max_jZ_j^2 (with \sigma=1). Deduce that they are at least 1, and use \E\max_jZ_j^2\ge(\E\max_j\lvert Z_jvert)^2 to explain why they grow without bound as m	o\infty.

title: 29.2 Mallows' Cp, AIC and BIC
content:
Mallows’ Cp, AIC and BIC A selection criterion assigns a number to each candidate model and picks the smallest. C_p estimates the prediction error of Section 29.1, AIC a likelihood-based discrepancy, and BIC the posterior probability of the model. The first two nearly always agree; the third answers a different question, and the difference shows up in large samples. Candidates The candidates are a finite collection of models \C(\X_k), k\in\mathcal K, with ank(\X_k)=p_k, each fitted by least squares: \hat{ mu}_k=\M_k\Y, with residual sum of squares 	ext{SSE}_k=
orm{(\I-\M_k)\Y}^2. Typically \X_k consists of the intercept and a subset of the columns of a full model matrix \X_F of rank P<n, and s^2=	ext{SSE}_F/(n-P) is the usual variance estimate from the full model. The data follow @eq-sel-model. By @thm-sel-optimism(c) the scaled risk of candidate k is J_k= rac{\E
orm{\hat{ mu}_k- mu}^2}{\sigma^2}=p_k+\gamma_k,\qquad \gamma_k= rac{
orm{(\I-\M_k) mu}^2}{\sigma^2}, {#eq-sel-scaled-risk} variance plus squared bias. The bias term \gamma_k is the noncentrality @eq-dep-gamma of the test of candidate k against any correct larger model. Mallows’ Cp [Mallows’ C_p] The C_p statistic of candidate k is C_k= rac{	ext{SSE}_k}{s^2}-n+2p_k . With \sigma^2 in place of s^2, \sigma^2(C_k+n)/n is the covariance-penalty estimate @eq-sel-covariance-penalty of the in-sample prediction error of candidate k. The scaling makes C_k comparable with p_k. [Properties of C_p] 1. Under @eq-sel-model, C_k^{\sigma}=	ext{SSE}_k/\sigma^2-n+2p_k is unbiased for J_k. 2. Assume normal errors,  mu\in\C(\X_F), \C(\X_k)\subseteq\C(\X_F) and n-P>2. Then \E(C_k)=J_k+ rac{2(P-p_k+\gamma_k)}{n-P-2}. 3. Let F_k=[(	ext{SSE}_k-	ext{SSE}_F)/(P-p_k)]/s^2 be the F statistic for testing candidate k against the full model (p_k<P). Then C_k=(P-p_k)(F_k-1)+p_k . In particular C_F=P, and C_k\le p_k iff F_k\le1. (a) By @thm-sel-optimism(c), \E(	ext{SSE}_k)=\sigma^2(n-p_k)+
orm{(\I-\M_k) mu}^2=\sigma^2(n-p_k+\gamma_k). (b) Write 	ext{SSE}_k=	ext{SSE}_F+(	ext{SSE}_k-	ext{SSE}_F). By @thm-glh-f-test(a), applied to \C(\X_k)\subseteq\C(\X_F), the two terms are independent, 	ext{SSE}_F/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-P), and (	ext{SSE}_k-	ext{SSE}_F)/\sigma^2 is noncentral \chi^2 with P-p_k degrees of freedom and noncentrality 
orm{(\M_F-\M_k) mu}^2/\sigma^2=\gamma_k, so its mean is P-p_k+\gamma_k. By @lem-cor-inverse-chisq, \E(\sigma^2/s^2)=(n-P)/(n-P-2). Hence  egin{aligned} \E\Bigl( rac{	ext{SSE}_k}{s^2}\Bigr)&=(n-P)+(P-p_k+\gamma_k)\, rac{n-P}{n-P-2}\ &=n-p_k+\gamma_k+ rac{2(P-p_k+\gamma_k)}{n-P-2}, \end{aligned} and subtracting n-2p_k gives the result. (c) By the definition of F_k, 	ext{SSE}_k/s^2=(n-P)+(P-p_k)F_k. Subtract n-2p_k. By (b), estimating \sigma^2 costs little unless the full model uses up most of the data. Mallows (1973) proposed plotting C_k against p_k: points near the line C_p=p have small bias, and the lowest point estimates the best predictor. By (c), adding q columns changes C_p by 2q-(	ext{SSE}_{	ext{small}}-	ext{SSE}_{	ext{big}})/s^2, so C_p prefers the larger model iff the F statistic of the added columns, with the full-model s^2, exceeds 2. AIC If g is the true density and f a model density, the Kullback–Leibler divergence \int g\log(g/f)\ge0 is zero iff f=g (Kullback and Leibler 1951), and up to a term free of f it is \E_g[-\log f(\Y^*)] for a new data set \Y^*\sim g. A fitted model f(\cdot\,;\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}) is therefore judged by the discrepancy \Delta=\E_{\Y^*} igl[-2\log f(\Y^*;\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}(\Y)) igr], with \Y^* independent of \Y. The maximized log-likelihood evaluates the same function at the data themselves, and is optimistic in the same way as the training error. [AIC and BIC] For a model with d_k free parameters and maximized log-likelihood \ell_k, 	ext{AIC}_k=-2\ell_k+2d_k,\qquad 	ext{BIC}_k=-2\ell_k+d_k\log n . In the normal linear model with unknown variance, d_k=p_k+1 and -2\ell_k=n\log(2\pi\,	ext{SSE}_k/n)+n (@thm-opt-mle), so up to a constant common to all candidates, 	ext{AIC}_k=n\log rac{	ext{SSE}_k}n+2(p_k+1),\qquad 	ext{BIC}_k=n\log rac{	ext{SSE}_k}n+(p_k+1)\log n . {#eq-sel-aic-normal} Akaike (1973, 1974) showed that 2d is the leading term of the optimism of -2\ell for a correct model fitted by maximum likelihood, in large samples. In the normal linear model the optimism can be computed exactly, without asymptotics. [The expected discrepancy of a normal linear model] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I) with  mu\in\C(\X_k) and n>p_k+2, and let \hat{\sigma}^2_k=	ext{SSE}_k/n. For the fitted density \Normal_n(\hat{ mu}_k,\hat{\sigma}^2_k\I), \E(\Delta_k)=\E igl[n\log(2\pi\hat{\sigma}^2_k) igr]+ rac{n(n+p_k)}{n-p_k-2} . Consequently 	ext{AICc}_k=-2\ell_k+2(p_k+1)+ rac{2(p_k+1)(p_k+2)}{n-p_k-2} {#eq-sel-aicc} is an unbiased estimate of \E(\Delta_k). For a new data set \Y^*= mu+ e^*, -2\log f(\Y^*)=n\log(2\pi\hat{\sigma}^2_k)+
orm{\Y^*-\hat{ mu}_k}^2/\hat{\sigma}^2_k, and as in @eq-sel-err-in \E igl(
orm{\Y^*-\hat{ mu}_k}^2 igm|\Y igr)=n\sigma^2+
orm{\hat{ mu}_k- mu}^2. So \Delta_k=n\log(2\pi\hat{\sigma}^2_k)+ rac{n\sigma^2+
orm{\M_k e}^2}{\hat{\sigma}^2_k}, using \hat{ mu}_k- mu=\M_k e when  mu\in\C(\X_k). Now 
orm{\M_k e}^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(p_k) and n\hat{\sigma}_k^2/\sigma^2=
orm{(\I-\M_k) e}^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-p_k) are independent (@thm-opt-sampling), and \E(\sigma^2/\hat{\sigma}^2_k)=n/(n-p_k-2) by @lem-cor-inverse-chisq. Hence the second term has mean n(n+p_k)/(n-p_k-2). For the second statement, -2\ell_k=n\log(2\pi\hat{\sigma}^2_k)+n, and the identity n(n+p)=(n-p-2) igl(n+2(p+1) igr)+2(p+1)(p+2) shows that n(n+p)/(n-p-2)=n+2(p+1)+2(p+1)(p+2)/(n-p-2). The corrected criterion AICc is due to Sugiura (1978) and Hurvich and Tsai (1989). Its extra term vanishes as n	o\infty with p_k fixed, which recovers AIC. It matters when p_k is not small compared with n. With n=20 and p_k=5, AIC charges 2(p_k+1)=12, while the exact charge in the proof is 2(p_k+1)\,n/(n-p_k-2)=18.46. A simulation of 100000 data sets gives a mean discrepancy of 68.11, equal to the theorem’s value to two decimals. AIC underestimates it by 6.46, and the underestimate favours the larger models. import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(2902) n_c, p_c, reps_c = 20, 5, 100_000 Xc = np.column_stack([np.ones(n_c), rng.normal(size=(n_c, p_c - 1))]) mu_c = Xc @ np.linspace(1, 2, p_c) # the model is correct H = Xc @ np.linalg.solve(Xc.T @ Xc, Xc.T) Yc = mu_c + rng.normal(size=(reps_c, n_c)) fit_c = Yc @ H s2ml = np.mean((Yc - fit_c) ** 2, axis=1) # ML variance estimate # discrepancy: expected -2 log-likelihood of an independent copy Y*, at the fitted values disc = n_c * np.log(2 * np.pi * s2ml) + (n_c + np.sum((fit_c - mu_c) ** 2, axis=1)) / s2ml target = np.mean(n_c * np.log(2 * np.pi * s2ml)) + n_c * (n_c + p_c) / (n_c - p_c - 2) print(f"E(discrepancy) {disc.mean():.2f}, formula {target:.2f}") print(f"penalty in AIC {2 * (p_c + 1)}, in AICc {2 * (p_c + 1) * n_c / (n_c - p_c - 2):.2f}") For a wrong candidate the penalty is no longer free of  mu, and 2d_k is an approximation, justified when the candidate is close to the truth (Konishi and Kitagawa 2008 discuss corrections). In practice AIC and C_p rank candidates almost identically (@exr-sel-aic-cp). BIC Suppose the candidates carry prior probabilities \pi_k, and the parameters  oldsymbol{\uptheta}_k of model k a prior density \pi( oldsymbol{\uptheta}_k\mid k). The posterior probability of model k is proportional to \pi_k\,m_k(\y), where m_k(\y)=\int f_k(\y\mid oldsymbol{\uptheta}_k)\,\pi( oldsymbol{\uptheta}_k\mid k)\,d oldsymbol{\uptheta}_k is the marginal likelihood of the model. For the conjugate normal prior of @thm-opt-bayes-conjugate the integral has a closed form. BIC is an approximation that needs no particular prior. [Sketch: where \log n comes from] This is a heuristic derivation; Schwarz (1978) proved the result for exponential families, and Kass and Raftery (1995) give conditions and error terms. Let \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}} maximize \ell( oldsymbol{\uptheta})=\log f_k(\y\mid oldsymbol{\uptheta}), and let \mathbf{J}_n=-
abla^2\ell(\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}) be the observed information, which for independent observations grows like n: \mathbf{J}_n=n	ilde{\mathbf{J}} with 	ilde{\mathbf{J}} of order one. Expanding \ell to second order about \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}} (Laplace’s method, Tierney and Kadane 1986),  egin{aligned} m_k(\y)&\approx f_k(\y\mid\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}})\,\pi(\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\mid k)\int e^{-( oldsymbol{\uptheta}-\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}})\T\mathbf{J}_n( oldsymbol{\uptheta}-\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}})/2}\,d oldsymbol{\uptheta}\ &=f_k(\y\mid\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}})\,\pi(\hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}\mid k)\,(2\pi)^{d_k/2}\det(\mathbf{J}_n)^{-1/2}. \end{aligned} Since \log\det\mathbf{J}_n=d_k\log n+\log\det	ilde{\mathbf{J}}, -2\log m_k(\y)=-2\ell_k+d_k\log n+O(1), where the O(1) collects the prior density at \hat{ oldsymbol{\uptheta}}, \det	ilde{\mathbf{J}} and 2\pi, none of which grows with n. So 	ext{BIC}_k approximates -2\log m_k, and with equal prior probabilities the model with the smallest BIC is approximately the most probable. The error is of order one, so \exp(-	ext{BIC}_k/2) is a crude estimate of a posterior probability, but the rate is right: each parameter costs \log n. For a “unit information” prior the error is of order n^{-1/2} (Kass and Wasserman 1995). Three criteria, one data set, one threshold Adjusted R^2 of Chapter 9 is sometimes used as a criterion too. [Adjusted R^2 as a criterion] Maximizing  ar{R}^2 over candidates that contain the intercept is minimizing s_k^2=	ext{SSE}_k/(n-p_k), and for two nested candidates the larger has the larger  ar{R}^2 iff its added columns have F>1. These are @prp-ss-adjusted-r2(d) and (c). The threshold 1 is lower than any of the others, so  ar{R}^2 chooses the largest models. Since \E(s_k^2)=\sigma^2(1+\gamma_k/(n-p_k)) (@thm-dep-omitted(c)), minimizing s^2_k aims at the smallest bias, not the smallest prediction error. For two nested candidates, each criterion is a test with its own critical value. Let the larger model add q columns, have residual degrees of freedom 
u, and let F=[(	ext{SSE}_{	ext{small}}-	ext{SSE}_{	ext{big}})/q]/(	ext{SSE}_{	ext{big}}/
u), so that 	ext{SSE}_{	ext{small}}/	ext{SSE}_{	ext{big}}=1+qF/
u.
